text:
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin says he feels for the family of a Haitian immigrant who died by apparent suicide earlier this week, but that his department isn't to blame.

Mullin was speaking during a visit to Warren County in Ohio to promote ICE cooperation with local law enforcement. He also said DHS won't stop using ankle monitors in its efforts to deport Haitians who no longer have Temporary Protected Status (TPS).

Pierre Damas Bel came from Haiti to Springfield in 2024. Shortly after TPS ended in late July, the 20-year-old received an ankle monitor from ICE. On Monday, his father says Bel called him to express emotional distress. Shortly after, the Ohio State Highway Patrol says Bel took his own life.

"It breaks my heart for the parents," Mullin said of Bel's death. "But we were following our procedures; we did our job. What happened when he went home... he wasn't in our custody. We're not responsible for that."

Bel was studying at Wright State University and, according to immigration advocates, was a member of the Marine's Junior Reserve Officer Training Corps.

ICE placed him and a number of other Haitians in Springfield on ankle monitors shortly after a July 27 federal court decision allowed the Trump administration to end TPS for Haitian immigrants. The protected immigration status was first granted to Haitians following a massive 2010 earthquake in the country that disrupted basic infrastructure and rule of law there.

The Trump administration argued the country is now safe to return to as its reason for ending Haitian TPS.

"TPS is just that — it's temporary," Mullin said Friday. "It was never designed to be permanent."

Critics point out, however, that Haiti is still high on the list of places the U.S. Secretary of State's office has declared unsafe to travel to.

Many Haitians living in Springfield and nearby were ordered to check in at ICE field offices and wear the monitors ahead of future immigration court dates. Those devices have caused many required to wear them to feel shame, according to immigration advocates.

"Someone will look at me like, 'This guy is a criminal,' " Springfield resident and Haitian immigrant Phillip Vil told WVXU after a recent check in.

Bel expressed similar feelings about the monitor in a social media post he made in late July.

"I came to this country to pursue my education," Bel wrote in an Instagram post. "I didn't come here to commit a crime or hurt anyone. Yet now I'm walking through the streets of the United States with a GPS monitor on my leg carrying a feeling of shame and humiliation I never imagined I would experience."

287(g) Contracts

Mullin was in Warren County to meet with regional ICE field office managers and Warren County Sheriff's Office officials for a roundtable discussion on 287(g) contracts. Those contracts allow local law enforcement agencies, like the Warren County Sheriff's Office, to conduct limited immigration enforcement actions.

Warren County's 287(g) agreement with ICE is under what is called the task force model, one of several ways local agencies can chose to work with federal immigration authorities.

Jail Division Captain Brian Payne told Mullin and other officials the county is currently holding 14 ICE detainees, all of whom were picked up on local misdemeanor or felony charges.

After the roundtable, Mullin answered questions on a number of other subjects, including an April incident in which off-duty police officers from Gratis, Ohio visited Cincinnati Public Schools looking for immigrant students. The visits caused the suspension of the department's 287(g) contract and led to the firing of the Gratis chief of police.

Mullin defended ICE contractors visiting schools looking for immigrant students, saying they weren't seeking arrests but merely doing welfare checks.

Asked about the tense situation in Springfield, which is home to as many as 15,000 Haitian immigrants, Mullin told reporters his agency intends to continue using GPS monitors and detaining and deporting Haitians who were relying on TPS.

"We've made 380 arrests in Springfield," he said. "We're going to continue to push."

Anyone considering suicide or in crisis can text or call 988 to reach the National Suicide and Crisis Lifeline.

text:
Updated Sept. 4, 2026, at 6:30 p.m.

Students at hundreds of schools across Colorado walked out of class around noon Friday to protest the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown and the agency leading it. Organizers say more than 200 schools, from Brush to Grand Junction, participated.

In Denver, hundreds of students from several area high schools gathered at La Alma-Lincoln Park for a mostly peaceful demonstration against the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

It was at times disrupted by a handful of anti-immigrant demonstrators seeking a reaction from the sidelines. At one point, students threw water bottles at one heckling demonstrator.

Social media brought student activists together

The event was organized by Colorado Youth Coalition, a student-led protest group co-founded earlier this year by Bre Kennedy, a 16-year-old junior at Grandview High School in Aurora, who said the event came together through social media.

“I posted something on Instagram about 20 schools that were participating,” Kennedy said. “The post got 200K views on Instagram and absolutely blew up. My Instagram DMs on the Youth Coalition were flooded, and I was able to get so many more schools plugged in and organized.”

Kennedy said the Youth Coalition campaign brought together student activists across the state who often feel isolated in their individual communities.

“I think this resonates with a lot of Colorado youth because there's a lot of ICE activity in our state, and it's absolutely disgusting to see,” Kennedy said. “Being a kid, people say, ‘Oh, you can't be into politics. You're too young. You can't vote. Your voice doesn't matter.’ I think kids are tired of hearing that. So getting everybody out here and plugged in is really cool to see.

Kiros calls students brave

Democratic congressional candidate Melat Kiros brought some star power to the event when she stopped by to deliver a short speech. She applauded the students, most of whom are still too young to vote, for their activism.

“These are very, very serious problems that we're facing right now,” Kiros said. “These students are brave. They're getting threatened with suspensions. They're getting harassed online right now. And they still chose to show up and fight for what they think is right. It's important for public officials to be standing alongside them.”

Students across the state walked out of classrooms between 10:30 am and noon Friday.

“I was in chemistry,” said Liliana Garcia-Martinez, a 15-year-old sophomore at Lincoln High School. She said she came to support friends and family who don’t have a voice and cursed at ICE. “And I walked out, and I left to the bus.”

Marvin McNeil, a 15-year-old junior, left during math class at Manuel High School and walked the 3 miles to La Alma-Lincoln Park with a handful of friends.

Setting examples

“I'm here today because youth need to have more examples of people who are willing to step up for what they believe in,” McNeil said. “A lot of people who are here today do not know how many people are on their side. I'm here to set an example for the people who believe that they want to do something, but just can't right now.”

Emunah Zalkin, 16, and a junior at Compassion Road Academy, an alternative high school near downtown Denver, said she joined the walkout along with roughly half of her classmates.

“I'm hoping to make a difference with everything that's going on in our world right now — with our president, with people getting deported, with the violence going on,” Zalkin said. “Even if I'm missing class, that's nothing compared to what a lot of these people are going through and what is continuing to go on in our country right now.”

Conflicts in Denver park

The demonstration turned tense at times, as a small number of counter-protesters agitated from the margins. One man, his face hidden by a mask, held a sign that said: “I Love ICE.” Another man carrying a microphone and apparently recording himself got a rise out of students by asking provocative questions.

“They were twisted questions like, ‘How do you feel about Arab immigrants coming and changing the culture here?’” Zalkin said. “And I'm like, ‘That's not why we're here today.’”

Some students yelled at and shoved the instigators, and hit them with water bottles, while teachers, adult organizers and Denver Public Schools security officers tried to hold them back and redirect their attention.

According to the Denver Police Department, no one was arrested, two were cited for graffiti and three people were sent to the hospital for unknown injuries. In a statement, DPD said there were at least five assaults or altercations during the protest.

"Officers contacted or identified several suspects in these altercations, and those investigations are ongoing," a DPD statement read.

The crowd dispersed by early evening with no further incidents.

Kirrabella Cruz, a 16-year-old junior, didn’t need to be told to give the agitators wide berth. She and her friends, who walked over from East High School, said they’d rather keep it safe. Cruz said her history class had recently learned about the 2017 Charlottesville demonstration where protesters were attacked by a motorist, and one died.

“I’m here because I am an immigrant descendant,” she said. “My great-grandparents are immigrants. I'm pretty sure they'd be disappointed to know that people are getting deported when they only wanted to live the American Dream.”

Editor's note: This story was updated to include a statement from the Denver Police Department.

text:
Part of the Series

Voting Wrongs

After dozens of violent raids and untimely deaths in squalid jails, as well as several high-profile killings at the hands of President Donald Trump’s immigration police, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters on Tuesday that he “can’t guarantee” Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents won’t be present at the polls when voters arrive to cast ballots in upcoming elections.

Trump ally Steve Bannon is calling for an “up-armored ICE presence” to “surround the polls come November,” and Democrats are increasingly worried about voter suppression as Republicans in Congress face a potential midterm rebuke from voters. With Trump once again raising false alarms about immigrants engaging in voter fraud, and a broader crackdown on free speech and dissent underway, the prospect of poorly trained ICE recruits intimidating people at polling sites in majority Black and Brown neighborhoods is a top concern.

While Mullin said ICE would respond to “specific threats” rather than “patrol the polling place,” he indicated that a report of an undocumented person could be reason enough to deploy agents at or near a polling site. Shortly after taking office, Trump officials ditched rules that prohibited immigration arrests at public locations such as schools that often host elections. In cruel displays that go viral online, masked ICE agents have arrested parents dropping kids off at school and at school bus stops.

“If we’re serving a warrant, we will be where we need to be,” Mullin said.

Midterm voters could play a major role in reining in ICE’s neighborhood invasions and deadly violence if they reject pro-ICE incumbents in the midterms and make Trump a true lame duck — but in order to do so they would need to overcome racist gerrymandering and efforts by the administration and right-wing forces to suppress turnout. Organizers have been preparing for this moment since at least June 2025, when Trump sent federal troops to occupy Los Angeles, California, as ICE conducted raids and mass protests erupted, according to Mary Corcoran, executive director of the Save America Movement.

“Just having the possibility of them showing up in the air could create a chilling effect on people’s willingness to come to the polls; we’ve seen situations where ICE shoots first and asks your immigration status later,” Corcoran told Truthout in an interview. “I think it’s not hard to understand why people who are not going to their jobs right now may not go to vote.”

Since the occupation of Los Angeles, ICE and, in several cases, federal troops have invaded Chicago, Minneapolis-St. Paul, New Orleans, Memphis, Charlotte, and other cities with large populations of immigrants and people of color. The resulting violence and mass incarceration of immigrant families and children with no criminal record in squalid detention camps has inspired serious political backlash, and many of the most impacted areas have seen mass protests and an explosion of mutual aid.

“But what we saw in all of those incidents is people coming together to speak up and take action and say, this has gone too far,” said Cristina Jiménez, co-founder of United We Dream and Connected Americans, a project connecting people impacted by ICE, in an interview with Truthout. “The same spirit and the same energy will be there for the election.”

As abuses have mounted and as Trump’s approval ratings have tumbled, organizers have decided that the possibility of armed federal agents showing up at voting precincts in largely Black and Latino communities is real, Corcoran said.

“As the numbers began to point to even more of a ‘blue wave,’ our perspective was that possibility would increase,” Corcoran said. “Having ICE show up for whatever false reason they are showing up for at the precinct is another way to intimidate voters.”

On September 2, the Save America Movement and a non-partisan coalition announced Vote Safe, a voter protection program and one of several activist efforts to counter racist voter suppression. Led by civil rights activist Rev. Al Sharpton and American Federation of Teachers President Randi Weingarten, Vote Safe is organizing hundreds of trained volunteers — veterans, clergy, firefighters, and other trusted local figures — to be at polls in key districts that are most likely to be targeted by ICE based on Trump’s previous efforts to subvert elections.

“What we asked ourselves is, what would Stephen Miller do?” Corcoran said. “Where would he send these folks if he was trying to impact an election outcome? And that is how we designed the program.”

While Vote Safe is non-partisan and supports voters of all backgrounds, the trained poll watchers will focus on swing districts with large numbers of Black, Latino, and Asian voters in Ohio, Georgia, North Carolina, and Michigan.

Weingarten said the right-wing majority on the Supreme Court gutted the Voting Rights Act “right on schedule” for the midterms, and now Republicans are leaning on fear to “finish the job.” By communicating with Black, Asian, and Latino voters before early voting begins and through Election Day with assurances that trusted neighbors and local leaders will have their backs at the polls, Vote Safe is designed to help potential voters overcome any fear or hesitancy about casting a ballot.

“The threat of armed federal agents descending on polling places is an attempt to intimidate us and control who gets to hold power in this country. It won’t work,” Weingarten said in a statement on Tuesday. “Vote Safe exists so that people know the community has their backs at the ballot box, with someone standing beside them who knows their rights and knows the law, so that fear doesn’t get the last word.”

Such a strategy has already been tested in Washington, D.C., where the DC Election Protection Coalition trained both volunteer poll watchers and voting rights attorneys to support voters during elections that were held in June. The city has been under a National Guard occupation ordered by Trump for more than a year, and Trump’s gaudy July 4 celebrations brought additional National Guard troops alongside federal and local police to public spaces across the city.

Carmen Daugherty, interim executive director of the Advancement Project, a civil rights group in the DC Election Protection Coalition, said volunteers monitored polling sites, watching for closures and observing areas where National Guard troops were already on patrol near polling locations. On Election Day, volunteers monitored the polling location, ready to call attorneys if troops were spotted near voters — or if troops attempted to enter a polling place in violation of local law. Poll watchers also took notes.

“It’s important to have those first-hand accounts to show the narrative, in order to say, look at what is happening in this authoritarian moment of voter suppression,” Daugherty said. “There are more of us who care about fair and free accessible elections than those who want to suppress our vote, so we have to show up in numbers.”

text:
2026 is on track to be a record-breaking year for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Utah. The agency made 3,467 arrests from January through July, up from 2,116 over the same period the previous year. That’s on top of a threefold increase in arrests in 2025 when President Donald Trump returned to office.

Here’s where the agency has been most active in Utah during the federal government’s current fiscal year, which began Oct. 1, 2025. The data runs through Aug. 5, 2026.

Utah cities with the most ICE arrests since Oct. 1

Federal government data obtained by the Deportation Data Project includes a field for the city where each arrest took place. In Utah, West Valley City has the most arrests this fiscal year, with 793. Then come Spanish Fork, South Salt Lake, Ogden and Salt Lake City.

All of these cities have a jail or prison, except for West Valley. Many ICE arrests — 58% in Utah this fiscal year — are transfers of people who were already in custody. Since there’s no jail in town, it’s unclear where custodial arrests occurred in West Valley City.

ICE did not answer KUER’s question about it but did provide a statement.

“DHS nor ICE have verified the accuracy, methodology or the analysis of the project and its results. ICE does not provide comment about unverified sources nor comment on its alleged findings. The bottom line is that the Deportation Data Project is not accurate.”

The Deportation Data Project gets its data directly from the federal government through Freedom of Information Act requests.

Seeing West Valley City at the top of the list was no surprise to Democratic state Rep. Angela Romero, who represents parts of Salt Lake City and West Valley City. She said half of her district is Latino, and the impacts of immigration enforcement are inescapable.

“I worry about just children being able to play outside because their parents are worried about them getting picked up,” she said.

To see where ICE has been most active, KUER looked at noncustodial, or at-large, arrests. Those happen out in the community, not transfers from other law enforcement agencies.

West Valley City also has the most noncustodial ICE arrests of any Utah city, followed by Salt Lake City, St. George, Ogden and Orem.

Comunidades Unidas, an immigrant advocacy nonprofit in West Valley City, has shifted to accommodate people who don’t want to come to the office. Brianna Puga, the lead community organizer, said people weren’t showing up for regular food pickups, one of the services they offer, so they deliver now. The nonprofit’s offices are just down the street from the region’s ICE field office on Decker Lake Drive, which serves four states.

And people are getting around differently. When residents do leave home, Puga said they’re taking public transit more to avoid being pulled over for a traffic violation. She meets them in their neighborhoods and at libraries, parks and malls.

The fear isn’t new, she said. Things have been different since President Donald Trump won reelection.

“Whenever I go to Rancho Market now, it feels quiet, it feels stiff, it feels dead,” she said. “It feels like there isn't any of that cheerfulness, any of that energy anymore because we're constantly now, like, watching our backs.”

More than a quarter of those arrested have no criminal background

Since Oct. 1, 27% of ICE arrests in Utah have been of people with no criminal charges or convictions. Looking only at at-large arrests in the community, that figure is much higher: 54%. For local law enforcement working with ICE in the 287(g) program, half of arrests have been of people with no criminal background.

Being in the U.S. illegally is a civil violation, not a criminal offense.

“I feel lied to,” said Ogden activist Kim Haslam. “Because I feel like the leaders in our community keep telling us that they're just going after the worst of the worst and getting criminals off the street, and people in the community have been letting them know that is not true.”

Haslam volunteers with a group called Ogden United, which helps local immigrant families get groceries, transport kids to and from school and pay for things like flights to reunite with a deported family member.

She was recently in touch with the wife of a man whose ICE arrest angered local activists. In body camera footage of the incident, an Ogden police officer makes a call, apparently to a supervisor, and explains what happened: an ICE agent in an unmarked car asked him to pull a driver over, and the officer said no. The driver of the suspected car then flagged down the Ogden officer and said he was being followed. The officer talked with the ICE agent and told him, “I'll just walk up and talk to him. If he’s stopped, if you want to just pull up behind him and make contact with him.” The ICE agent then arrested the man.

“We've been told that people can trust OPD,” Haslam said, “but I think that video has caused a breakdown of trust.”

Rep. Romero worries people who need help won’t call the police because they’re afraid.

Haslam and other activists want clear guidelines from Ogden police on how officers interact with ICE. Mayor Ben Nadolski said during a recent city council meeting that a policy was already in the works.

Park City stands out for non-custodial arrests per capita

For community arrests per 1,000 residents, Park City tops the list. Arrests there spiked in April, in line with local news reports. That’s based on KUER’s analysis of cities with five or more noncustodial arrests.

Maggie AbuHaidar, executive director of the Wasatch Immigration Project, is skeptical that all 28 noncustodial arrests tagged with Park City actually happened within city limits — as opposed to nearby neighborhoods like Kimball Junction, which would affect the per capita figure.

“Based on my experience and having my ear on the ground, these numbers feel off to me,” she said.

Still, she said more than 70% of clients are changing their daily habits due to fears of ICE, according to a survey the Wasatch Immigration Project conducted in the spring. And two high-profile ICE operations occurred during the data’s timeframe, with about 10 people detained at each, she said.

West Valley City is second for arrests per capita, followed by Washington and St. George. Arrests in southwest Utah shot up this spring, when ICE began flying detainees through the St. George airport.

While she gets emotional speaking about ICE in her community, Romero is grateful for local activists. She doesn’t think ICE would have called off its plan to build a detention center in Salt Lake City without the protests.

“I see these people who are not from the Latino community organizing these watches, putting pressure on us as elected officials to do something, and it amazes me of the power of community,” she said.

But state lawmakers are limited in what they can do. She wants residents to keep pressuring their federal representatives to reform the immigration system and “hold the president accountable,” she said.

Macy Lipkin is a Report for America corps member who reports for KUER in northern Utah.

text:
After Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer Christian Castro shot Julio C. Sosa-Celis in Minneapolis on January 14, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) portrayed that use of potentially lethal force as fully justified. "Fearing for his life and safety as he was being ambushed by three individuals," it said in a press release the next day, Castro "fired a defensive shot to defend his life," striking Sosa-Celis in the leg.

As the DHS told it, Castro "attempted to apprehend" Sosa-Celis, "a criminal illegal alien from Venezuela," who "began to resist and violently assault the officer." Castro was on the ground, wrestling with Sosa-Celis, when two other men "came out of a nearby apartment and attacked the law enforcement officer with a snow shovel and broom handle." Then Sosa-Celis "got loose and began striking the officer with a shovel or broom stick." Kristi Noem, then the DHS secretary, described "an attempted murder of federal law enforcement" in which Castro "was ambushed and attacked by three individuals who beat him with snow shovels and the handles of brooms."

According to an indictment that a federal grand jury approved on Wednesday, none of that was true: Castro made the whole thing up. Compounding Castro's dishonesty, the DHS uncritically accepted his version of events, and Noem went further, embellishing his story by multiplying the number of imaginary weapons that his supposed assailants allegedly used to attack him.

That is par for the course at the DHS, which has a history of reflexively defending its employees, rushing to judgment before all the relevant facts are known. This is by no means the only case in which the government's initial account of a DHS shooting has unraveled in the face of contrary evidence. But it is unusual in one respect: The government ultimately admitted that its account was based entirely on a DHS employee's self-serving lies.

What actually happened that day? According to the DHS press release, "federal law enforcement officers were conducting a targeted traffic stop in Minneapolis for Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis," who "fled the scene in his vehicle, crashed into a parked car, and proceeded to flee on foot." But the very next day, FBI agent Timothy Schanz told a different story in an affidavit supporting federal charges against Sosa-Celis and Alfredo A. Aljorna, who shared a duplex apartment with Sosa-Celis and supposedly joined him in assaulting Castro.

According to Schanz, Castro and another ICE officer spotted "a silver/grey Ford Focus" with a license plate registered to Joffre Barrera. Records indicated that Barrera "was illegally in the United States." The officers assumed the man driving the car, Aljorna, was Barrera, even though Aljorna was 50 pounds heavier, five inches taller, and about a decade older. In any event, it was Aljorna, not Sosa-Celis, who "fled the scene" when ICE tried to pull him over and "hit a light pole" (as opposed to "a parked car") on North 24th Avenue after a car chase that lasted "15 to 20 minutes." Then Aljorna ran toward his home.

As Castro chased Aljorna, Schanz said, he "saw a separate Hispanic male," later identified as Sosa-Celis, "standing on the porch" of the duplex. After Aljorna "slipped and fell," Castro caught up with him and "began tussling with him on the ground." Then Sosa-Celis grabbed "a red-handled broom" and "began hitting" Castro with it "in the face," saying "something to the effect of, 'Let him go.'" Castro saw "a third Hispanic male approach with a snow shovel." That man "began striking" Castro with the shovel. When Aljorna "wiggled out of his shirt or sweater and freed himself" from Castro's grip, the ICE officer called out for help from his partner but realized he was not there.

Castro, who estimated that he "had been fighting/tussling" with Aljorna for three minutes, "was exhausted, alone, on the ground, and in fear of his safety," Schanz said. Sosa-Celis "passed the broom" to Aljorna, who "attempted to hit" Castro "in the face or head." Castro, who "was struck repeatedly by the broom," "used his left hand to block a strike," which "caused a cut or gash to the palm of his left hand." While "blocking strikes with his left hand," Castro "struggled to draw his service pistol with his right hand and pointed it in the direction of his assailants."

When the men saw Castro "draw his pistol," Schanz said, they "dropped the broom and the snow shovel" and "began to run" toward the duplex where they lived. Castro "simultaneously fired one round from his service pistol towards the vicinity of the assailants," who "ran inside" the building and "closed the front door."

If three men participated in the alleged attack on Castro, why were only two charged? Schanz did not say. But as he could have discovered if he had bothered to investigate Castro's claims, the ICE officer's account was inconsistent with video and physical evidence. Surveillance camera footage of the incident did not show any assault with a broom or a snow shovel. Nor did it document a prolonged violent struggle like the one that Castro described.

The struggle with Aljorno lasted about 12 seconds, and Castro "was not hit by a shovel or a broom," Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty would later note. "In fact, he was not hit at all." After Aljorna and Sosa-Celis escaped into their home, she added, they "presented absolutely no threat to him or anyone else." And contrary to what Castro claimed, that was when he fired his gun, as a bullet hole through the front door showed.

After charging Aljorna and Sosa-Celis with assault and various other felonies, federal prosecutors belatedly noticed the problems with Castro's story. "Newly discovered evidence in this matter is materially inconsistent with the allegations" against Aljorna and Sosa-Celis, Daniel N. Rosen, the U.S. attorney for Minnesota, told U.S. District Judge Paul A. Magnuson on February 12, nearly a month after the shooting. The next day, Magnuson granted Rosen's request to dismiss the charges with prejudice, meaning they could not be filed again.

"Video evidence has revealed" that Castro "appears to have made untruthful statements," Acting ICE Director Todd Lyons said the day the charges were dismissed. "Lying under oath is a serious federal offense. The U.S. Attorney's Office is actively investigating these false statements."

That investigation culminated in this week's indictment, which remains sealed but reportedly charges Castro with six counts of making false statements to FBI agents, a federal felony punishable by up to five years in prison. That charge implies that Castro was not justified in shooting Sosa-Celis, meaning he may also be guilty of "willfully" violating Sosa-Celis' Fourth Amendment rights under color of law, a federal felony punishable by up to 10 years in prison when it causes "bodily injury."

Federal prosecutors in Minnesota "pressed for more serious civil rights charges but said that their Washington counterparts had so far been unwilling, limiting the indictment to accusations of lying," The New York Times reports, citing "two people with knowledge of the case." According to "a Justice Department official," the Times says, "federal prosecutors are still investigating the shooting and have not ruled out adding civil rights charges."

On Tuesday, ProPublica reports, the prosecutor assigned to Castro's case, Assistant U.S. Attorney Matthew Evans, said in an email that he "objected in the strongest possible terms" to a decision by Rosen and "Main Justice" against charging Castro with violating Sosa-Celis' constitutional rights. CBS News reports that Evans was fired after that dispute.

In May, Moriarty announced state charges against Castro. The ICE officer "was not under any physical threat when he fired his weapon, or even beforehand," Moriarty said, explaining her decision to charge Castro with four counts of second-degree assault and one count of falsely reporting a crime.

That case has stalled. After the shooting, ICE transferred Castro to Texas, where Gov. Greg Abbott resisted Minnesota's extradition request, saying he needed more time to consider it. Although Castro was arrested based on that request, he was released last week after three months of detention, the maximum allowed by state law in extradition cases.

It remains unclear whether Castro will be held accountable for his unjustified use of force as well as his mendacity. But either way, the case highlights the perils of believing anything the DHS says after its employees fire their weapons.

A week before Castro shot Sosa-Celis, ICE officer Jonathan Ross fatally shot Minneapolis protester Renee Good. A couple of weeks after that, DHS employees fatally shot Alex Pretti, another Minneapolis protester. In both cases, the story that the DHS told, which cast Good and Pretti as would-be murderers, was inconsistent with video of the incidents.

Although the outcome was less serious in this case, the DHS followed the same playbook, depicting Aljorna and Sosa-Celis as bent on homicide—a claim that likewise was contradicted by video evidence. Beyond the issue of whether the shooting was justified, the DHS was egregiously sloppy in reporting the basic facts of what had happened, confusing Sosa-Celis with Aljorna, who in turn was misidentified as the initial ICE target.

The DHS not only credulously accepted Castro's fictional claims. It added made-up details, pluralizing the single broom and single snow shovel he described. It also implied that Aljorna and Sosa-Celis had previously shown violent tendencies. These were "criminal illegal aliens," it said. Yet Aljorna's "crime" was illegally entering the United States, while Sosa-Celis' criminal record was limited to a conviction for driving without a license and an arrest for "giving a false name to a peace officer."

In a sense, the federal case against Castro sets the record straight. But far from apologizing for misleading the press and the public, the DHS has not even bothered to retract or correct its statement about the shooting, which remains on the department's website with all the original errors and misrepresentations.

text:
INDIANAPOLIS — The Archdiocese of Indianapolis is weighing in after days of immigration enforcement activity across the city.

The Archdiocese is offering a dispensation, or exemption, from attending Mass.

“The vibe I’m getting is things are pretty tough here in the city, and I think we don’t want to make people feel like they have to go out at this time,” said Father Todd Goodson, the lead pastor at Our Lady of Greenwood Catholic Church.

FOX59/CBS4 spoke with Fr. Goodson after he presided over a wedding at St. Mary’s Catholic Church in downtown Indianapolis.

St. Mary’s has served the city’s immigrant community for nearly 170 years. However, the pews may be a little less full this Sunday.

The exemption is for parishioners who may feel unsafe due to ICE activity.

Our Lady of Greenwood also offers Spanish-language Mass.

“A lot of the immigrant community is catholic and devotedly so. And we just want them to feel like at this time if you’re nervous you can stay home,” said Fr. Goodson.

Earlier this week, ICE ramped up enforcement across the city. The action forced many businesses on the east side to close. The business owners cited the safety and well-being of their employees. And the catholic church is saying the same.

“It’s not something we take lightly, for sure,” said Father James Brockmeier, the rector at Saints Peter and Paul Cathedral in Indy.

Fr. Brockmeier said granting exemptions in the Catholic faith is rare, but the requests came from individual pastors.

“We say that Mass is the source and summit of our lives as Catholics. And Catholics take that very seriously,” said Fr. Brockmeier.

The business community is also calling out the ICE activity.

Calvin Fletcher’s Coffee Company in Fletcher Place posted to social media Friday that the activity is a financial drain and disrupts local economies. They also said it’s not good for our safety.

Back at St Mary’s, the exemption lasts until the end of the month.

“I think people are nervous, and I think that’s why we issued the statement. We feel they should not be obliged to go outside if they don’t feel safe to leave their homes at this time,” said Fr. Goodson.

text:
DENVER — Hundreds of students across Colorado walked out of class Friday to make a point against U.S. Immigration Enforcement and President Trump's immigration crackdown.

"A lot of these students, they themselves or, have known of somebody that has been affected by ICE, and a lot of these students are done with it," said Christy Aguilar, event organizer and Co-Captain of The Brown Berets of the Tepetlán. The group worked alongside The Youth Coalition to host the demonstration.

Denver7 reporter Danielle Kreutter was at those protest and has reaction in the video below:

Hundreds of students across Colorado walk out of class to protest ICE

There were speakers, moments of community and marches at an event at La Alma-Lincoln Park in Denver. Students from across the metro area showed up.

"This is something that's really important to me. I asked my dad, I'm like, 'Hey, would you be able to take me down here?' He was like, 'Yeah, absolutely,'" said Yuri Novac, who came from Boulder.

His father, Andrei, immigrated to the U.S. when he was a toddler.

"You have people getting pulled off the street. That's not something that should happen in this country," said Andrei.

Even though the majority of the students aren't old enough to vote, they still want their voice heard. Students say they realize some people may criticize their efforts to protest during the school day.

"If you look back in history, like the march from Selma to Montgomery, the March on Washington, the Montgomery bus boycotts. All those people — they didn't know if what they were doing was going to help at all," said Yuri. "Just because we don't think anything will happen from this, you might as well try, because something might."

The day was not without several tense moments between the students and adult counter-protesters at the event.

One counter-protester who was recording a group of demonstrators was eventually kicked and pushed while on the ground after what appeared to be a camera was knocked out of his hand.

Later, another man holding a pro-ICE sign walked into the event as demonstrators yelled at him to leave. When he returned later, a crowd of students followed him. Student demonstrators were seen throwing a metal water bottle at his head. He ran away after being hit in the head.

Throughout the day, organizers urged the students to remain peaceful and ignore the men.

Denver police told Denver7 there were five assaults/altercations at the event.

According to police, three people were transported to the hospital for injuries. They could not comment on the extent of those injuries.

Another person was treated on scene with unknown extent of injuries. Officers say a fifth person was hurt who left the area before officers could talk to them. They are asking that person to contact DPD at 720-913-2000 to initiate a report.

DPD officers say they have contacted or identified several suspects in the assaults/altercations and those investigations are ongoing. Two other people were ticketed for graffiti.

"It is important to note that this was an unpermitted demonstration organized without a safety plan, which contributed to an unsafe environment for participants," a spokesperson for Denver Police said via a statement.

Organizers told Denver7 they hope the actions of some don't take away from the many who came out to peacefully protest a cause that means so much to them.

"A lot of these students are really willing to fight for their justice and really willing to fight for everything that's right in this country," said Aguliar.

text:
The death toll from a U.S. missile strike on a wedding party in Iran has risen to five. Among the dead is a 6-year-old boy. A funeral for the victims was held on Thursday. Nearly 70 others were wounded in the U.S. bombing that struck a home in the Iranian city of Kuhestak on Tuesday, one of dozens of U.S. attacks on Iran earlier this week. Reuters reports it was likely a direct hit by a U.S. munition, and not a ricochet off another target. Other news outlets, including The New York Times and the BBC, came to similar conclusions.

On Thursday, Vice President JD Vance said the U.S. will investigate the missile strike but that he doubts the U.S. was behind the attack.

Vice President JD Vance: “I will say that the Iranian state media has not been a very good scribe about what’s happened in the conflict thus far, so I’m extremely skeptical of this.”

Vance’s pledge to investigate the bombing of the wedding party comes six months after U.S. cruise missiles struck an elementary school in Minab. That attack killed over 150 people, most of them students. The Pentagon has yet to publicly release a report on the strikes. Meanwhile, Vance was asked by CNN’s Kaitlin Collins whether the war would continue into November.

Kaitlan Collins: “Will this war be over by the time of the midterm elections?”

Vice President JD Vance: “Well, Kaitlan, again, I don’t — I wouldn’t call it a war. Right now there is no active shooting. I recognize there is — there have been places where this has flared up. Major combat operations — again, major combat operations lasted for about six weeks.”

Israel’s far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir has outlined a plan to remove all Palestinians from the Gaza Strip. He called for the next government to form a ministry in charge of emigration to carry out his plan of mass expulsion.

Itamar Ben-Gvir: “Two hundred fifty thousand in the first year, is it possible? It is possible. One-point-one million within three years, and within seven years, we can reach almost 1.9 million, which will accumulate. It is possible. It is realistic. It is in our hands. It is within our capabilities.”

This comes as Israel continues to carry out deadly attacks in Gaza, killing at least three Palestinians on Thursday despite the U.S.-brokered so-called ceasefire. Meanwhile, Amnesty International has accused Israel of brazenly confiscating land in the occupied West Bank as part of what the group calls Israel’s “annexation agenda.”

Federal authorities have once again deported asylum seekers from the U.S. to Haiti, despite an epidemic of gang violence that’s displaced nearly 1.5 million people. It was the third consecutive Thursday that a deportation flight landed in the northern city of Cap-Haïtien. Haiti’s main international airport in Port-au-Prince is considered too dangerous. In June, the Supreme Court ruled 6 to 3 to allow the Trump administration to cancel temporary protected status for more than a third of a million Haitians living in the U.S. UNICEF warns one in 13 children in Haiti are suffering from acute malnutrition.

An Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer who shot a Venezuelan immigrant in Minnesota was taken into federal custody late Thursday on charges of making false statements to investigators. That’s according to CBS News, which reports a federal grand jury returned a six-count indictment against the agent, Christian Castro. He’s expected to appear in court today. This comes after Texas Republican Governor Greg Abbott refused to extradite Castro to Minnesota to face more serious charges of second-degree assault and falsely reporting a crime.

Meanwhile, ProPublica reports a U.S. prosecutor in Minnesota planned to file federal civil rights charges against Castro but was overruled by higher-ups at the Justice Department. Assistant U.S. Attorney Matthew Evans wrote in an email reviewed by ProPublica, “This is being directed by the Main Justice and the US Attorney. I objected in the strongest possible terms and fought it as hard as I could. It wasn’t enough.”

In Nepal, rescue workers pulled two survivors from a hydropower tunnel Friday morning, nine days after the partial collapse of a glacier triggered a massive flood and landslide. Rescue work is continuing, as authorities believe dozens of others remain trapped in similar tunnels. On Thursday, authorities said the disaster had killed at least 1,280 people on both sides of the China-Nepal border, with more than 5,600 still missing. The United Nations warns the Himalayas are warming twice as fast as the global average, accelerating the retreat of glaciers and increasing the risk of devastating landslides and floods.

The United Nations warns that nations will fail to limit global heating to 1.5° Celsius above preindustrial levels, falling short of a cornerstone of the Paris Climate Agreement. A new report by the U.N. Environment Programme finds that even under the most optimistic scenario, global temperatures are set to rise by at least 1.8 degrees, with catastrophic consequences. This is UNEP Director Inger Andersen.

Inger Andersen: “Above 1.5 degrees centigrade, we can expect an intensification of extreme weather, of glacier melt, of ecosystem loss and of sea level rise. And human health, and food and water security, cities and infrastructure will come under an increasing strain. So, put simply, there is no good outcome if we remain above the 1.5.”

The report concludes that the best remaining option is to exceed current climate goals on the road to net-zero greenhouse gas emissions.

text:
Arlington police have opened an investigation into an immigration arrest on Columbia Pike that reportedly left a man with serious injuries.

Detectives met with the man, José Mejía Hernandez, last week, NBC4 reported. This prompted a swift response from Sens. Tim Kaine and Mark Warner and Reps. Don Beyer, Suhas Subramanyam and James Walkinshaw today (Friday).

“We strongly support the Arlington County Police Department’s decision to open this investigation, which is essential to establishing how José Mejía Hernandez suffered serious injuries,” the Democratic members of Congress wrote. “These included internal bleeding and a brain injury after an encounter with ICE agents.”

ACPD confirmed to ARLnow that Mejía Hernandez filed a police report the same day he and his counsel addressed protesters outside the Arlington County Courthouse last Friday.

“The investigation into the circumstances of the incident is ongoing,” police spokesperson Ashley Savage told ARLnow.

Mejía Hernandez has alleged that he was injured after masked ICE officers approached him without warning while he was walking to the bus on the morning of Aug. 11. He says that he fled and they shot him from behind with a Taser in a parking lot in an apartment complex at Columbia Pike and S. Courthouse Road.

Mejía Hernandez, a Mexican immigrant, has said that he has a gap in his memory between getting hit with a stun gun and waking up in a hospital bed. He says that he lost consciousness, although bystander video of the incident shows him sitting upright and ultimately standing up, surrounded by ICE agents.

In the days after the incident, Mejía Hernandez was diagnosed with a traumatic brain injury resulting in brain swelling and a brain bleed, according to his attorneys.

“It is unfortunate that the Trump Administration has abandoned its responsibilities to hold federal agents under their command accountable, leaving state and local jurisdictions to do the job the Administration refuses to do to maintain law and order and protect the public,” members of Congress wrote in today’s letter.

“That failure is fueling a pattern of unchecked violence, rights violations, and chaos, in some cases with deadly consequences,” they continued. “If this investigation finds that ICE agents’ misconduct caused Mr. Mejía Hernandez’ injuries or impeded his medical treatment, they must face consequences.”

The Department of Homeland Security told HuffPost that Mejía Hernandez is undocumented and that he “attempted to flee from the scene, requiring ICE to use necessary force to gain control of the situation.”

Mejía Hernandez’s police report alleges aggravated malicious wounding, malicious wounding, failure of a driver in an accident to stop, reckless driving and assault and battery, Savage said.

In a letter to ACPD, Mejía Hernandez’s attorneys alleged that witnesses reported him being struck by an officer’s vehicle while he was on foot. However, available videos only show the aftermath of whatever happened.

Commonwealth’s Attorney Parisa Dehghani-Tafti has called for “a complete and impartial review of the facts” in the case.

“Allegations of significant harm must be examined carefully, transparently, and without regard to an individual’s position or authority,” Dehghani-Tafti said in a statement last week. “No one is above the law, and I will do my part to ensure that in my community.”
