text:
By ZACH LAIRD, InDepthNH.org

The WMUR Democratic primary debate between incumbent U.S. Rep. Maggie Goodlander (D-NH), and challenger State Rep. Paige Beauchemin, D-Nashua on Thursday night covered their positions on key issues such as immigration, housing, and the looming possibility of data centers.

The two are running for New Hampshire’s 2nd Congressional District. Before being elected to represent New Hampshire’s Second District in Congress in November 2024, Goodlander served as a senior advisor at the White House, though she began her career working as a foreign policy advisor to U.S. Senator John McCain in the United States Senate per her website.

Goodlander’s challenger, Beauchemin, has worked to help expand people’s access to healthcare (and) New Hampshire’s paid family and medical leave program. She also works on measures that promote transparency, civil liberties, and human rights per her campaign website.

Commentators began by asking what could be done to build homes that Granite Staters can actually afford.

Goodlander said Congress passed the most significant piece of housing legislation in a generation, citing the 21st Century Road to Housing Act. She said she was proud to work on several critical areas of the bill, which focused on cutting red tape to allow building more homes for working-class families. She also said the bill was helpful in cutting down abusive practices by big corporations that have jacked up housing costs for everybody.

Beauchemin responded that when she thinks about the housing crisis, she looks at it with a multi-pronged approach.

“First of all, we need to stop the problem in its tracks, which means we need to get private equity out of housing. Private equity is the core of everything that is wrong with housing right now, and it is the reason that there’s a shortage of housing, especially for first-time home buyers,” Beauchemin said.

She continued that another problem is corporations continuing to buy houses and land around the state. She added how often it’s not even affordable to build homes right now. Beauchemin said there has to be a plan, including things like subsidies as well as using existing infrastructure more creatively.

Should Congress do anything to help the average struggling renter? Commentator Steve Bottari noted the average monthly rent for a one-bedroom apartment in New Hampshire is up to $2,000.

Beauchemin said more regulations need to be put in place for renters’ protections, because “right now, people can be living in very unsafe, very unhealthy conditions, and they can’t do anything about it, because they know if they say something, they can be evicted.”

Goodlander emphasized that more homes need to be built which would “help us bring down the costs for renters and home-buyers,” and recalled how her time working in the Justice Department she focused on how “big corporate monopolies are using algorithms and something called surveillance pricing to fix the price of rent more effectively than ever before.”

She said she aims to crack down on “precisely this kind of abusive corporate practice that is jacking up rent for hardworking people all across this state.”

The next question was centered around whether the candidates would support the development of any artificial intelligence data center in CD 2.

Goodlander said some communities around the country are seeing more than 200% increases in their energy prices as a direct result of data centers coming into their towns or cities. She said she believes deeply that people and communities “have got to have the ultimate say in whether a data center comes into their community.”

She said there has to be transparency, accountability, and the corporations that are responsible for setting up the data centers pay the price rather than taxpayers.

Beauchemin explained she looks at A.I. and data centers from a nuanced perspective, noting that “the toothpaste is out of the tube. We know technology is happening,” but said she supports stopping the construction of any data centers until legislation can be introduced to regulate the issue accordingly.

“Those kinds of regulations need to ensure that environmental impact studies initially and ongoing, they need to ensure that utility costs are paid for by the companies and not from the other folks, and we also need to make sure that the local folks have their own local control,” Beauchemin said.

Bottari turned the conversation toward immigration and referenced the Laken Riley Act that mandates the detention of illegal immigrants who commit certain crimes. He said a majority of voters in 2024 favored a tougher stance on immigration, and asked why Democrats should go back to policies “that helped them lose the last election.”

Beauchemin argued that it was absolutely not the reason why Democrats lost the election and that there are a lot of other reasons for the defeat. She said the reality is Laken Riley Act is one of the worst pieces of legislation that has come out of the current administration.

“Unfortunately, my opponent is one of only 46 Democrats who voted against party lines for that act. That act had many warnings about it; the ACLU put out warnings about it. They did know that what’s happening right now was going to happen, those are the facts,” she said.

Goodlander responded that we are a nation of immigrants, and that we’re also a nation of laws. She said it’s her approach that if you are in this country unlawfully and commit a crime, then there should be immigration consequences. She said that principle led to her vote on the Laken Riley Act and that she stands by her vote.

She said what we’re seeing happen in America today with immigration has nothing to do with any law on the books, but that we’re seeing a President who is completely lawless, undermines due process. She added that Trump has given blank check after blank check to ICE, and has created a gestapo-like force that defies every norm in law enforcement in this country.

Commentators pointed out how in a previous debate Goodlander was called out for participating in a social media video calling on troops to refuse illegal orders. Having served 11 years in the United States Navy Reserve, Goodlander said she learned the bedrock principle that “you do not blindly follow orders, you follow the law,” and that she stands by that principle.

During the early hours of Sunday morning, legal advocates with the Tennessee Immigrant & Refugee Rights Coalition awakened to buzzing cellphones.

More than 120 men and women had been rounded up by immigration agents inside the Memphis nightclub, El Corralón. Their families and friends needed help.

“Parents didn’t come home. Roommates and friends stopped answering the phone. Workers and business owners didn’t show up on Monday morning and cars were left in the parking lot of the nightclub,” said Lisa Sherman Luna, the coalition’s executive director.

The raid, executed through at least two search warrants obtained by the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation in Shelby County Criminal Court, and reviewed by the Tennessee Lookout, was among the largest immigrant roundups in recent Tennessee history.

The incident occurred amid an escalation in immigrant arrests nationwide that began at the start of summer, following a temporary decline in activity after the January shooting deaths by ICE agents of two Minneapolis residents.

Homeland Security confirms 121 immigrant arrests in Memphis nightclub raid

Trump administration officials have touted the immigration crackdowns, in Memphis and elsewhere, as both part of a broader public safety push and a fulfillment of the president’s campaign promises to stem illegal immigration.

“Thanks to President Trump’s leadership, crime in the city of Memphis has plummeted,” a statement from Department of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said this week.

“A big part of that success comes from arresting and deporting illegal aliens in the city,” the statement said.

On Thursday, Sherman Luna joined national immigration advocates during a press conference to discuss the Memphis raid and other recent events in Tennessee that, they said, highlight the state’s increasingly pivotal role in the Trump administration immigration enforcement and deportation agenda.

The Memphis nightclub raid is among a recent string of events in Tennessee tied to the Trump administration’s immigration policies.

In May and June, four Black men were fatally shot in separate incidents by members of the Memphis Safe Task Force, a concentrated crime fighting effort that has brought multiple federal and state agencies, and the Tennessee National Guard, to Memphis. The task force includes Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Homeland Security Investigations, which both enforce immigration law. A Homeland Security Investigations officer fired her weapon during one of the four fatal encounters, according to the TBI. No charges have been brought against officers in any of the fatal shootings.

Late last month, the Lookout first reported the federal government’s $63 million contract with the Alaska-based Koniag corporation to establish a 24-7 ICE call center in Tennessee to more closely coordinate with local law enforcement across the country to locate and detain immigrants, including children.

ICE changes location of Tennessee call center site from Adams to Nashville

(Contract documents initially placed the ICE coordination center in Adams, Tenn. before being updated to reflect Nashville is its planned location). A spokesperson for Koniag this week did not respond to a request for more information. A spokesperson for ICE declined to discuss details of the planned coordination center.

The federal activities, paired with a slew of state-level legislation introducing immigration status verification into routine interactions with state and local government, “are turning Tennessee into a national hub for the mass deportation machine,” Sherman Luna said.

Hadi Sedigh, senior strategist with the National Immigration Law Center called Tennessee a “testing ground” for the Trump administration as it puts into place similar task force collaborations between federal and local law enforcement elsewhere. Sedigh also highlighted a key priority of the Trump administration to expand so-called 287(g) agreements that delegate immigration arrest powers to local police and sheriffs.

The administration’s goal has been codified into law in Tennessee, with legislation enacted this year requiring all sheriffs and police departments to enter the agreements by 2027. Tennessee was among the first states to implement the requirement as part of a package of legislation targeting immigrants that grew out of meetings between Tennessee House Speaker Cameron Sexton and White House advisor Stephen Miller.

“The mechanisms that helped make the midnight raid in Memphis possible, namely the 287(g) agreements and the joint federal task force model are, in effect, rapidly increasing in a number of jurisdictions throughout the country,” he said.

text:
A federal judge in Maryland has blocked the Trump administration from applying President Donald Trump’s latest birthright citizenship order to a class of U.S.-born children, finding that the Supreme Court already settled their constitutional right to citizenship earlier this year.

U.S. District Judge Deborah L. Boardman issued a preliminary injunction Wednesday, September 2, preventing federal agencies from enforcing Trump’s August 6 executive order against children covered by an existing class-action lawsuit. Boardman said the new order is “almost certainly unconstitutional” as applied to the class because the Supreme Court ruled June 30 that children born in the United States to parents who are unlawfully or temporarily in the country are citizens at birth.

“The Supreme Court has spoken,” Boardman wrote. She said no presidential executive order can undo the Court’s determination that the children covered by the lawsuit satisfy the requirements of the Citizenship Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.

The ruling marks a significant change from Boardman’s decision just days earlier. On August 28, she declined to immediately block the new executive order because the plaintiffs’ existing complaint challenged Trump’s earlier 2025 birthright citizenship order, not the replacement issued this summer.

Boardman allowed the plaintiffs to supplement their lawsuit that same day. They quickly filed an amended challenge to the August 6 order and renewed their request for an injunction. After reviewing the new claims, Boardman concluded that the plaintiffs were highly likely to succeed on their constitutional challenge.

Trump issued Executive Order 14418, titled “Continuing to Protect the Meaning and Value of American Citizenship,” on August 6, approximately five weeks after the Supreme Court rejected his administration’s broader attempt to restrict birthright citizenship.

The new order sought to identify narrower categories of children whom the administration contends fall outside the Fourteenth Amendment’s citizenship guarantee. It directs federal agencies not to recognize citizenship when neither parent is a U.S. citizen, and certain additional conditions apply.

Among them are children whose parents are classified as “alien enemies,” children of certain foreign government employees, and children whose parents allegedly engaged in fraud or a commercial transaction intended to obtain birthright citizenship. The order specifically includes arrangements in which parents pay for travel or other services intended to ensure that a mother is in the United States when she gives birth.

The administration described the latter category as an effort to curb “birth tourism,” in which foreign nationals travel to the United States to give birth so their children receive American citizenship.

Boardman found that the administration’s new categories do not resolve the central constitutional problem for children already covered by the lawsuit.

The certified class includes children born in the United States after February 19, 2025, whose mothers were unlawfully present and whose fathers were neither U.S. citizens nor lawful permanent residents, as well as children whose mothers were lawfully but temporarily present and whose fathers lacked citizenship or permanent resident status.

That class is effectively identical to one involved in Trump v. Barbara, the Supreme Court case decided June 30.

In that 6-3 decision, the Supreme Court held that children born in the United States to parents who are unlawfully or temporarily present are “subject to the jurisdiction” of the United States and therefore citizens at birth under the Fourteenth Amendment. The Court said the constitutional rule is broad and carries only narrow historical exceptions, including children of certain foreign diplomats and children born to enemies occupying U.S. territory.

Trump’s new order relies on language from the Supreme Court decision concerning those exceptions. The administration argues that additional categories of children may fall outside the citizenship guarantee when circumstances create what the order calls an “extraterritorial fiction.”

Boardman rejected that reasoning as a basis for denying citizenship to members of the certified class.

She wrote that even a preliminary review of the new order showed that several of its proposed exceptions bore “little to no resemblance” to the narrow historical exceptions recognized by the Supreme Court.

Her ruling did not resolve every possible constitutional question raised by the August order. Instead, Boardman focused on the narrower question of whether the administration could apply it to children whom the Supreme Court had already determined are citizens.

She concluded it could not.

Justice Department attorneys had argued that the lawsuit was premature because federal agencies had not yet issued detailed guidance explaining how the new order would be enforced. The executive order gives agencies 30 days to publish implementation guidance.

Boardman rejected that argument, reasoning that the executive order itself directs agencies to deny citizenship documents to broad categories of children regardless of what the forthcoming guidance ultimately says.

The implementation issue has already taken on practical significance.

Reuters reported this week that the State Department had drafted guidance that could require parents applying for passports for U.S.-born children to provide documents showing their own citizenship or immigration status. The proposal was designed in part to determine whether a child falls within one of the categories established by Trump’s August order.

Boardman’s injunction prevents the State Department, Department of Homeland Security, Social Security Administration and other federal defendants from enforcing the August order against members of the certified class or otherwise refusing to recognize their citizenship.

The ruling has limits.

Boardman did not prohibit federal agencies from issuing the implementation guidance required by the executive order. She also left untouched a provision addressing people born in U.S. territories or territorial waters where citizenship is not granted by federal statute because that provision does not affect members of the class before her.

The preliminary injunction also does not amount to a final ruling invalidating every provision of Trump’s August order for every person who might be affected. Boardman expressly limited her decision to the certified class and said she did not need, at this stage, to decide the constitutionality of each individual exception claimed by the administration.

Even so, her reasoning presents a substantial obstacle to the administration’s renewed attempt to narrow birthright citizenship.

The Fourteenth Amendment states that all people born or naturalized in the United States and “subject to the jurisdiction thereof” are citizens. In Trump v. Barbara, the Supreme Court concluded that children born here to parents unlawfully or temporarily present generally fall within that language.

Boardman said the August executive order cannot remove citizenship from children already protected by that decision simply by assigning them to newly defined categories.

The case now returns to litigation over the administration’s revised policy, less than three months after the Supreme Court appeared to resolve the central constitutional dispute surrounding Trump’s original birthright citizenship order.

text:
WASHINGTON — Congress has given the Trump administration hundreds of billions of dollars for immigration enforcement while placing relatively few restrictions on how the money can be used, according to an opinion by immigration policy analyst Dara Lind published by the American Immigration Council.

Lind argues that the November 2026 midterm elections could determine whether Congress continues providing broad financial support for the administration’s immigration agenda or begins using its authority to impose tighter controls on Immigration and Customs Enforcement and U.S. Customs and Border Protection.

Her analysis, published Sept. 3 under the headline “Congress Has Let Trump Go Wild. The Midterms Could Fix That,” focuses on congressional funding, oversight of ICE and the potential consequences of a change in the composition of Congress.

The American Immigration Council describes itself as a nonprofit, nonpartisan organization. Lind is a senior fellow at the organization.

$239.5 billion in immigration-enforcement funding

Lind cites a combined $239.5 billion in funding for ICE and CBP approved by Congress through legislation passed in 2025 and 2026.

She argues that much of the funding was approved through the budget reconciliation process, allowing the measures to pass the Senate with a simple majority rather than the 60 votes generally required to overcome a filibuster.

According to Lind, the result was an unusually large allocation of resources to immigration enforcement without extensive conditions governing how the agencies could spend the money.

She describes this approach as Congress effectively giving the Trump administration a “blank check” for immigration enforcement.

ICE’s electric-shock glove contract

One of the principal examples in Lind’s argument is ICE’s purchase of electric-shock gloves.

ICE awarded a $16.7 million contract for 6,000 pairs of the gloves in August. Reuters reported that the agency moved forward with the purchase despite opposition from human-rights advocates.

Federal procurement documents described the devices as “conductive distraction and de-escalation devices.” CBS News reported that ICE said the gloves were intended as a use-of-force tool for situations involving resistance and that the agency viewed them as an alternative to more serious or lethal weapons.

Lind uses the purchase to illustrate her broader criticism of congressional oversight. She argues that lawmakers who oppose particular ICE practices have not necessarily attached binding conditions to the funding that allows the agency to make such purchases.

Lind criticizes Congress’ oversight of ICE

Lind focuses particular attention on Sen. Susan Collins, Republican of Maine, who chairs the Senate Appropriations Committee.

According to Lind, Collins has expressed disagreement with some ICE spending while pointing to congressional funding for de-escalation measures and body cameras.

Lind argues that appropriations would have greater effect if Congress explicitly required agencies to spend the money in particular ways. In her view, funding an initiative without making it a statutory requirement leaves the agency with substantial discretion.

The opinion also argues that Congress has other tools available, including hearings, investigations and subpoenas.

Lind says a Congress willing to conduct aggressive oversight could investigate the actions of ICE and the Justice Department, including the federal response to incidents involving immigration enforcement that she identifies in the article.

These are arguments made by Lind in the opinion rather than findings of an independent congressional investigation.

What a new Congress could do

Lind argues that the next Congress could impose conditions on immigration-enforcement funding even if it does not control the White House.

Among the possibilities she identifies are restrictions on the use of appropriated funds for certain enforcement and surveillance equipment, additional requirements for immigration agents and conditions intended to protect constitutional and due-process rights.

She also argues that Congress could seek to recover or restrict funds that remain unallocated from earlier appropriations.

At the same time, Lind acknowledges that a new Congress would face a significant limitation: much of the money has already been appropriated.

Even without additional funding, she writes, the resources provided during 2025 and 2026 could allow ICE and CBP to continue large-scale immigration enforcement during the remainder of Trump’s term.

The potential effect of the midterm elections would therefore depend not only on which party controls Congress but also on whether lawmakers are willing to use their appropriations and oversight powers.

Immigration legislation could face a different path

Lind also examines how a change in congressional leadership could affect immigration legislation.

She highlights the American Dream and Promise Act, which would provide permanent legal status to certain people who have benefited from programs including Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals and Temporary Protected Status.

According to Lind, the legislation is currently the subject of a House discharge petition because House leadership has not brought it to the floor, despite bipartisan support.

She argues that a change in House leadership could give such legislation an opportunity to receive a floor debate.

Lind also points in the opposite direction, arguing that divided government could make it more difficult for Congress to pass legislation expanding immigration enforcement.

The midterms as a test of congressional power

The central argument of Lind’s opinion is that Congress retains significant authority over immigration enforcement even after approving large amounts of funding.

She argues that lawmakers can influence ICE and CBP through appropriations, spending restrictions, oversight investigations and legislation. Whether those powers are used will depend largely on the political composition of Congress after the November 2026 elections.

text:
New capacity-building hub will provide training, practice advisories, and resources for attorneys, partner organizations, and immigrant communities

CHICAGO — The National Immigrant Justice Center (NIJC) is excited to announce its new Advocate Training Center, a capacity-building hub offering trainings, practice advisories, and other resources to defend immigrant communities.

NIJC’s Advocate Training Center will expand legal resources for community partners, pro bono attorneys, and immigrants. The Advocate Training Center will respond to the rapidly changing immigration landscape and equip advocates to address emerging challenges.

To formally initiate this work, the Advocate Training Center will host a series of trainings on appeals before the Board of Immigration Appeals this fall. This will include a virtual training for pro bono attorneys on September 16 and an in-person convening for partner organizations in Chicago in early October.

NIJC has long offered sessions on critical topics such as fighting prolonged detention, defending due process as immigration judges try to pretermit cases without a full hearing, and protecting the parental rights of community members in detention. Additionally, NIJC has offered introductory courses on representing asylum seekers, survivors of crimes and trafficking, and people in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention along with dozens of other trainings. Through the Advocate Training Center, NIJC will both create new substantive offerings and expand access to these existing opportunities.

Later this year, NIJC will launch a learning management system that will serve as the online home for Advocate Training Center’s trainings, materials, and resources. The portal will make it easier for advocates to find practical support for their work with immigrant communities. NIJC will also expand its “office hours” offerings to make more slots available for other legal service providers in the region.

“The Advocate Training Center enables NIJC to continue the work NIJC was founded to do: equip legal advocates with the trainings and resources necessary to provide high-quality representation to immigrants. In a rapidly changing environment, immigrants and their legal advocates need resources they can trust. Through the Advocate Training Center, NIJC and our pro bono and community partners will continue responding to emerging needs and serving immigrants at scale.” said Charlotte Sall, Pro Bono Manager at NIJC.

“NIJC is fortunate to have deep expertise across so many areas of immigration law. The Advocate Training Center gives us a way to put that knowledge to work for the broader movement,” said Elizabeth Gibson, Managing Attorney for Capacity Building at NIJC. “We want to empower the next generation of advocates while also helping legal experts, community partners, and immigrants keep pace with the overwhelming barrage of legal updates, policy changes, and case law.”

The Advocate Training Center will build on NIJC’s history of providing pro bono and community support to strengthen the community of advocates rising to meet the challenges of this moment. Funding for the Advocate Training Center was provided by Walder Foundation.

text:
A supervisor overseeing background checks warned last year that Immigration and Customs Enforcement was hiring many new officers who had not undergone basic vetting, violating federal rules and putting the agency at risk of misconduct, a newly released whistleblower complaint shows.

The official was a unit chief in ICE’s Office of Professional Responsibility, where background checks were backlogged as ICE added thousands of new officers to carry out President Donald Trump’s mass deportation campaign.

ICE’s human resources division was making final job offers before preliminary vetting steps had been completed, including fingerprints, identity verification and credit checks, the official’s complaint warned.

“This unprecedented lowering of standards sacrifices proper risk mitigation for expediency, placing DHS at risk of infiltration and insider compromise,” the official wrote in a memo to the Department of Homeland Security’s Office of Inspector General dated August 2025.

The New York Times first reported on the whistleblower complaint Thursday. The Associated Press obtained the complaint and a related memo from the now-retired ICE official’s lawyer, Kevin Owens. The official’s identity was redacted from the complaint. The Times said the official was a 17-year-agency employee and longtime Republican who had voted for Trump in 2020 and 2024.

ICE announced in January that it had hired 12,000 new officers in less than one year, a spree financed by a $75 billion infusion from Congress to increase the agency’s arrests and deportations.

The rapid pace of the hiring, fueled by a $50,000 signing bonus, raised concerns about the quality of the new employees. An investigation by The Associated Press found that some of the new hires had serious financial problems in their backgrounds, had been accused of misconduct in prior jobs, and had checkered employment histories.

In July, Tom Homan, the White House border czar, said ICE would investigate apparent shortcomings in the vetting of an officer who shot and killed a 25-year-old motorist in Maine.

The whistleblower complaint said that “systemic breakdowns in vetting” violated several federal rules and standards designed to ensure candidates are suitable for sensitive law enforcement and national security positions.

The complaint said the lack of vetting created “increased vulnerability to insider threats, infiltration and foreign influence,” undermined ICE’s law enforcement operations and eroded public confidence in the agency.

It asked the inspector general to investigate the personnel vetting failures and for the agency to immediately suspend the improper practices, hold accountable those responsible for the violations and to review all recent hires to identify potential “insider threats.”

The Office of Inspector General has previously announced that it is investigating ICE’s hiring and training process, as well as security clearances granted to contractors and political appointees.

In a statement, ICE said Thursday the whistleblower was no longer with the agency.

“The ICE Office of Professional Responsibility diligently applies the proper personnel vetting regulations, including guidelines for national security, and evaluates all available information for every applicant based on these factors,” the statement said.

As the AP previously reported, ICE acknowledged that some applicants received “tentative selection letters” after their initial applications and interviews. Some were allowed to begin training before their background investigations were completed.

The whistleblower is the second insider to call out ICE’s rush to put more officers on the streets as reckless.

A former agency lawyer and instructor at the ICE academy, Ryan Schwank, said the agency cut training on the use of force, firearms safety, and the rights of protesters last year. The Department of Homeland Security has since increased the amount of training for new officers.

text:
Federal prosecutors have charged U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent Christian Castro with making false statements about the shooting of Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis in Minneapolis Jan. 14, the New York Times reported Thursday, citing an unnamed person familiar with the case.

The Times reported that the indictment will be unsealed after Castro is taken into custody.

The federal charge against an ICE agent is a rare move for the administration of President Donald Trump, which still has not charged any of the agents involved in the January killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti.

The single charge against Castro is far less than the civil rights violations originally sought by local federal prosecutors. But officials at the Department of Justice in Washington D.C. insisted the charges be significantly downgraded, according to reporting from ProPublica.

Castro is also charged in Minnesota with four counts of second-degree assault and one count of falsely reporting a crime. He is accused of firing his gun through the closed front door of a north Minneapolis home, hitting Cesar-Solis in the leg and endangering other people in the home.

Castro accused Sosa-Celis and another Venezuelan immigrant of assaulting him with a broom and a snow shovel before Castro opened fire, leading to assault charges against the two men that were dropped after surveillance footage proved Castro’s statements false.

In an email obtained by ProPublica, Matthew Evans, the assistant U.S. attorney in Minnesota in charge of the case, told attorneys for Sosa-Celis and other victims that he “objected in the strongest possible terms” to his bosses’ decision not to pursue civil rights charges.

Castro was released from a Texas county jail on Aug. 27, 90 days after his arrest by Texas Rangers, a state law enforcement agency, pursuant to the warrant related to his Minnesota charges.

Texas Gov. Greg Abbott blocked Castro’s extradition to Minnesota, prompting a lawsuit from Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison. A federal judge in that case declined to force the extradition, paving the way for Castro’s release.

Minnesota authorities told the federal court that Castro was in a romantic relationship with a woman in Mexico and owned property there, making him a flight risk.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security issued a statement later Thursday that indicated they are right about continuing enforcement operations.

Blumenthal conducted a public forum on the campus of Western Connecticut State University to receive testimony Thursday from the Danbury community about last week's ICE enforcement operations for the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations.

Members of Danbury United For Immigrants said after the forum that the local immigrant rights group documented that ICE agents arrested or detained 65 immigrants last week based on reports from loved ones and community members who witnessed arrests. But they said they also believe the number is higher but it has proven difficult to discern a more precise figure because ICE often does not release information on most of its arrests.

New Haven immigration attorney Glenn Formica recounted during the forum how he and other attorneys were denied access to detainees from Danbury they believed were being held in Hartford. He said some detainees were moved to unspecified "dark sites" that were inaccessible to their lawyers before being transferred out-of-state.

"We cannot have people denied access to lawyers. We cannot have dark sites as we had last weeks, dark sites where people were swept up, put in unknown locations, and we weren't able to access them as a lawyer," said Formica, a board member of the National Immigration Law Center and a founder of The American Immigrant Legal Clinic, a state-based nonprofit providing free legal defense for detained immigrants in Connecticut.

Blumenthal denounced the ICE operation in Danbury last week at the outset of the Thurday's forum at WCSU.

“I will just say what I've seen here in Danbury repeats a lot of what we seen in other cities, Minneapolis, Chicago, Los Angeles, where cruelty is the point," Blumenthal said. "Cruelty is the point. Fear and terror are the goal. I don’t recognize America in what I saw in Danbury last week."

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security said in a statement following the Danbury forum that ICE enforcement actions will continue under President Donald Trump and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin despite protestations from Blumenthal

A DHS spokesperson blasted Blumenthal in the statement that also referenced stolen valor allegations against Blumenthal over his past admitted misstatements about having served in the Vietnam War, which Trump has repeatedly criticized the Connecticut senator for making.

"We would remind Senator Blumenthal, perhaps most well-known for fabricating a military service record during the Vietnam War, that he has the ability to change the law if he doesn’t like it. ICE is enforcing the law as written by Congress and we will not be stopping," the DHS representative stated. “Under President Trump and Secretary Mullin, if you break the law, you will face the consequences. Criminal illegal aliens are not welcome in the U.S. We will find you, we will arrest you, and we will deport you."

The DHS spokesperson also ripped Connecticut and Gov. Ned Lamont over state laws limiting state and local cooperation in federal immigration enforcement, including honoring civil requests from federal authorities to detain immigrants in state or local custody.

“ICE is again calling on pro-criminal alien politician Senator Blumenthal to put Americans first and to tell Governor Lamont to honor our detainers so we can take custody of illegal aliens who pose a public safety threat in our communities,” the DHS spokesperson said.

State law generally requires state and local police to only honor administrative warrants and civil detainers for immigrants unless accompanied by a signed judicial warrant. There are exceptions for immigrants convicted of the two most serious classes of state-level felonies, or identified on the federal government's terrorist

No Danbury immigrants testified during Thursday's roughly hourlong forum; only five invited panelists participated. Before the public session, Blumenthal and Alves met privately with a small group of family members of detained immigrants, local immigrant advocates who witnessed ICE actions last week firsthand, and immigration attorneys representing detainees.

"That meeting we had just earlier today, so gripping and riveting, so powerfully emotional, the stories that we heard, but, rightly and understandably, people are worried that coming forward publicly will endanger their loved ones who are in detention right now," Blumenthal said.

Immigrant advocates and Alves said during the public forum that the members of the immigrant community in Danbury without and without legal status remain anxious and alert following last week's ICE operation. Fears of being picked up and a sense of powerlessness are prevalent, they said.

"The only time that this city is not safe is when ICE is here, and I am confident that everyone sitting up here with me today would agree with that," said panelist Carina Bandhauer, a sociology professor at WCSU and a board member for Danbury United For Immigrants. "Last week was horrifying."

Panelist Margaret Henderson, another Danbury United For Immigrants activist, recalled a school resource officer for a middle school near her home approaching her and some neighbors on her street after they started blowing whistles after spotting ICE agents to alert people nearby to their presence.

"So, we started doing that, and a school resource officer in a uniform came across the street and asked us to quit because we'd be scaring the children inside the school because they didn't know what it means, and ICE left that day without taking anybody," she said.

Alves, the state Democratic chairman, also predicted that ICE agents will being swarming Danbury on and off over the next two months until the Nov. 3 election. Formica said the same thing will be happening in places all across the country.

"We need to brace for it. We need to fight back on it, and we need to hold on," Formica said.

text:
MEMPHIS, Tenn. — An 81-year-old Iranian man held in federal immigration custody in West Tennessee was released on Thursday.

Hasan Besharat has been held at the West Tennessee Detention Center since February despite his attorney saying he spent decades complying with ICE requirements.

Besharat came to the United States legally from Iran in 1974 on a student visa.

An immigration judge issued an order of removal in 2001, but his attorney says Besharat had been living under an ICE “order of supervision” since 2004 and attended every required check-in.

That changed earlier this year when ICE detained him in Nashville.

His attorney said the agency told them it now had the means to enforce that decades-old removal order. His attorney says age and health quickly became major concerns for the father of two U.S. citizen sons.

“He has high blood pressure, and he barely weighs 100 pounds right now. It’s difficult for him to get around,” said Brandon Viele, Besharat’s attorney.

Now, seven months after Besharat’s detainment, a judge has granted a petition for his release from a holding facility in Mason, TN.

“Suddenly at the end of February, he was detained by ICE and his order of supervision was revoked and the only explanation that was given was that ICE now had the means to enforce that order of removal,” Viele said four months ago to WREG.

“There have been a lot of administrations that have come and gone since that time, and the requirements haven’t remained static. In fact, they’ve become significantly more complex, especially with the recent changes made,” said Viele.

He walked out of that facility Thursday at around 1 p.m., Besharat’s attorney confirmed with WREG. Besharat is heading to Nashville to be reunited with his family. His attorney continues working through the immigration process to help him seek legal status.

“We’re thrilled and so happy that he’s able to be reunited with his family,” said Viele. “Its involved so much litigation and effort on our part as his legal team and his family and friends have also gone through a lot in the time that he’s been in Mason.”

“We believe that he should have been home in Nashville this entire time. But right now, we’re thankful for this victory. And we hope to continue to make progress on his pathway towards status through USCIS,” said Viele.

Attorney Viele says it’s wonderful and inspiring to see the outpouring of support that Besharat has received from the community. After months of persistence, sacrifice, and much litigation, Attorney Viele said everyone involved feels a sense of relief Thursdsay night.

text:
Area residents gathered outside the Gainesville Police Department Thursday to protest a new general order requiring officers to report interactions with individuals they reasonably suspect are unauthorized immigrants.

The Gainesville Immigrant Neighborhood Inclusion Initiative committee called on Gainesville residents to gather at 4 p.m. and demand the cancellation of General Order 82.4. Protestors assembled outside police headquarters holding posters and signs with anti-immigration law messages opposing the new policy.

Ethan Maia de Needell, 32, a member of the Gainesville Immigrant Neighbor Inclusion Initiative leadership committee, said the protest aimed to raise awareness about GPD’s new policy and demand its cancellation.

“We are also using this protest as a way to invite the community at large to call into our city manager and the chief of police demanding the cancellation of this policy. We have a QR code that is available for anyone who's interested in putting an end to this racial profiling, show-me-your-papers policy,” Maia de Needell said.

GPD issued the order on Aug. 27. The policy, which applies to all sworn department officers, requires them to report certain interactions with people they suspect are “unauthorized aliens,” the term used in the order.

Officers must complete a Suspected Unauthorized Alien Contact Form when they believe someone is an authorized alien and the person is not being arrested. The contact form requires a photo of the individual and must be submitted by the end of the GPD agent’s shift.

If the officer has lawful interaction with a suspect and intends to arrest that person under a criminal charge, the officer must complete the same form and include the person’s photo. The authority must also include an FDLE notification in the arrest report identifying the person as a suspected unauthorized alien.

The order states that personal characteristics, such as limited English proficiency, are not enough on their own to warrant an investigation. However, depending on the circumstance, it may contribute to an officer’s reasonable suspicion.

If the official finds an immigration warrant or order of detention by immigration enforcement, the order directs the officer to detain the individual and request assistance from a designated immigration officer. GPD does not have a designated immigration officer.

People attending the protest also raised their voices in support of immigrant families facing complicated circumstances.

Jonah Starling, 18, a Gainesville High School Student, attended the protest mainly to support one of his classmates, Sebastian Jimenez Peroza, who was recently detained with his family for more than a week by immigration officials.

“I met him. We talked. He's a good kid. He's a nice kid. Doesn't do wrong,” said Starling.

The intersection of Northwest Sixth Street and Northwest Eighth Avenue in front of GPD headquarters was lined with people calling for the equality and human rights of all immigrants.

Valerie Fauldauer, 76, a retired hospital administrator, held a sign in support of immigrants she said are entitled to legal protection even if they allegedly crossed the border illegally.

“They are entitled to due process under our constitution, and they should not be rounded up, treated improperly, and put in prisons,” Fauldauer said. “The fact that our government is not able to provide that due process is not the fault of the immigrant.”

Among the protesters was Joe Rojo, 66, a Gainesville resident who said he is concerned that those in power could arrest people they consider enemies.

“I don't believe that the government has any authority to abduct people and transfer them all over the country without any kind of hearing, any kind of legal help,” Rojo said.

Maia de Needell said the specific policy goes beyond what state law requires and could discourage immigrants from interacting with local police.

The Gainesville Immigrant Neighbor Inclusion Initiative said the group’s goal is to continue raising awareness about the policy despite the fear and anger surrounding immigration enforcement.

Maia de Needell said the issue has implications beyond immigration and urged residents to continue contacting city officials about the order.

Protesters of all ages remained outside the police department after 5 p.m.

text:
A judge in Alabama granted Leo Garcia Venegas, an American citizen and construction worker, a first-round victory in his federal lawsuit aimed at stopping unconstitutional raids and detentions by immigration officers. Judge Jeffrey Beaverstock rejected the government’s attempt to dismiss the case after a hearing in Mobile. Leo is represented by the Institute for Justice (IJ).

PREVIOUSLY:

Baldwin County man sues seeking injunction to bar ICE work site raids after 3 detentions

Federal agents accused of unlawful raids on Baldwin County worksites: lawsuit

“The court’s decision was an important first step,” said IJ Senior Attorney Jared McClain. “We know the Department of Homeland Security thinks it can raid construction sites without a warrant, round up all the workers, and refuse to credit their government-issued IDs. Now we’ll have the chance to prove these violations of the Fourth Amendment.”

Leo, a construction worker in Baldwin County, Alabama, has been detained three times since the spring of 2025 despite presenting an Alabama-issued REAL ID each time. In May and June of last year, Leo was detained by officers who entered his private job sites without warrants. Both times, officers refused to believe Leo was a citizen or recognize his REAL ID as proof of legal status. Earlier this year, officers followed Leo home and confronted him in his driveway. Even though Leo was trying to show officers his REAL ID, he was ripped from his car, tackled to the ground, handcuffed, shackled, and locked in the back of a car.

“Americans cannot be stopped and held by law enforcement when they are doing nothing wrong,” said Leo. “I’m glad my case is moving forward, and I hope it can make lasting change.”

At a May hearing to consider the motion for a preliminary injunction, a DHS official testified that agents do not treat REAL ID as reliable proof of legal presence. But DHS certifies and administers the READ ID Act and then-Secretary Kristi Noem spent considerable time last year encouraging people to get their REAL ID.

The DHS also testified that agents treat construction sites as “open fields” that they can enter without a reason or warrant. Leo’s second detention, inside of a mostly-constructed home, shows just how far the government’s theory reaches.

The court has yet to rule on Leo’s request for a temporary injunction against the raids and detentions. IJ attorneys reiterated at Wednesday’s hearing that the government has not disavowed using unconstitutional tactics in Alabama.

text:
Last week, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) published a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) that would impose a $103,265 fee on all cap-subject H-1B petitions. The fee would apply to all petitions filed by private sector employers, the majority of petitions filed, but not to “cap-exempt” filers, like universities and nonprofit organizations.

Technology companies have routinely abused the H-1B guest worker program to displace American STEM workers and depress wages by paying foreign workers – mainly from India and China – substantially less than their U.S. counterparts. The Trump administration has issued several regulations aimed at reforming it while also investigating fraudulent H-1B applications used to acquire green cards. The NPRM is the administration’s second attempt at imposing a fee on new H-1B petitions, after the original $100,000 fee was vacated by a federal district judge on statutory and procedural grounds, a decision pending appeal in the First Circuit.

Applied to 85,000 petitions per fiscal year, the annual visa cap, DHS projects that this new fee would generate approximately $8.8 billion annually. These funds would be distributed across agencies within DHS as well as the Departments of State, Labor, and Justice. By making H-1B petitions more expensive the NPRM would also incentivize employers to hire U.S. workers, especially recent STEM graduates, over foreign nationals.

The NPRM is part of the administration’s broader effort to reform employment-based visas and protect the American labor market. Upcoming regulations include reforms to Optional Practical Training (OPT), a program that allows foreign students to work in the United States for up to three years after graduation, and H-4 work authorizations, provided to spouses of H-1B recipients. Despite both programs lacking any congressional authorization, DHS is proposing to end the practice of granting H-4 work authorizations while simply imposing a fee on OPT.

text:
A federal prosecutor in Minnesota who was investigating an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer for possible civil rights crimes has been fired, four sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Matthew Evans was investigating ICE officer Christian Castro over the shooting of a Venezuelan immigrant earlier this year. The Justice Department ultimately charged Castro this week with making false statements about the incident, but the indictment remains sealed, CBS News has previously reported.

Earlier this week, ProPublica reported that Evans told attorneys for the man who was shot, Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis, and other victims to prepare for Castro to only be charged with making false statements, which would carry lesser penalties than criminal charges that he violated people's constitutional rights under color of law.

ProPublica quoted directly from an email it said Evans had sent to the attorneys.

"This is being directed by the Main Justice and the US Attorney," the email from Evans reportedly said. "I objected in the strongest possible terms and fought it as hard as I could. It wasn't enough." (CBS News has not obtained the email reviewed by ProPublica.)

Three sources told CBS News that Evans is under investigation by the Justice Department. Two sources said the investigation focuses on allegations of leaking.

CBS News has reached out to Evans for comment.

A federal grand jury returned a six-count indictment against Castro on Wednesday, multiple sources familiar with the matter told CBS News. He was taken into custody in Texas on Thursday and will make an initial court appearance Friday, a source said.

The case revolves around a January incident involving Castro and Sosa-Celis, who officials say is in the U.S. illegally, during the Trump administration's immigration crackdown in the Minneapolis area.

After Sosa-Celis was shot in the leg, federal prosecutors charged him and one other man — Alfredo Alejandro Aljorna — with forcibly assaulting, resisting or impeding federal officers. But the federal government's description of the leadup to the shooting has shifted, and ICE later accused its agents of lying about the incident.

Initially, the Department of Homeland Security said Sosa-Celis fled a traffic stop on foot, and when an ICE agent tried to arrest him, two other men attacked the agent with a shovel and a broomstick. DHS said Sosa-Celis then broke free and started attacking the agent, too, leading the agent to fire a "defensive shot to defend his life."

But an FBI affidavit filed in the criminal case against Sosa-Celis and Aljorna alleged Aljorna, not Sosa-Celis, was the one who fled a traffic stop, and said Sosa-Celis had initially struck the ICE agent with a broomstick while the agent tried to arrest Aljorna. The agent described it as a three-minute-long tussle, according to the affidavit.

Cellphone video shared by a Democratic state senator also showed a woman telling 911 her husband was chased by ICE agents before he reached his home, and was shot in front of his family. And a video later released by The New York Times showed the altercation involving Aljorna and Sosa-Celis lasted far less than three minutes.

A month after Aljorna and Sosa-Celis were charged, the Justice Department dropped the case and said "newly discovered evidence" was "materially inconsistent" with the allegations against them.

Todd Lyons, who led ICE at the time, said a review of video evidence showed two ICE officers had made "untruthful statements" in sworn testimony. He said the officers would be placed on administrative leave and could face prosecution.

Springfield resident Sean Moorman is a volunteer ICE watcher, who monitors the public activities of immigration agents. ICE watchers take pictures or videos from a distance.

For weeks Moorman has been taking pictures and videoing ICE agents as they apprehend Haitian immigrants.

His attorney David Carey is with the ACLU of Ohio. He said Moorman is motivated by compassion.

"He sees his neighbors being taken away, and he's concerned about what's happening to them," Carey said.

According to the lawsuit, Moorman said his actions have sparked repeated menacing and intimidating retaliation from masked agents.

WYSO reached out to the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE. In an email response the agency said, "ICE is aware of the lawsuit filed by the ACLU in Ohio and is reviewing appropriate next steps in coordination with the Department of Justice.”

In late August, Moorman photographed several ICE agents in a parking lot. Per Moorman, they got back into their SUV’s, and attempted to box him in. Finally one officer gestured to Moorman to follow him. Carey said Moorman complied and another officer followed him.

"The ICE vehicles went to his house. He called his wife who was at home and she was terrified," Carey said. "One of the officers waved out the window to get Sean's attention and then pointed at his house, then took some pictures, pictures of the house, pictures of his wife's car in the driveway, and then slowly drove away. And then the other officer who was following behind Sean did the same, slowed down, took some pictures, as if to say, 'we know where you live'."

According to Carey, the agents are infringing on Moorman’s First Amendment rights to record law enforcement activities in public.

"The First Amendment to the Constitution guarantees Sean's right to record ICE, to monitor what they're doing in public, which is what he does, peacefully, lawfully," Carey said. "A number of agents have harassed or intimidated him in what we would describe as an escalating campaign designed to get him to stop doing what he's doing."

Moorman's lawsuit asks the court to identify the seven ICE agents. It also requests an emergency temporary restraining order to prevent ICE agents from intimidating Moorman.

The case is being heard in Dayton before Justice Michael Newman in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Ohio.

It prioritizes the arrest and detention of people in the country illegally who are accused or convicted of crimes.

ICE offers law enforcement agencies three models for enforcing immigration law:

Task Force Model: While patrolling their communities, law enforcement officers can question and "exercise limited immigration authority" on people they suspect of violating civil immigration laws. Officers can place a 48-hour hold on non-citizens, allowing ICE officers to transfer the person to an immigration detention center.

Warrant Service Officer Model: ICE trains and deputizes officers to execute ICE administrative warrants within an agency’s jails or correctional facilities.

text:
A judge has rejected the federal government’s attempt to dismiss a case involving a Baldwin County construction worker who was arrested by immigration officials on three separate occasions.

Leo Garcia Venegas, represented by the Institute for Justice, filed a lawsuit last year challenging the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) immigration enforcement practices. He is requesting a preliminary injunction against DHS related to immigration enforcement at job sites, accusing immigration officials of violating his and others' constitutional rights.

In his lawsuit, Venegas says immigration officials apprehended him three separate times, twice at construction sites where he worked and once when driving home. He alleges that officials rejected his Alabama-issued REAL ID when he presented it to them, dismissing it as fake. He has not received any criminal charges following his encounters with immigration officials.

In a victory for Venegas, Southern District of Alabama Judge Jeffery Beaverstock, a Trump appointee, denied the government’s motion to dismiss his lawsuit following a hearing in Mobile. Beaverstock previously ruled that Venegas has enough ground to sue, with a hearing involving both him and the government being held at the U.S. District Court in Mobile in May.

“The court’s decision was an important first step,” Jared McClain, Institute for Justice senior attorney, said Sept. 3 in a statement. “We know the Department of Homeland Security thinks it can raid construction sites without a warrant, round up all the workers and refuse to credit their government-issued IDs. Now we’ll have the chance to prove these violations of the Fourth Amendment.”

Beaverstock has not yet ruled on Venegas’ request for a temporary injunction against the raids and detentions that occur within the court’s jurisdiction.

“Americans cannot be stopped and held by law enforcement when they are doing nothing wrong,” Venegas said. “I’m glad my case is moving forward, and I hope it can make lasting change.”

GCM has reached out to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) for comment.

text:
A supervisor overseeing background checks warned last year that Immigration and Customs Enforcement was hiring many new officers who had not undergone basic vetting, violating federal rules and putting the agency at risk of misconduct, a newly released whistleblower complaint shows.

The official was a unit chief in ICE’s Office of Professional Responsibility, where background checks were backlogged as ICE added thousands of new officers to carry out President Donald Trump’s mass deportation campaign.

ICE’s human resources division was making final job offers before preliminary vetting steps had been completed, including fingerprints, identity verification and credit checks, the official’s complaint warned.

“This unprecedented lowering of standards sacrifices proper risk mitigation for expediency, placing DHS at risk of infiltration and insider compromise,” the official wrote in a memo to the Department of Homeland Security’s Office of Inspector General dated August 2025.

The New York Times first reported on the whistleblower complaint Thursday. The Associated Press obtained the complaint and a related memo from the now-retired ICE official’s lawyer, Kevin Owen. The official’s identity was redacted from the complaint. The Times said the official was a 17-year-agency employee and longtime Republican who had voted for Trump in 2020 and 2024.

ICE announced in January that it had hired 12,000 new officers in less than one year, a spree financed by a $75 billion infusion from Congress to increase the agency’s arrests and deportations.

The rapid pace of the hiring, fueled by a $50,000 signing bonus, raised concerns about the quality of the new employees. An investigation by The Associated Press found that some of the new hires had serious financial problems in their backgrounds, had been accused of misconduct in prior jobs, and had checkered employment histories.

In July, Tom Homan, the White House border czar, said ICE would investigate apparent shortcomings in the vetting of an officer who shot and killed a 25-year-old motorist in Maine.

The whistleblower complaint said that “systemic breakdowns in vetting” violated several federal rules and standards designed to ensure candidates are suitable for sensitive law enforcement and national security positions.

The complaint said the lack of vetting created “increased vulnerability to insider threats, infiltration and foreign influence,” undermined ICE’s law enforcement operations and eroded public confidence in the agency.

It asked the inspector general to investigate the personnel vetting failures and for the agency to immediately suspend the improper practices, hold accountable those responsible for the violations and to review all recent hires to identify potential “insider threats.”

The Office of Inspector General has previously announced that it is investigating ICE’s hiring and training process, as well as security clearances granted to contractors and political appointees.

In a statement, ICE said Thursday the whistleblower was no longer with the agency.

“The ICE Office of Professional Responsibility diligently applies the proper personnel vetting regulations, including guidelines for national security, and evaluates all available information for every applicant based on these factors,” the statement said.

As the AP previously reported, ICE acknowledged that some applicants received “tentative selection letters” after their initial applications and interviews. Some were allowed to begin training before their background investigations were completed.

The whistleblower is the second insider to call out ICE’s rush to put more officers on the streets as reckless.

A former agency lawyer and instructor at the ICE academy, Ryan Schwank, said the agency cut training on the use of force, firearms safety, and the rights of protesters last year. The Department of Homeland Security has since increased the amount of training for new officers.

___

This story has been updated to correct the spelling of Kevin Owen, not Owens.

text:
A federal judge has temporarily blocked Donald Trump’s latest attempt to restrict birthright citizenship – the longstanding principle that all babies born in the US are guaranteed American citizenship.

The decision came nearly a month after the president tried for a second time to limit via executive order which people born in the US can become American citizens. The supreme court ruled in late June that Trump’s previous sweeping order denying birthright citizenship to the children of undocumented immigrants or temporary visitors was unconstitutional.

Trump’s latest order, issued on 6 August, denied automatic citizenship not only to the children of ambassadors or “foreign ministers” but to the children of other foreign citizens. Including employees at a foreign embassy and employees of international organizations including the United Nations and the World Bank. The new order also denied birthright citizenship to children of parents the government deemed “alien enemies” and parents who “engage[d] in a commercial transaction to ensure that the person’s mother is present in the United States, or a territory of the United States, to give birth”.

The federal government has yet to issue guidelines on how these restrictions would work in practice. For instance, how the government would discern between a parent that buys plane tickets to visit on vacation and one who is engaging in what the administration called “birth tourism” – visiting the country for the sole purpose of giving birth in the US.

Judge Deborah Boardman ruled on Wednesday that the supreme court had already settled some of the questions raised by Trump’s new order, writing: “No presidential executive order can undo what the Supreme Court has done.”

In a 35-page opinion, she also wrote that the new executive order could have the effect of rescinding citizenship from children who were already protected by the supreme court decision, if – for instance – the administration arbitrarily moved to designate parents as “alien enemies”. The government has already used the sweeping label of “alien enemy” to designate dozens of Venezuelan nationals with no criminal records as terrorists, justifying their deportation to a Salvadoran megaprison last year.

“The Supreme Court has spoken: Children in the certified class are ‘citizens at birth’,” she wrote. The court’s decision, she said, “is the law of the land. The President must follow it.”

The plaintiffs in this latest challenge include Casa and the Asylum Seeker Advocacy Project (Asap), two non-profits that provide immigrant services, as well as individuals who could be affected by the new executive order. The new orders are worryingly vague, said Conchita Cruz, co-founder of Asap – which was also part of the lawsuit challenging the president’s original birthright restrictions last year. “Immigrant families should not have to rush back into court on an issue that has already been resolved by the supreme court,” she said.

The pregnant women who partook in that first suit, who gave birth as the supreme court was deciding the fates of their newborns, have once again been plunged into uncertainty, she said.

One of the original plaintiffs, a Venezuelan asylum seeker, had told the Guardian she felt relief after the country’s highest court ruled that her baby boy was unambiguously a US citizen.

“But I know this isn’t over,” she said in a statement after the ruling on Thursday. “The threat to birthright citizenship is still out there. I’ll keep fighting for permanent protection for my child, and for every child born in this country.”

text:
For Immediate Release: September 3, 2026

Contact: press@presidentsalliance.org

WASHINGTON, D.C. — Today, the United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts heard oral argument in the case brought by a coalition of higher education associations and unions that challenges the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) final rule ending the Duration of Status (D/S) framework for international students, exchange visitors, and representatives of foreign media. The final rule also imposes new limits on academic flow and educational mobility. The following are statements by some of the co-plaintiffs:

Miriam Feldblum, President and CEO, Presidents’ Alliance, said:

“Today’s hearing laid out the serious and irreparable harms this rule would cause to international students, scholars, higher education institutions, our communities, the economy, and U.S. research and innovation. It also underscored the government’s failure to adequately engage in the rulemaking process at every stage. We appreciate the court’s careful consideration of these issues and look forward to its ruling.”

Fanta Aw, PhD, Executive Director and CEO of NAFSA: Association of International Educators said:

“We remain steadfast in our belief that DHS’s decision to end Duration of Status is a misguided and unnecessary policy shift that injects uncertainty, bureaucracy, and fear into a system that has long worked effectively. At a time when global competition for talent is intensifying, this policy is not just bad for higher education, it is bad for American innovation, economic growth, workforce development, and global leadership. Our hope is that higher education institutions and international students and scholars know that we remain committed to fighting for what is right and what is in the best interest of our students, our institutions, and our nation.”

Jon Schleuss, President of The NewsGuild-CWA, said:

“I was proud to be in court today to represent our members, which include international journalists working in the U.S. We are part of a strong labor coalition, including international students and scholars, fighting recent DHS rules that shorten the duration of F, J, and I visas and undermine our right to free speech and a free press. What DHS is doing is illegal. We must stand up against a president who continually undermines our First Amendment. I never dreamed I would be spending so much time in court suing a president violating our constitution and the rule of law.”

About the Lawsuit

NAFSA: Association of International Educators; the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration; the Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts (AICUM); the American Federation Of Teachers (AFT); Graduate Labor Organization, AFT Local 6516 (GLO); International Union, United Automobile, Aerospace and Agricultural Implement Workers of America (UAW); United Auto Workers Local 2322; and The NewsGuild-CWA filed a complaint and a motion for preliminary injunction in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts challenging the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) final rule ending the Duration of Status (D/S) framework for international students, exchange visitors, and representatives of foreign media.

Plaintiffs are represented by McDermott Will & Schulte.
