title: This U.S. citizen is suing ICE for arresting him three times. His lawsuit is moving forward.
authors: Autumn Billings, Veronique de Rugy, Matthew Petti, Robby Soave, Tosin Akintola
description:
A federal judge ruled on Wednesday that his lawsuit against the Trump administration for violating his Fourth Amendment rights can move forward.
Venegas quickly began recording on his phone after one of the officers physically assaulted his brother, another worker at the construction site.
Venegas exclaims as the officer grabs him by the arm and tries to force him to the ground.
While pinned to the ground by three officers, one of the men grabbed Venegas' wallet out of his back pocket, according to the lawsuit.
And, once again, officers refused to let Venegas go after he presented his REAL ID.
text:
Leo Garcia Venegas, an American citizen and construction worker, has been arrested and detained by federal immigration officers, not once, not twice, but three times since the spring of 2025, despite carrying and presenting an Alabama REAL ID each time. A federal judge ruled on Wednesday that his lawsuit against the Trump administration for violating his Fourth Amendment rights can move forward.

Venegas was working early on May 21, 2025, laying the foundation for a new home in Foley, Alabama, southeast of Mobile, when he saw "five armed men in camouflage" jump the property line fence and run toward the construction workers, according to his complaint filed in the Southern District of Alabama. Venegas quickly began recording on his phone after one of the officers physically assaulted his brother, another worker at the construction site.

Video of the incident shows another officer approach Venegas. "Yes, immigration," the masked officer says. Venegas sidesteps the man, trying to get clear footage of his brother's ongoing arrest. "You're making this more complicated than you want to," the officer says while following Venegas. "Don't touch me! I'm a citizen!" Venegas exclaims as the officer grabs him by the arm and tries to force him to the ground.

"I'll show you my papers now! I'm a citizen!" pleads Venegas. Additional officers run over to assist in the tackle. "Get on the fucking ground now!" one yells, and Venegas falls to the ground.

While pinned to the ground by three officers, one of the men grabbed Venegas' wallet out of his back pocket, according to the lawsuit. But despite carrying his valid REAL ID–compliant driver's license—which requires proof of citizenship or lawful presence to be issued—the officers refused to accept the ID as proof that he was in the country legally. Instead, the officers accused Venegas of having a fake ID and placed him in handcuffs.

After pleading with officers to check his Social Security number for over an hour in the hot Alabama sun, "one of the officers finally relented, made a phone call, and confirmed that [Venegas'] Social Security Number was valid," writes the complaint. Venegas was released with no charges.

But just three weeks later, it happened again. While working alone inside a "partially constructed home," armed, masked federal officers entered the private property without permission and detained Venegas. And for the second time, according to the complaint, the officers told Venegas that his REAL ID could be fake and therefore was not enough to prove his citizenship or legal status.

Venegas was eventually released after officers confirmed, again, that he was a citizen.

Represented by the Institute for Justice, a nonprofit law firm, Venegas filed suit in September 2025, arguing the two warrantless detentions lacked probable cause and were instead based only on his ethnicity. In response, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has defended the immigration officers' actions, arguing that Americans have no reasonable expectation of privacy while working on privately owned construction sites and that REAL IDs can't be trusted to prove U.S. citizenship.

But as his case works its way through the courts, Venegas has been forced to live with the reality of the Trump administration's immigration policies. And on May 2, almost one year after his initial immigration arrest, he was detained for a third time. Without asking any questions or issuing any lawful commands, the agents confronted Venegas after parking in front of his own home, pulled him from his car, tackled him to the ground, and placed him in handcuffs, according to his declaration following the incident. And, once again, officers refused to let Venegas go after he presented his REAL ID.

text:
Sources said the confrontation unfolded during the afternoon of Sept. 2 on 24th Avenue between 97th and 98th streets in East Elmhurst. Video obtained by amNewYork shows a man approaching a vehicle and pressing his cellphone against the driver’s side window and shouting, “Get out of the neighborhood. Get the f**k out of the neighborhood.” Filming ICE interactions from a public street is protected by the First Amendment, provided those doing the filming are not obstructing any official actions.

The armed individual inside the vehicle — whom sources identified as an ICE agent — then drew a handgun equipped with a mounted flashlight and pointed it toward the man filming.

“You pointed a gun at me?” the cameraman asked, stunned.

“You tried to break my window with a weapon,” the individual inside the vehicle replied.

“It’s not a weapon,” the cameraman responded.

“It is a weapon,” the armed individual answered.

The encounter has left immigrant rights advocates and ICE watchdogs astonished over what they called a dangerous provocation. An ICE watcher familiar with the incident described the encounter to amNewYork.

“A community defender was standing beside the driver’s side window of the vehicle when the ICE agent could be seen lifting a pistol and pointing it directly toward the community defender to the point that you could see directly down the barrel of the gun,” said the watcher, who requested anonymity for this article.

Looking down the barrel of ICE agent’s gun

The watcher also condemned ICE’s presence in New York.

“A concerned neighbor looked down the barrel of a gun yesterday. ICE is a violent paramilitary force and is an imminent danger to our communities. This level of violence will only get worse until they are abolished,” the watcher added.

Murad Awawdeh, president and CEO of the New York Immigration Coalition, called the incident “an abuse of power” and said the agent should face disciplinary action.

“Every American and every New Yorker has a legal and ethical right to film law enforcement, military or public officials without fear of arrest, violence or retaliation,” Awawdeh said. “Pointing a gun at any person for exercising their legal right to record is an abuse of power and a direct attack on our individual rights. We have seen the devastating consequences of putting armed ICE agents in our communities, from Minneapolis to Texas, where bystanders lost their lives. No New Yorker should have to fear being shot, threatened or killed because they are documenting the actions of ICE.”

Awawdeh added that the agent “was clearly attempting to threaten and intimidate community members into silence” and said the officer should be “at the very least reprimanded, if not taken off active duty.”

The incident came a day after Mullin held a press conference at 26 Federal Plaza, where he announced that ICE had arrested about 2,100 immigrants in New York over the past month.

Mullin — who falsely claimed New York was a “crime-ridden city” despite overwhelming evidence to the contrary — also threatened to deploy more federal immigration agents to the city if Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Gov. Kathy Hochul continue to prevent local law enforcement from cooperating with federal immigration authorities.

“We will send as many people as we have possible to make sure that we’re restoring law and order,” Mullin said. “President Trump made this very, very clear. He loves New York. He made that very clear over and over again. He wants to see law and order restored.”

amNewYork reached out to DHS regarding Wednesday’s incident in Queens, and is awaiting a response.

text:
Federal prosecutors in the United States have charged an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer accused of lying under oath to investigators regarding the shooting of a Venezuelan man during an immigration crackdown this year.

Prosecutors alleged that Christian Castro lied to federal investigators about the events that led up to him firing on 24-year-old Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis through the door of a Minnesota home in January.

Recommended Stories

list 2 of 3US judge declines Minnesota’s effort to force Texas to extradite ICE agent

list 3 of 3Ex-ICE agent charged over shooting is freed by Texas authorities

end of list

The Associated Press news agency and The New York Times reported the indictment, quoting a person familiar with the matter who was not authorised to discuss the investigation publicly. It was expected to be unsealed when Castro is detained.

Castro, a former Department of Homeland Security agent, also faces multiple state felony charges in Minnesota related to the nonfatal shooting, including assault with a dangerous weapon.

Authorities in the Midwestern state had sought to extradite Castro from Texas to face trial. Texas Governor Greg Abbott, a Republican and President Donald Trump loyalist, declined to cooperate with the request.

The ensuing standoff left Castro detained in Texas for 90 days before his release last week. Under Texas law, the state cannot hold the subject of an extradition order for longer than that. His whereabouts were unclear as of Thursday.

The charges mark a rare move by the Department of Justice under Trump.

Trump’s top officials have repeatedly argued that immigration agents maintain broad protections while conducting enforcement, a position rejected by many legal experts.

For example, no one has been charged in the fatal shootings by immigration agents of Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis in January.

An Associated Press review conducted in February found about two dozen ICE employees and contractors had faced criminal charges since 2020.

An American Civil Liberties Union report released in July documented instances of violent tactics or other civil rights violations in about a third of 1,200 immigration enforcement incidents reviewed in 2025 alone.

Video evidence contradicts statement

The Trump administration distanced itself from the Castro case after video emerged contradicting the agent’s initial accounts of the confrontation.

Castro told investigators that Sosa-Celis had attacked him, which the surveillance footage showed did not happen.

Todd Lyons, then acting head of ICE, said at the time that the footage “has revealed that sworn testimony provided by two separate officers appears to have made untruthful statements”.

Castro and a fellow agent chased Alfredo Aljorna, a Venezuelan national, after a traffic stop, according to charging documents.

Aljorna fled to the home he shared with Sosa-Celis. After a brief scramble, the two men ran inside. Castro then shot through the closed door, “knowing [the home] was occupied by several people”, the documents said.

One witness said there were two children in the house when Castro opened fire. Sosa-Celis was hit in the leg.

Federal authorities have since suspended Castro and dropped all charges against Sosa-Celis and his co-defendant, who were both initially accused of forcibly assaulting an ICE officer. The other agent involved in the incident was also suspended, but has not yet been charged.

Thursday’s indictment comes after ProPublica this week reported that Department of Justice (DOJ) officials had blocked prosecutors from pursuing more serious civil rights charges against Castro, including “deprivation of rights under color of law”.

However, a source close to the investigation told the AP the active investigation could still result in civil rights charges.

The Trump administration has scaled back the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division and dismantled several Biden-era police oversight initiatives since returning to office in January 2025.

That has come as the administration has revved up its mass deportation campaign across the country.

In August, immigration agents detained 50,925 people with the Department of Homeland Security hailing it as a new record for the “highest number of illegal aliens arrested in a single month”.

text:
TOPEKA — Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach slammed the U.S. Supreme Court majority that blocked President Donald Trump’s effort to unravel birthright citizenship, suggesting its decision “may not stand the test of time.”

Testifying before a U.S. House subcommittee Wednesday, Kobach encouraged Congress to pass a law that would cement Trump’s Aug. 6 executive order that targeted “birth tourism.” He made the urging hours before the executive order was blocked Wednesday by a federal judge.

Kobach was one of at least 25 state attorneys general who supported the government’s position in the U.S. Supreme Court case Trump vs. Barbara that upheld birthright citizenship, the constitutional guarantee that people born in the United States are United States citizens regardless of the parents’ citizenship.

He called the court’s June decision “weakly reasoned.”

But Kobach praised Justice Clarence Thomas’ 91-page dissent and said it was “truly bizarre” that the majority opinion rested “on this futile notion that you are attached to the lord of the soil.”

“I suggest that this decision may not stand the test of time,” Kobach said.

He added: “This one, because it is so weakly reasoned, is particularly vulnerable.”

Democrats on the U.S. House Judiciary’s subcommittee on the Constitution and Limited Government expressed frustration and confusion as to the purpose of the hearing, since the Supreme Court decision precludes Congress from altering birthright citizenship in the way Trump envisioned.

But Kobach encouraged Congress to consider narrowly tailoring a federal law to address “birth tourism,” or the act of entering a country while pregnant to secure U.S. citizenship for one’s child once born. Mimicking Trump’s Aug. 6 executive order in statute could pass muster, he said.

Then, a federal judge Wednesday blocked the Trump administration from enforcing the order that attempted to redefine birthright citizenship. U.S. District Judge Deborah Boardman referred to the Supreme Court’s June decision in her own decision, calling Trump’s order “almost certainly unconstitutional.”

Kobach appeared alongside Ken Cuccinelli, former acting deputy secretary of the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and former Virginia attorney general; Rosemary Jenks, policy director at the Immigration Accountability Project; and Jonathan Weinberg, Wayne State University law professor.

Kobach, Cuccinelli and Jenks shared the sentiment that the Supreme Court got its decision wrong.

Weinberg said it would be “chaos” to implement Trump’s vision for eradicating birthright citizenship. Applying it prospectively, as the president intended, would be chaotic on its own, Weinberg said, and he theorized Trumps theory would render every current U.S. citizen’s status questionable.

“We’d all have to look around and find out whether we’re citizens or not, trace our lineage back and see if our parents or our grandparents could pass the test set by President Trump’s executive order,” Weinberg said.

text:
An ICE officer is facing federal charges for allegedly lying to federal investigators about the shooting of a Venezuelan immigrant during immigration enforcement operations in Minneapolis earlier this year.

A federal grand jury on Wednesday returned an indictment charging the officer, Christian Castro, with making false statements to the FBI about the Jan. 14 shooting that left Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis with a gunshot wound in his leg, a source familiar with the investigation told NBC News.

A separate investigation into whether Castro should face a more serious civil rights charge in the shooting is ongoing, the source added.

The Associated Press first reported on Castro’s latest federal charges.

The federal charges come a week after Castro was released from jail in Texas despite an extradition warrant from Minnesota prosecutors seeking his transfer. He’s facing state charges in Minnesota accusing him of assault and false reporting of a crime related to the same shooting.

Federal authorities had initially accused Sosa-Celis and another man of beating an immigration officer with a broom handle and a snow shovel in a confrontation that preceded the shooting, but federal prosecutors dropped the charges they filed against the men after video evidence showed the ICE officers may have lied about the encounter.

Castro was arrested in May in the Minnesota case. He was held in custody in Brownsville, Texas, until his release last week after a judge and Gov. Greg Abbott refused to sign his extradition warrant — citing fraud investigations involving social services programs in Minnesota, which the Trump administration used to justify his immigration crackdown there.

Andrew Mahaleris, Abbott’s press secretary, told NBC News that “state law enforcement stands ready and willing to assist federal partners in facilitating Mr. Castro’s arrest if needed.”

Mahaleris added that “details of any federal indictment are best addressed to the U.S. Department of Justice.”

The Department of Homeland Security and the Minnesota Attorney General’s Office referred any queries to the DOJ.

An attorney for Castro did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

As news broke of Castro’s latest indictment, a federal prosecutor working on the case against Castro was fired, two sources familiar with the matter told NBC News.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Matthew Evans had told lawyers for Sosa-Celis that DOJ officials have blocked efforts to bring the more serious civil rights charge against Castro, ProPublica reported on Wednesday.

Evans did not immediately respond to a request for comment, and his DOJ email address returned an automated reply saying he was on leave.

description:
Illinois immigrants and leaders rejoice as Supreme Court affirms birthright citizenship, rejecting Trump’s order “The Supreme Court has spoken: Children in the certified class are ‘citizens at birth,’” Boardman, appointed by President Joe Biden, wrote in Wednesday’s ruling.
Birthright citizenship is guaranteed under current law for anyone who is born on U.S. soil, with a few exceptions.
The law stretches back to 1868, when the 14th Amendment was ratified in the aftermath of the Civil War.
But Trump has long wanted to end birthright citizenship, issuing a previous executive order declaring that children born to people who are in the United States illegally or temporarily are not American citizens.
“No matter what the guidance says, the 2026 Executive Order commands agencies to deny citizenship documents to several broad categories of children,” Boardman wrote.
text:
A federal judge has blocked President Donald Trump’s latest attempt to limit birthright citizenship, granting a preliminary injunction against an executive order that the administration said would target “birth tourism.”

U.S. District Judge Deborah L. Boardman in Maryland on Wednesday issued the injunction until a class-action lawsuit brought by immigrant families and advocacy groups is resolved.

Illinois immigrants and leaders rejoice as Supreme Court affirms birthright citizenship, rejecting Trump’s order

“The Supreme Court has spoken: Children in the certified class are ‘citizens at birth,’” Boardman, appointed by President Joe Biden, wrote in Wednesday’s ruling.

Birthright citizenship is guaranteed under current law for anyone who is born on U.S. soil, with a few exceptions. The law stretches back to 1868, when the 14th Amendment was ratified in the aftermath of the Civil War.

But Trump has long wanted to end birthright citizenship, issuing a previous executive order declaring that children born to people who are in the United States illegally or temporarily are not American citizens. The Supreme Court struck down that attempt in June.

In August, the president tried again with a narrowed executive order that appeared to restrict automatic citizenship for specific categories of people, including children born to adults with connections to foreign embassies or organizations or to anyone considered an “alien enemy” of the United States.

The order defined birth tourism as someone who enters the United States on a “nonimmigrant visa for the purpose of giving birth on American soil.” Birth tourism is already considered fraud and grounds to restrict a visa if someone seeks one specifically to obtain U.S. citizenship for a child.

The order sought to deny citizenship to children born to adults who “engaged in a commercial transaction to purchase or access birthright citizenship,” and some families said they feared their children could be denied citizenship simply because they purchased airfare to come to the U.S. and got pregnant after they arrived.

Families and organizations who sued over the birthright citizenship restrictions told the court that the executive branch has taken a broad view of who qualifies as an alien enemy, sometimes relying on speculation or misinformation to make that determination.

Others said they feared their children would be denied citizenship because a member of the parents’ extended family was connected to a gang in their home country, even though the parents were not gang members.

Uncertainty surrounding the order left them with confusion and fear, the families said.

They were joined in the lawsuit by We Are CASA, the Asylum Seeker Advocacy Project and the Institute for Constitutional Advocacy and Protection.

The administration’s attorneys argued that the request to block the order was premature and said the federal agencies tasked with enforcing it would use “appropriate measures” to do so, relying on official guidance that hasn’t been issued yet.

The judge rejected that argument.

“No matter what the guidance says, the 2026 Executive Order commands agencies to deny citizenship documents to several broad categories of children,” Boardman wrote.

“The White House must recognize it will not succeed in stripping children of their right to citizenship, evading binding court decisions or placing the president’s anti-immigrant agenda above the Constitution,” Shana Khader, legal director at We Are CASA, said in a prepared statement.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Associated Press reporter Valerie Gonzalez contributed.

text:
A US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer has been indicted on charges of lying to investigators about the events leading up to the shooting of a Venezuelan man during the Minneapolis immigration crackdown earlier this year, according to multiple reports.

A source told the Associated Press that Christian Castro, the officer accused of shooting Julio Sosa-Celis in the leg in January, has been charged by US federal prosecutors with making false statements to federal investigators. He had been previously charged in state court.

The ICE officer was released from jail last week after Texas’s Republican governor, Greg Abbott, refused to immediately sign an extradition warrant that would surrender him to the Minnesota authorities that had charged Castro separately with assault and false reporting of a crime related to the same shooting.

The Department of Justice was contacted for comment. No attorney is listed for Castro in the case brought by Minnesota, and it was not immediately clear if he had a lawyer to speak on his behalf.

The Trump administration launched what it called “Operation Metro Surge” in the Twin Cities in early December 2025. The operation sent thousands of federal agents to arrest immigrants at bus stops, grocery stores and churches, leading to ongoing protests and countless clashes between demonstrators and immigration enforcement officers. Castro was one of those thousands of agents who swarmed Minnesota.

Sosa-Celis was one of three people shot by federal immigration agents during the administration’s operations in Minnesota. Two US citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, were shot and killed by agents during the crackdown.

Robin Wolpert, the attorney representing Sosa-Celis, said in a statement: “Mr Castro has been indicted for making false statements. But he made them to cover up the fact that he shot my client through the door of an occupied house without a self-defense justification. Although the evidence strongly supports civil rights charges, the federal government has grossly undercharged this case. Mr Sosa Celis wants Mr Castro to be held fully accountable for his crimes.”

Federal authorities initially accused Sosa-Celis of attacking the agents with a shovel and broom. Kristi Noem, the then-secretary of homeland security, described the incident as “an attempted murder of federal law enforcement”.

Federal prosecutors charged Sosa-Celis with assaulting a federal agent, but the charges were dropped after the US attorney’s office cited evidence that was “materially inconsistent” with preliminary hearing testimony. Video released by the city of Minneapolis showed Sosa-Celis dropping the shovel and both men running inside as an agent fired in their direction.

In July, Minnesota prosecutors said they had obtained new evidence in the cases of Good and Pretti, as well as the shooting of Sosa-Celis.

Earlier this week, a federal prosecutor working on the case told lawyers for Sosa-Celis that justice department officials had blocked the prosecutor’s plans to bring civil rights charges against Castro, ProPublica reported.

Sanofi Vaccines U.S. Inc., a decision from the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of California that dismissed all claims against prescription drug manufacturers without leave to amend. The court found the plaintiff's claims were barred by California's two-year statute of limitations and preempted under federal law. In particular, the court held that the plaintiff failed to allege newly acquired evidence that would have permitted a labeling change through the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's (FDA) Changes Being Effected (CBE) process, resulting in dismissal of the failure-to-warn claims. The court also determined the negligent design claim was preempted because manufacturers cannot unilaterally alter a drug's design and rejected the implied warranty claim because California does not recognize such claims for prescription drugs. Eric highlights the decision as a notable example of a California federal court applying preemption principles at the motion-to-dismiss stage and declining to give a plaintiff another opportunity to replead deficient claims.

(CN) — Federal prosecutors charged a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer this week with lying to investigators about the events leading up to a January shooting in Minneapolis where the agent shot a Venezuelan man, reports say.

The federal charge remained sealed Thursday but comes one week after 52-year-old Christian Castro was released from a Texas jail after U.S. District Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr., a Donald Trump appointee, declined to extradite him to Minnesota to face state charges.

Reports indicate the indictment will be unsealed once Castro is in custody.

In May, Minnesota prosecutors charged Castro with four counts of assault and one count of falsely reporting a crime after the agent shot Julio Sosa-Celis, a Venezuelan national, during an attempted immigration arrest on Jan. 14.

Prosecutors say Castro fired his service weapon through the front door of an occupied North Minneapolis home, striking Sosa-Celis in the leg before the bullet lodged in a child’s bedroom wall.

The Justice Department originally filed federal charges against Sosa-Celis and Aljorna, but hastily dropped them in February after “newly discovered evidence” refuted what was laid out in a sworn affidavit.

Minnesota officials claim both men were “lawfully” in Minnesota at the time of the shooting and victims of a mistaken identity incident.

ICE told Courthouse News in April both officers involved were placed on administrative leave without pay pending an investigation into the potentially false statements — adding lying under oath is a serious federal offense.

Texas Rangers arrested Castro in May on the Minnesota charges, holding him in Brownsville, Texas, while Minnesota officials sought extradition. State leaders have shown concern that Castro may flee to Mexico now that he’s been released.

Texas Governor Greg Abbott, whom Minnesota sued to compel extradition of the agent, wrote in a July 31 letter he had “serious doubts that the prerequisites for extradition have been met” — later praising the judge’s decision to deny Minnesota’s request.

“The court was right to reject Governor Walz’s absurd claim,” Andrew Mahaleris, Abbott’s press secretary, told Courthouse News. “The Constitution requires deliberate consideration of extradition requests and tasks Governor Abbott to ‘decide, upon such evidence as he may deem satisfactory’ whether ’the person demanded is a fugitive.’ Today’s order rebuffs Minnesota’s efforts to conscript federal courts into commandeering the authority of Governor Abbott’s office.”

Following the ruling, Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison accused Abbott of turning Texas into a sanctuary state for violent criminals in a statement, reiterating that Castro will face judgment in Minnesota.

Castro is the second ICE agent Minnesota has charged for actions committed during Operation Metro Surge, but is the first known instance of an agent being charged by the Justice Department for the Minnesota operation.

In April, Minnesota prosecutors charged ICE agent Gregory Donnell Morgan Jr. with second-degree assault for pointing a gun at the heads of two civilians in a vehicle while driving illegally on the shoulder of a highway.

Morgan Jr. has yet to make a court appearance.

The Justice Department did not respond to an initial request for comment and clarification of Castro’s charges.

text:
ICE is plotting to award a multi-million-dollar contract to create a giant national voter database as part of President Donald Trump's scheme to federalize elections and sow distrust in the midterms, a new report reveals.

The Trump administration has spent more than a year trying to obtain states' complete, unredacted voter rolls—which contain sensitive voter data—despite widespread opposition from the states and the courts.

The administration claims it needs the data to fight voter fraud, though court records and independent audits have repeatedly found that electoral fraud is vanishingly rare.

Now, the Department of Homeland Security and ICE are preparing a contract to handle and securely deliver publicly available "voter registration files and voter history files" to help detect fraud, according to a document published last week.

Either data set could potentially include party affiliation, which experts say would likely violate U.S. voters' privacy rights, according to Wired, which first reported on the contract document.

The document says the contractor "shall not collect, process, or deliver party affiliation data… unless explicitly directed in writing by the contracting officer," suggesting an initial prohibition on collecting political party data could change.

The successful contractor will initially be given a list of states to mine. However, it must be able to eventually obtain data for "each federal election specified by the Government, including general, primary, runoff, and special federal elections" in all 50 states, plus the District of Columbia and U.S. territories. That means navigating a patchwork of data-collection procedures, because each state has its own rules for how public voter data is obtained.

The contract is expected to be worth $2 million to $5 million, according to an acquisition planning forecast.

DHS did not respond to the Daily Beast's request for comment.

The move comes six months after Trump signed an executive order giving DHS and the U.S. Postal Service extraordinary roles in election administration, despite the Constitution giving states the authority to administer elections.

The executive order instructs DHS to create state-specific lists of U.S. citizens eligible to vote and directs USPS to deliver mail-in ballots only to people whose names appear on the lists.

A federal judge has temporarily blocked the order, and it has been challenged in court.

In the meantime, DHS has assigned agents from Homeland Security Investigations, the branch of ICE that usually investigates human trafficking and drug smuggling, to gather evidence of Trump's voter fraud claims.

However, the agents have struggled to back up the administration's claims that hundreds of thousands of potential noncitizens were registered to vote in Nevada, California, New Jersey, and Pennsylvania, CNN reported this month.

The department has also threatened to withhold grant funding from states that refuse to turn over their voter rolls and expressed a willingness to send ICE agents to polling places—even though federal law prohibits armed agents at places where elections are held.

text:
An immigrant rights group sued the Trump administration Wednesday to block the U.S. Department of Homeland Security from using federal databases that it alleged are being used to target naturalized citizens who are eligible to vote.

The lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court in Washington on behalf of the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights, alleges that DHS and the U.S. Justice Department are interfering with fair elections by using inaccurate federal databases in an attempt to buttress allegations of voter fraud.

The federal government is engaging in an “attack on the freedom to vote,” Angelica Salas, the coalition’s executive director, said at a downtown Los Angeles news conference. “This is voter intimidation.”

The lawsuit — filed on behalf of the coalition by the UCLA Voting Rights Project — becomes part of a swirl of legal moves that states, including California, have taken to fend off federal actions that threaten to create confusion during the midterms.

“It's not an accident the federal government is trying to interfere with the right to vote. ... They believe they can intimidate naturalized U.S. citizens,” said Xavier Becerra, the Democratic nominee for California governor who is acting as a senior adviser to the voting project.

Part of a broader effort to search for noncitizens on voter rolls

The lawsuit alleges that the administration might be comparing voter rolls with undisclosed government databases. Those systems can include outdated information and be riddled with errors, it said, and could produce inaccurate results that disproportionately affect naturalized voters.

“Comparing government databases to try and arrive at a list of noncitizen registrants has been shown to result in erroneous data,” the lawsuit said. “Congress has never authorized such activities and in fact has ... prohibited invasion of voter privacy through government data matches in this way.”

The Trump administration has been targeting noncitizen voting to allege it could be a source of significant fraud during the midterm elections, even though actual voting by people who are not citizens is rare. He is pushing for the U.S. Postal Service to send mail ballots only to voters verified as U.S. citizens, and his Justice Department has sued to force the release of detailed voter data in 30 states and the District of Columbia, though it has not yet succeeded in those cases.

Asked to respond to the lawsuit, a DHS spokesperson said in an email: “The department accessed publicly available data from states’ voter rolls and cross-referenced them with known illegal aliens in our systems. It’s not rocket science; it’s an easy step to secure our elections.”

“DHS is laser focused on prosecuting and removing aliens who vote and preventing the dilution of the votes of U.S. citizens,” the statement added.

Judge had previously halted use of a federal citizenship database

In June, a federal judge ruled that a recently revamped version of a federal tool can no longer be used, which critics had referred to as an unlawful centralized federal database of voter information.

U.S. District Court Judge Sparkle L. Sooknanan sided with advocacy groups that argued the recent upgrades to the program, called Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, or SAVE, aggregated Americans’ sensitive personal data in a way that could result in voters being wrongly purged from voter rolls.

The lawsuit said it isn’t clear if the administration used that system to generate projections about noncitizens on voting rolls in the states or if other unknown datasets were involved.

By May, the Trump administration had run millions of voter registrations through government databases to determine their eligibility, a process that critics feared could purge valid voters from the rolls before the November elections. At least 67 million registrations, primarily from Republican-controlled states, have gone through a beefed-up verification program, or SAVE, at the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, and tens of thousands of those have been flagged as potential noncitizens or people who have died.

State officials push back against DHS noncitizen claims

Specifically, the lawsuit by the immigrant rights group asks the court to stop the administration from pursuing a review of California’s voter list and to rescind the letter sent to the state requesting voter information. It also asks the court to declare the administration’s actions unconstitutional.

Trump’s Department of Homeland Security is claiming without providing evidence that 250,000 noncitizens might be on the rolls in just four states, including 190,832 in California.

California’s secretary of state, Democrat Shirley Weber, said in response, “I have serious doubts about the reliability of your data and accuracy of your claims, since my office has not shared our statewide voter registration list with DHS or any other federal agency or official.”

According to the lawsuit, federal officials have not disclosed evidence supporting those figures.

text:
New data shows there have been nearly 5,000 ICE arrests in Kentucky since the beginning of the Trump administration, and a growing number are the direct result of 287(g) agreements between local law enforcement agencies and the U.S. Department of Homeland Security. There are now 55 local agencies in Kentucky with a 287(g) agreement, 50 of which are the problematic Task Force Model that deputizes local law enforcement officers to question, detain and arrest people for civil immigration violations while performing their regular duties.

Since last November, at least 257 ICE arrests in Kentucky were through the 287(g) program. In the first five days of August 2026 alone, there were 73 ICE arrests, 12 of which were through the 287(g) program.

Number of 287(g) agreements in Kentucky nearly doubled in past six months

The number of 287(g) partnerships between ICE and state and local law enforcement agencies has exploded in recent months, in part due to financial incentives in the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” (OBBBA) that went into effect October 1 of last year. In Kentucky, there are now 55 287(g) agreements across 53 agencies — up from 30 agreements across 24 different agencies back in February.

Task Force Model

The 287(g) Task Force Model empowers state or local law enforcement to make immigration arrests during routine policing and was discontinued from 2012 until January 2025 due to documented civil rights abuses. text:
A federal case is now closing in on an ICE officer already facing state charges after a January shooting in north Minneapolis that left a man wounded and raised questions about what investigators were first told.

ICE officer Christian Castro has been federally charged with making false statements to investigators about the shooting of Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis. The federal charges remain under seal, but sources said they stem from Castro’s account of the shooting.

Castro, 52, was already charged in Minnesota with four counts of second-degree assault and one count of falsely reporting a crime. Authorities allege he fired through the front door of a Minneapolis home during a Jan. 14 ICE operation, striking Sosa-Celis in the leg. Prosecutors said the bullet later lodged in a child’s bedroom wall.

Homeland Security officials initially said Sosa-Celis and another Venezuelan man, Alfredo Alejandro Aljorna, attacked an ICE officer with a snow shovel and broom handle after Sosa-Celis fled a traffic stop and ran into the home. Those federal assault charges were later dismissed after video and eyewitness accounts did not corroborate the agents’ version of events, prompting an investigation into whether two ICE agents lied under oath.

Castro was arrested in Texas in May on Minnesota’s warrant and held in a Brownsville detention center. He was released last week after a federal judge ruled he could not block the release or compel Texas Gov. Greg Abbott to approve Minnesota’s extradition request.

Under Texas law, Castro had to be released after 90 days in custody unless he was extradited. Minnesota officials have said they fear he could flee to Mexico.

The Justice Department is still considering whether to bring separate civil rights charges against Castro, according to a person familiar with the case.

text:
The Trump administration illegally deported a 19-year-old man to El Salvador this week in violation of court orders, attorneys said — the second time this year he’s been illegally removed from the country.

The man, referred to in Wednesday’s court filing only by the initials ELA, was in a Louisiana immigration detention facility this week expecting to undergo the second day of a psychological evaluation in preparation for his asylum proceedings, according to attorneys representing a class of young asylum seekers.

Instead, he was put on a flight to El Salvador, his attorneys said.

ELA was on a manifest for a flight that landed the afternoon of Sept. 1, attorneys for the government confirmed in a separate filing.

It’s the latest instance of the Department of Homeland Security — and the Trump administration more broadly — being accused of ignoring court orders. In a separate case last month, churches in Minneapolis accused US Immigration and Customs Enforcement of sending undercover agents into their spaces in violation of court orders.

Class attorneys said they intend to seek remedies for the government’s “profound malfeasance.” Judge Stephanie Gallagher ordered the government to answer a series of questions about the timeline of ELA’s removal, aiming to clarify who made the decision to take him out of the country and their plan for “promptly rectifying this error.”

In response, Justice Department attorneys handling the case said Thursday they only learned that ELA might have been removed when the class attorneys alerted them Sept. 1 via email. They later contacted Department of Homeland Security officials and confirmed ELA had been put on the flight out of the country.

DOJ’s filing says the defendants, which include DHS and US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, are “considering appropriate steps to rectify the communication errors that led to ELA’s erroneous removal” but doesn’t mention plans to bring ELA back, once again, to the US.

ELA had previously been “removed” to El Salvador earlier this year, but attorneys confirmed he was a class member and the government agreed to bring him back. He was returned to a Louisiana detention center last month.

Only after his evaluation was canceled did the class attorneys learn he’d been flown out of the country yet again — in violation of multiple court orders protecting class members, their filing states. Among other directives, Gallagher, of the US District Court for the District of Maryland, last year ordered the government not to remove certain class members from the country.

The underlying class action involves unaccompanied minors who sued in 2019 for the right to have their asylum applications heard while they remain in the US. A settlement agreement was entered in 2024, toward the end of the Biden administration, but last year Gallagher found the government violated that agreement by deporting at least one class member who had a pending asylum application.

Gallagher in July found the government in contempt of her orders and directed them to put a system in place to flag potential class members and potential wrongful deportations.

The plaintiff class is represented by Goodwin Procter LLP, Public Counsel, the National Immigration Project, and Kids in Need of Defense.

The case is JOP v. Dep’t of Homeland Security, D. Md., No. 8:19-cv-01944.

text:
A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer who was arrested in Texas earlier this year has been federally charged with lying to investigators about a January shooting in Minneapolis, according to The Associated Press.

ICE agent Christian Castro has been charged with making false statements to federal investigators, the AP reported Thursday, citing a person familiar with the investigation who wasn't authorized to publicly discuss the case.

The Texas Newsroom reached out to the U.S. Department of Justice and the U.S. Attorney's Office in Minnesota on Thursday for confirmation and additional information but didn't immediately receive a response.

Andrew Mahaleris, a spokesperson for Gov. Greg Abbott, referred questions about the reported charge to the Justice Department.

"State law enforcement stands ready and willing to assist federal partners in facilitating Mr. Castro's arrest if needed," Mahaleris said on Thursday.

The reported charge comes a week after Castro was released from a Texas jail amid an ongoing legal dispute between Minnesota and Texas Gov. Greg Abbott over whether Castro should be extradited to face separate state charges.

Minnesota prosecutors charged Castro in Maywith assault and falsely reporting a crime over the Jan. 14 shooting of Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis during an immigration enforcement operation in Minneapolis. Prosecutors say evidence contradicted Castro's accountthat Sosa-Celis and others attacked him before he opened fire. Sosa-Celis was shot in the leg.

Texas Rangers arrested Castro on May 29 after Minnesota issued a nationwide warrant. Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz later requested his extradition, but Texas Gov. Greg Abbott hasn't approved or denied the request and has questioned whether Castro qualifies as a fugitive.

Minnesota sued Abbott in an effort to force him to act, but a federal judge declined to intervene. Castro was released from jail last week after reaching Texas' 90-day detention limit for holding someone while awaiting extradition. The Minnesota charges and extradition request remain pending.

The AP also reported Thursday that a federal prosecutor who worked on the case was fired.

The prosecutor had previously told attorneys that Justice Department officials blocked an effort to pursue a more serious civil rights charge against Castro, according to previous reporting from ProPublica. But a person familiar with the investigation disputed that account and told the AP that the prosecutor is now under investigation for alleged obstruction of a grand jury investigation.

Editor’s note: This article was updated on Sept. 3 to include a statement from Texas Gov. Greg Abbott’s office.

text:
A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) official warned the agency about cutting corners in vetting officer candidates as the agency surged its hiring under the Trump administration.

The whistleblower report filed in August 2025 cited significant issues in how the department was reviewing its new hires, including making offers to candidates who had not yet passed background checks.

The filing asked the Office of Inspector General for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to investigate the matter.

The New York Times on Thursday was the first to report the whistleblower report, filed by a high-ranking career ICE veteran who retired in July.

In the report, which was also obtained by The Hill, the whistleblower flags “systemic breakdowns in vetting.”

“This unprecedented lowering of standards sacrifices proper risk mitigation for expediency, placing DHS at risk of infiltration and insider compromise,” they wrote.

The whistleblower filing accuses the agency of ignoring “derogatory” information collected on candidates and even pointed to political appointees, saying they were able “to ‘jump’ agencies and secure law enforcement credentials.”

The concerns from the whistleblower come after lawmakers and other DHS officials raised alarms about the speedy hiring process.

Those have taken new urgency since the July killing of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero who was shot in Maine by ICE officer David Brouillette, who has faced a string of complaints, including from an ex-wife who had accused him of abusive behavior.

The Office of Inspector General in August announced it would be reviewing ICE hiring and training.

The DHS said Tuesday it would not comment on matters regarding former personnel but defended its current hiring regime.

“The ICE Office of Professional Responsibility diligently applies the proper personnel vetting regulations, including guidelines for national security, and evaluates all available information for every applicant based on these factors,” the DHS said in a statement.

“Applicants may receive a Tentative Selection Letter following their initial application and interview. Additionally, individuals may receive an offer of temporary status to begin training pending a full background investigation.”

Another DHS whistleblower testified before Congress in February, telling lawmakers that in condensing the timeline for training for new ICE officers, the agency was cutting significant material.

Ryan Schwank, a former lawyer for ICE, said training for new officers had been pared down to the point where it is “deficient, defective and broken” during a forum organized by congressional Democrats about “constitutional violations and abuses” within ICE policies. He accused ICE leaders of shielding training shortcuts from the public.

“For the last five months, I watched ICE dismantle the training program, cutting 240 hours of vital classes from a 584 hour program, classes that teach the Constitution, our legal system, firearms training, the use of force, lawful arrests, proper detention and the limits of officers’ authority,” Schwank told lawmakers.

Tuesday’s statement from the DHS also referenced training standards.

“ICE training will now be extending to 72 days. The change, effective June 2, 2026, will apply to all new academy classes beginning July 1, 2026. All graduates of the previous academy curriculum will attend follow-on training at the Advanced Field Officer Training Program,” the agency said.

description:
Over and over, this Congress has proved itself incapable of exercising any restraint or even basic accountability over ICE and the Trump administration’s immigration agenda.
Its legacy has been to shovel unfathomable amounts of money at immigration enforcement – with predictably abusive results.
How the next Congress can rein in ICE Congress could be doing more — which means that the next Congress, the one set to be elected in November’s midterm elections, can also do more.
Potential checks on funding Congress can also attach requirements to any funds it appropriates.
Of course, the Trump administration may be tempted to simply disregard Congress’ instructions about how money may be spent.
text:
Last month, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) signed a contract for $16.7 million to buy 6,000 pairs of electric shock gloves for officers. The gloves apply a painful electric shock directly to the skin of someone the officer is already holding; in the notice published by ICE, they are called, euphemistically, “distraction and de-escalation devices.”

Sen. Susan Collins (R-ME), the chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, is responsible for sending ICE the money the agency is using to buy shock gloves — part of a combined $239.5 billion that Congress has handed to ICE and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) in a pair of massive no-strings-attached funding bills.

Collins has told reporters that she doesn’t agree with the way ICE is spending the money she sent them. She claimed that she got the agency to agree to spend $2 million on “deescalation” — which she apparently envisioned as training officers on how not to hurt people, rather than giving them gloves to hurt people more efficiently. But nothing in the text of the bill her committee passed actually made that a requirement. No matter how Collins may feel about ICE’s choices, she has steadfastly refused to do anything in her power, as the head of the relevant committee, to stop the agency from making them.

Over and over, this Congress has proved itself incapable of exercising any restraint or even basic accountability over ICE and the Trump administration’s immigration agenda. Its legacy has been to shovel unfathomable amounts of money at immigration enforcement – with predictably abusive results.

This Congress gave immigration enforcement a blank check

Twice, in 2025 (via the One Big Beautiful Bill Act) and 2026, Congress used the reconciliation process to appropriate a combined $239.5 billion to ICE and CBP. By using reconciliation, leadership in both chambers was able to pass the bills by a simple majority (rather than the Senate needing to meet a 60-vote threshold to pass a cloture vote, as is usually the case with appropriations or other legislation). With no need for bipartisan negotiations, Congress gave President Trump and his administration much of what it asked for — as a more-or-less blank check.

Unsurprisingly, ICE is now acting with no restraints — budgetary, legal, or moral.

ICE has adopted policies that contradict years of constitutional and statutory interpretation, such as claiming that suspected unauthorized immigrants have no Fourth Amendment right against unreasonable search and seizure. When its agents have killed people on the street for standing up for their immigrant neighbors, the Trump Department of Justice has not only failed to prosecute them itself but has frequently refused to cooperate with state and local criminal investigations. Whether or not every member of Congress who voted for reconciliation is happy about these outcomes, they have failed to prevent them and are failing now to hold the administration accountable.

When Susan Collins, for example, is pressed about the abuses ICE has engaged in with the money she sent them, she likes to tout the $2 million for de-escalation and a $20 million earmark in a funding bill from earlier this year to buy body cameras for immigration agents. But ICE has now released its policy over when to make bodycam footage public — and it says it will only do so when it’s in the agency’s own “best interest.” In other words, the body camera appropriation will most likely only be used to produce administration propaganda rather than holding officers accountable for what they do in the field.

How the next Congress can rein in ICE

Congress could be doing more — which means that the next Congress, the one set to be elected in November’s midterm elections, can also do more. Congressional leaders could be the only meaningful alternative to the diminished influence of the courts in providing a check on the Trump administration’s abuses when it comes to immigration enforcement and the management of our legal immigration system.

Without a majority of members in both chambers willing to keep writing blank checks to the Trump administration, Congress will be unable to use the reconciliation process to throw even more money at ICE and CBP. However, even without additional funds, the funding bonanza of the last two years could still be enough to keep both agencies running a mass-deportation operation through Trump’s term. But if enough members of the new Congress feel that the money already appropriated for Trump’s deportation machine is too much, they have the power to implement restrictions on how funding is used or theoretically “claw back” any funds still unallocated from the 2025 and 2026 bills — although whether the leadership of the next Congress would be willing to take that step will probably depend on the election results themselves (and how they are interpreted).

The difference a new Congress could make, in other words, is the difference between continued expansion of mass-deportation operations and forcing the Trump administration to scale back its existing plans and working to hold executive branch officials accountable for some for the most horrific things we’ve witnessed in the nearly two years since Trump regained office.

Potential checks on funding

Congress can also attach requirements to any funds it appropriates. It can, for example, prohibit funds from being used to purchase additional enforcement and surveillance equipment intended for use in the field. It can insist that immigration agents adhere to higher legal standards and bar agents from being put into the field before background checks are even complete. It can prohibit the administration from enforcing its radical interpretations of the Constitution to deprive noncitizens of their Fourth Amendment and due process rights.

Of course, the Trump administration may be tempted to simply disregard Congress’ instructions about how money may be spent. However, the majority party in Congress has the power to conduct oversight of the executive branch. It could set up new special committees with additional staff to investigate past and present abuses, and subpoena administration officials to testify under oath. A Congress that cared about oversight could, for example, subpoena officials at both ICE and DOJ for an investigation into the agencies’ responses to the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis last winter, and the killings of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Texas and Johan Sebastian Guerrero in Maine this summer.

Potential legislative solutions from the next Congress

In theory, of course, Congress could also pass legislation to fix the underlying problems with the system that have forced so many communities into constant fear of deportation. That is unlikely to happen under this president — the second Trump administration has shown even less willingness to negotiate with Congress than the first one did, and it is unlikely that an opposition party would get veto-proof supermajorities in both houses.

However, if an opposition party controls even one chamber of Congress, it has the power to bring bills to the floor that advance an alternative vision on immigration — making it clear to the American public that there are solutions to repair the current immigration system that don’t require letting ICE run amok in their communities. The American Dream and Promise Act, for example — a bill which would offer permanent status to people who have lost TPS or are in danger of losing DACA — is currently the subject of a discharge petition in the House of Representatives, because current House leadership refuses to bring it to the floor despite bipartisan support. If leadership changes, bills like the American Dream and Promise Act can actually be debated on the floor of Congress.

Additionally, under divided government, it will be harder for Congress to pass laws that further curtail immigrants’ rights — such as H.R. 2, which would (among many other things) mandate long-term detention of immigrant families and put any adult relative of an unaccompanied child into deportation proceedings. Congressional Republicans have been split over some provisions of the bill, and it is unlikely to come to the floor this year — but with a bigger majority (or even just a more unified one), it could be reintroduced and brought to the floor in the next Congress.

This Congress has all but abdicated its authority to keep the executive branch in check. But if the next Congress is made up of people who take that duty more seriously, both immigrant communities and the American system of government will be far better off.

text:
Washington — Federal prosecutors have charged an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer who shot a Venezuelan immigrant in Minnesota with making false statements to investigators about the incident, multiple sources familiar with the matter tell CBS News.

The officer, Christian Castro, was charged in May by local prosecutors, but Texas Gov. Greg Abbott has refused to extradite him, prompting a legal battle. He was released from a Texas jail last week.

A federal grand jury returned a six-count indictment Wednesday, but the case has not yet been unsealed, the sources said. Law enforcement officers are currently trying to locate Castro, one source said. The Associated Press first reported Castro had been charged by federal prosecutors.

The shooting at the center of the case occurred during the Trump administration's federal immigration surge in Minnesota, just a week after agents killed Renee Good.

In January, two men, Alfredo Alejandro Aljorna and Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis, were hit with federal charges of forcibly assaulting, resisting or impeding federal officers. Sosa-Celis, a Venezuelan immigrant, had been shot by an ICE agent in the leg.

Accounts of the interaction that led to the shooting shifted in the immediate aftermath. The Department of Homeland Security initially said Sosa-Celis fled a traffic stop, crashed the vehicle and fled on foot. DHS said two men emerged from a nearby apartment and attacked the agent with a broom handle and snow shovel. Sosa-Celis allegedly broke free and also started striking the officer, DHS said, adding that an officer then fired a "defensive shot to defend his life."

But an FBI affidavit filed to support the charges against the two men said Aljorna was the one who fled, and that Sosa-Celis initially struck Castro with a broomstick while the agent tried to arrest Aljorna. And cellphone video shared by a Democratic state lawmaker showed a woman telling 911 that her husband was chased by ICE agents before he reached his home, and was shot in front of his family.

The charges against Aljorna and Sosa-Celis soon unraveled. Federal prosecutors dropped the case in February, citing "newly discovered evidence" that was "materially inconsistent" with the allegations against them. The charges were dismissed with prejudice, meaning they could not be reintroduced.

Todd Lyons, then the acting head of ICE, said that video evidence contradicted statements made under oath by Castro and a second officer. Both were placed on leave. Castro has since been suspended without pay.

"Video evidence has revealed that sworn testimony provided by two separate officers appears to have made untruthful statements," Lyons said at the time. "Both officers have been immediately placed on administrative leave pending the completion of a thorough internal investigation. Lying under oath is a serious federal offense."

text:
MOBILE, Ala.—A judge in Alabama granted Leo Garcia Venegas, an American citizen and construction worker, a first-round victory in his federal lawsuit aimed at stopping unconstitutional raids and detentions by immigration officers. Judge Jeffrey Beaverstock rejected the government’s attempt to dismiss the case after a hearing in Mobile. Leo is represented by the Institute for Justice (IJ).

“The court’s decision was an important first step,” said IJ Senior Attorney Jared McClain. “We know the Department of Homeland Security thinks it can raid construction sites without a warrant, round up all the workers, and refuse to credit their government-issued IDs. Now we’ll have the chance to prove these violations of the Fourth Amendment.”

Leo, a construction worker in Baldwin County, Alabama, has been detained three times since the spring of 2025 despite presenting an Alabama-issued REAL ID each time. In May and June of last year, Leo was detained by officers who entered his private job sites without warrants. Both times, officers refused to believe Leo was a citizen or recognize his REAL ID as proof of legal status. Earlier this year, officers followed Leo home and confronted him in his driveway. Even though Leo was trying to show officers his REAL ID, he was ripped from his car, tackled to the ground, handcuffed, shackled, and locked in the back of a car.

“Americans cannot be stopped and held by law enforcement when they are doing nothing wrong,” said Leo. “I’m glad my case is moving forward, and I hope it can make lasting change.”

At a May hearing to consider the motion for a preliminary injunction, a DHS official testified that agents do not treat REAL ID as reliable proof of legal presence. But DHS certifies and administers the READ ID Act and then-Secretary Kristi Noem spent considerable time last year encouraging people to get their REAL ID.

The DHS also testified that agents treat construction sites as “open fields” that they can enter without a reason or warrant. Leo’s second detention, inside of a mostly-constructed home, shows just how far the government’s theory reaches.

The court has yet to rule on Leo’s request for a temporary injunction against the raids and detentions. IJ attorneys reiterated at yesterday’s hearing that the government has not disavowed using unconstitutional tactics in Alabama.

text:
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent has been federally charged with lying about the events leading up to his shooting of a Venezuelan immigrant in the leg earlier this year, according to multiple people familiar with the matter.

The charges against ICE officer Christian Castro are not yet publicly available, but a person familiar with the matter told CNN that he is facing several counts of making false statements.

This is the first time the Justice Department has charged an officer for conduct that occurred on-duty during highly publicized immigration operations nationwide. Local prosecutors in Minnesota had already charged Castro with second-degree assault and making a false report earlier this year.

CNN attempted to reach a lawyer for Castro for comment.

The Justice Department is still considering whether to bring civil rights charges against Castro, one of the sources said.

Castro also faces the separate state charges in Minnesota. He was released from a Texas jail last week after the governor there declined to immediately approve his extradition to Minnesota.

Federal prosecutors initially charged 24-year-old Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis, whom Castro shot, and another man with attacking an ICE officer with a snow shovel and broom stick. But those charges were dropped after investigators reviewed surveillance footage and other material from the incident that conflicted with Castro’s account.

Castro and a second agent were soon placed on administrative leave. Federal prosecutors told the judge overseeing the case against Sosa-Celis that the agents had made “false statements” under oath, and former ICE Director Todd Lyons said later the Justice Department was investigating the “untruthful statements.”

Prosecutors in Minnesota, who charged Castro in May, allege that he shot Sosa-Celis in the back of the leg through the door of Sosa-Celis’ apartment.

The shooting occurred after ICE officers had attempted to pull over a truck belonging to an undocumented immigrant named Joffre Barrera, the state alleged. Sosa-Celis’ cousin and DoorDash driver, Alfredo Alejandro Aljorna, was behind the wheel and drove off from the officers, they said.

According to Sosa-Celis, Aljorna ran from the truck and was tackled steps away from Sosa-Celis’ apartment by an ICE agent. Sosa-Celis called for Aljorna to get inside and, once both cousins were behind the door, a shot rang out, Sosa-Celis said.

“I closed the door and as I was locking it, I heard the shot, and that’s when I realized I had been shot in the leg,” Sosa-Celis told CNN at the time during a Facebook livestream from a hospital.

This story has been updated with additional information.

text:
The Trump administration is proposing that parents applying for U.S. passports for their children provide proof of their own citizenship or immigration status, a new requirement tied to President Donald Trump’s latest effort to restrict birthright citizenship.

Draft State Department guidance would require parents or legal guardians to submit documents showing their status. U.S. citizens could provide a valid passport or birth certificate, while noncitizens could be asked for records such as an I-94 arrival document or permanent resident card. The proposed requirement has not been finalized.

The information would be used to determine whether a child is entitled to U.S. citizenship under an executive order Trump signed Aug. 6. Current State Department procedures already require parents or guardians to present valid identification when applying for a child’s passport, along with proof of the child’s U.S. citizenship and the parent-child relationship. The proposed guidance would go a step further by requiring parents to separately document their own citizenship or immigration status.

The proposal comes as the executive order behind the planned passport checks faces a federal court challenge.

U.S. District Judge Deborah Boardman in Maryland on Wednesday issued a preliminary injunction barring federal agencies from enforcing the order against children covered by an existing class action challenging Trump’s birthright citizenship policies.

Boardman prohibited agencies including the State Department, Department of Homeland Security and Social Security Administration from denying or interfering with the citizenship of children covered by the case.

She allowed federal agencies to continue preparing guidance to implement the policy. The State Department can continue developing the proposed passport procedures while enforcement remains blocked for children protected by the injunction.

Trump’s Aug. 6 directive was issued after the Supreme Court rejected his broader attempt to restrict birthright citizenship in June.

The new order directs federal agencies not to recognize citizenship for certain U.S.-born children when neither parent is a U.S. citizen and a parent falls within specified categories. Those include some foreign government employees, people classified as alien enemies, and parents accused of fraud or commercial arrangements intended to obtain citizenship for a child.

The administration has described the policy in part as an effort to target “birth tourism,” in which foreign nationals travel to the United States to give birth so their children receive U.S. citizenship.

Trump’s previous order went further. It would have denied citizenship to children born in the United States when neither parent was a U.S. citizen or lawful permanent resident, and the mother was unlawfully or temporarily in the country.

The Supreme Court rejected that policy 6-3 in Trump v. Barbara on June 30, ruling that children born in the United States to undocumented immigrants and temporary visitors are citizens at birth under the Fourteenth Amendment.

Boardman cited that decision in blocking enforcement of Trump’s latest directive against the class of children before her court, finding that the Supreme Court had already established their citizenship.

Justice Department lawyers argued that the new challenge was premature because federal agencies had not yet published instructions explaining how the Aug. 6 order would be carried out. Boardman rejected that argument.

text:
On Saturday, Aug. 8, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) raided, without a warrant, a group of construction workers at a private residence in Cornwall. Migrant Justice, a human rights organization for Vermont immigrant farmworkers, sent out a “rapid response alert” to which I and others responded. Although several workers had escaped the raid, two workers had already been detained by the time many of us arrived. The workers were then sent to Massachusetts, away from their families and support systems.

Those workers who remained were traumatized, but received fast and thorough support and protection by neighbors, community members and Migrant Justice organizers. Later, a GoFundMe page was set up to help with legal fees for workers with future court dates.

Such an outpouring of local support was impressive and was received with gratitude from the victims of this unlawful raid. But let’s not assume that this will be the last ICE incident in our local community. Across the country, immigration enforcement agents continue to patrol, surveil, detain, arrest, disappear, injure and kill civilians. Agents are denying people their constitutional rights by searching vehicles and homes without consent or the appropriate warrants.

You can help fight against this injustice by supporting Migrant Justice Vermont at migrantjustice.net, or become involved in your local Indivisible organization, the closest one being Indivisible Middlebury. Contact by email at: indivisiblemiddlebury@gmail.com.

But the person familiar with the investigation disputed the prosecutor’s characterization, saying the probe is continuing and no final decision has been made about whether additional charges will be brought.
