text:
FAIR shows President’s authority is more than adequate

WASHINGTON—Today, the Federation for American Immigration Reform (FAIR) filed a brief in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit defending President Trump’s imposition of a hundred-thousand-dollar fee for H-1B visas. The state of California and other states have sued over the fee, claiming the President’s proclamation establishing it has no good reason, and therefore is arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act. As FAIR shows in its brief, however, under the law, the President, not courts, is the sole judge of whether his restrictions on the entry of aliens are in the national interest.

In 1952, Congress passed a statute that gives the President the power to suspend the entry of any class of aliens, or all aliens, into the country, or put any restrictions on their entry, if he deems such suspensions or restrictions in the national interest. As FAIR shows in its brief, the Supreme Court has firmly upheld this law, and its deference to the President’s decisions, in prior cases. It is also clear, FAIR shows, that the President, not being an agency, is not subject to the Administrative Procedure Act, and neither are his subordinates when they carry out a proclamation under this 1952 statute.

FAIR also demonstrates in its brief that the H-1B program has been used by companies not to obtain needed foreign “talent,” but to replace American tech workers with cheaper workers from abroad. The hundred-thousand-dollar fee will discourage this abuse, while still allowing companies to hire any foreign workers they really need for high-end jobs. Thus, even if the court could second-guess Trump’s determination that his fee is in the national interest, the court should agree that it is.

“American tech workers are far and away the best in the world, and they have been hit hard by the H-1B program for decades,” said Christopher J. Hajec, deputy general counsel of FAIR. “We are pleased the President has taken this step to put their interests and the interests of the nation first, and hope the court recognizes that it has no legal or factual basis to override his judgment.”

The case is California v. Mullin, No. 26-1699 (First Circuit).

text:
The Chinese government is pressing for answers after a Chinese man died hours after being taken into custody by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in a U.S. territory.

Lianyong Wei, 51, died Aug. 23 at a hospital in the Northern Mariana Islands, ICE announced Tuesday. Wei was arrested Aug. 21 by the Northern Mariana Islands Department of Public Safety on criminal charges stemming from an alleged assault on a family of five at their home, according to ICE. He was taken into ICE custody the next day pending removal proceedings.

ICE said a guard at the lockup in Saipan found Wei unresponsive during routine morning checks. He was taken to a hospital emergency room, where he was pronounced dead after “life-sustaining interventions were initiated,” the agency said, noting that the cause of his death is under investigation.

Wei entered the U.S. territory in February 2019 and was authorized to stay for two weeks, according to ICE. U.S. authorities began removal proceedings in July, and Wei’s next hearing had been scheduled for this month.

The Chinese Consulate General in Los Angeles said it had been notified of Wei’s death.

“We have expressed serious concerns to the relevant U.S. authorities over this incident and required a timely and thorough investigation into the cause of Mr. Wei’s death, notification of the findings, measures to prevent any recurrence of similar incidents, and assistance to the family of the deceased in handling the aftermath,” the consulate said in a statement.

Wei is at least the fifth Chinese national who has died in the custody of ICE or the U.S. Border Patrol since March 2025, according to tracking by the Associated Press. Two of the first four deaths have been ruled suicides and the other two were the result of medical complications.

At least 57 ICE detainees have died since President Trump returned to office in January 2025, a death rate that has alarmed public health experts, advocates for immigrants and the Mexican government.

ICE hasn’t said whether Wei received the medical intake screening, which the agency promises to detainees within their first 12 hours in custody. Medical experts say a thorough screening is critical to preventing deaths.

It’s unclear why it took ICE more than a week to acknowledge Wei’s death, which was announced by authorities in the Northern Mariana Islands on Aug. 24. ICE has said it aims to issue a news release on detainee deaths within two business days.

The lockup in Saipan has held an average of 18 ICE detainees on any given day this year, according to ICE data. Roughly 50,000 people live in the Northern Mariana Islands.

“Following this incident, the Department is reviewing relevant procedures and will implement any necessary corrective actions to strengthen prevention and response measures,” Northern Mariana Islands Corrections Commissioner Anthony Torres said in a statement.

text:
A Kendall man who gained the trust of one of the hemisphere’s most notorious anti-Castro militants and lived in South Florida for years has been deported because he was actually spying for Havana, immigration officials said Wednesday.

Fernando Armando Valdes Perez, a 61-year-old permanent U.S. resident, was arrested at Miami International Airport on July 10. Immigration and Customs Enforcement deported him to Guatemala on Aug. 7. He did not reveal that he was a “Cuban intelligence asset” or his links to Havana when he applied for lawful permanent residency in the United States, the agency said.

Valdes even became part of the circle of trust of controversial Cuban militant Luis Posada Carriles, who died of throat cancer in 2018 in Hollywood. Cuba accused Posada of being behind the bombing of a Cubana Airlines jet in 1976 while it was in flight from Barbados to Havana, killing all 73 aboard.

Valdes was so close to Posada, he was quoted in the late militant’s obituary for the Miami Herald. “I spoke with him yesterday and felt he was strong,” Valdes, who had also organized Posada’s last birthday party, said at the time of his death.

He “remained in close proximity to other well-known Cuban and Cuban American figures in South Florida until his arrest,” ICE said in a statement.

Investigators determined Valdes had been involved in intelligence gathering for Cuba since at least the mid-1990s, ICE said. However, it’s unclear Wednesday which federal agency made that determination.

READ MORE: Anti-Castro militant Posada Carriles is dead at 90

Valdes was also a Guatemalan citizen, ICE said. A Herald public records search found a Kendall address for Valdes, as well as a hunting and fishing license. He bought the town house in June 2016, according to the property records, and was identified as a married man in the warranty deed.

There is also a cigar company, Sr Valdes Cigars, registered to the same address, according to Florida’s Division of Corporations. The company’s social media says it’s headquartered in Guatemala and Miami.

The deportation is part of the targeting of South Florida residents linked to espionage or human rights violations in Cuba and Venezuela under President Donald Trump. It comes a week after the federal government announced the deportation of Rafael José Quero Silva, a former Venezuelan official accused of torturing protestors who lived in Miramar.

READ MORE: ICE detains in Miami sister of head of GAESA, the military firm that runs Cuba’s economy

ICE arrested 57-year-old Daniel Morejon Garcia, whom the U.S. says was a member of Cuba’s Interior Ministry, in April 2025. It also revoked the green card and arrested Adys Lastra Morera, a Miami woman whose sister runs the military firm in control of the Cuban economy, in May.

READ MORE: ICE deports Venezuelan official accused of torture. He lived in South Florida

“Individuals who conceal ties to foreign intelligence services and exploit our immigration system pose a serious threat to the integrity of that system and to our national security,” said Miami ICE chief Matthew Elliston.

ICE, U.S. Customs and Border Protection and the Miami office of the FBI were involved in Valdes’ arrest.

CHICAGO (WLS) -- Robot dogs, already used by some law enforcement across the country, could soon be deployed by ICE agents on the streets. They can be used to search for suspects in dangerous situations, assess explosives, and more, costing taxpayers $2 million, according to federal contract records.

"I think people will be concerned if you send robotic dogs with facial recognition capabilities into crowds and have them scanning across crowds in the hopes of locating people who whose immigration status has expired. I think there's going to be real concerns about using robotic dogs to chase down suspects and to employ lethal or non-lethal force," said former Homeland Security Acting Undersecretary for Intelligence and ABC News contributor John Cohen.

He told the ABC7 I-Team as new technologies are implemented, there must be accountability.

ABC7 Chicago is now streaming 24/7. Click here to watch

"The challenge facing ICE right now is that people just don't trust them. ICE specifically has to be very transparent and clear how they're going to use these new technologies," Cohen said.

A nearly $17 million government contract was just awarded for more than 6,000 electrified gloves for ICE. Those can be used to incapacitate targets.

"The question for ICE is: Are they going to use those gloves appropriately, or are they going to use them in a manner which is you know amounts to excessive force?" asks Cohen.

Since the start of the second Trump administration DHS has also made heavy investments in advanced social media monitoring tools. As the I-Team previously reported, Chicagoan Marimar Martinez was surveilled online by immigration agents, her social media post tagged as a threat days before she was shot by a federal agent in Chicago.

"When I was at the Department of Homeland Security. We needed to be able to tie that that online activity to threat-related or criminal activity. We had to be able to articulate those connections. Hopefully, that's also what the those are also the rules that ICE is operating under," Cohen told the I-Team.

DHS released statements saying robotic dogs will increase the ability to respond to incidents involving dangerous difficult-to-access areas and improve officer safety. Regarding the electrified gloves, they say officers are highly trained in de-escalation tactics and receive ongoing use of force training.

DHS issued the following statements:

"Robotic dogs will be used for border and infrastructure security.

"This capability helps improve officer safety, supports informed operational decision-making, and enhances DHS's ability to respond to incidents involving dangerous, confined, unstable, or difficult-to-access areas."

"ICE is constantly assessing the needs of our officers in the field to ensure they have the tools and equipment necessary to safely arrest and remove criminal illegal aliens from our country. Every decision is made with careful consideration and appropriately reviewed to ensure that any technology ICE utilizes is consistent with all applicable law enforcement policies and standards.

"Our officers are highly trained in de-escalation tactics and regularly receive ongoing use of force training. The latest ICE use of force policy is available here.

"Under President Trump and Secretary Mullin, ICE is targeting the worst of the worst. Since Day One, ICE law enforcement has been delivering on President Trump's promise to the American people to arrest and deport criminal illegal aliens including murderers, rapists, pedophiles, gang members, and terrorists. Nearly 70% of ICE arrests are of dangerous illegal aliens charged or convicted of a crime in the U.S. While ICE law enforcement works to remove these public safety threats from American communities, they're also facing a 1,300% increase in assaults, a 3,300% increase in vehicle attacks, and an 8,000% increase in death threats."

text:
It's been a month since the Trump administration severed a multimillion-dollar contract with aid organizations representing unaccompanied children in immigration court.

Congress created the federal legal aid program almost two decades ago and has directed funds to it every year. But on July 31, the roughly $200 million annual contract to do that work came to an end.

Roxana Avila-Cimpeanu is the deputy director of the Florence Immigrant and Refugee Rights Project, which represents about 600 children in Arizona. She says her group will continue to represent those children, but without the government funding, they can’t take on new cases.

“What we’ve seen since spring of this year is an increase in the number of hearings children have to go to and an acceleration of the cases to get to that deportation point,” she said.

There are roughly 1,800 children in government custody nationwide, Avila-Cimpeanu says that includes dozens in Arizona — many of whom have not been given the Know Your Rights presentation required under federal trafficking laws. The legal aid groups estimate roughly 20,000 children have immigration cases pending in the U.S.

Avila-Cimpeanu says direct representation services for children have lapsed since the contract ended July 31, despite an agreement the Trump administration says it has with a group called the U.S. Commission for Refugees and Immigrants (USCRI).

“They have been showing up to some detained children’s dockets and just showing up on camera, rarely speaking and sometimes not showing up at all. SO even some of the non-representational services such as Friend of Court are not being complied with,” she said during a press conference Tuesday.

During a hearing last month in Arizona, a 1-year-old boy and his mother appeared in court alone without a lawyer. Avila-Cimpeanu said although a USCRI representative was present, they did not speak up in any capacity.

The baby and his mother, a 17-year-old who is also an unaccompanied minor, appeared in court again at the end of August and were given an extension to file an asylum claim or face deportation.

USCRI did not respond to questions about that case or its role in immigration cases for unaccompanied children more broadly, and directed KJZZ to U.S. Health and Human Services, the government agency in charge of immigrant children.

As NPR reports, last month the Trump administration awarded a six-month, no-bid contract to Our Rescue, a Utah-based group headed by a former ICE officer, though it’s not clear whether the group has attorneys on staff, or whether they’ll provide direct representation.

text:
A Springfield, Ohio, man is suing seven U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers for alleged harassment.

The lawsuit, filed by the ACLU of Ohio, claims the officers violated the man's First Amendment right to film them in public.

The man alleges ICE agents chased his car, drove by his home and shouted his name at him in traffic.

A Springfield, Ohio, man is suing seven federal immigration officers, alleging a "terrifying campaign of retaliatory harassment" against him for recording their activities in his hometown.

Sean Moorman's federal lawsuit, filed by the ACLU of Ohio, says officers of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement violated his First Amendment right to act as an ICE observer.

Moorman, a 41-year-old electrical engineer, has been the target of "flagrant and escalating" ICE harassment since he began volunteering as an ICE observer on Aug. 19, the suit says.

"Sean's case is a particularly egregious example of a group of ICE agents, acting individually and in concert with each other .. to torment him, to terrify him," American Civil Liberties Union attorney David J. Carey said.

ICE did not immediately respond to a request for comment about Moorman's allegations.

Reached by phone, Moorman declined to comment, referring questions to the ACLU.

Harassment includes chase at Cracker Barrel, drive by home

Moorman's suit says ICE agents harassed him during five of the six times he photographed or filmed them in Springfield between Aug. 19 and Sept. 1. He alleges that agents:

Chased his car through the parking lot of a local Cracker Barrel restaurant and adjacent properties for 10 to 15 minutes. Three ICE vehicles blocked and surrounded his car repeatedly, taking photos of his license plate, the suit says.

Drove to his home in a three-car caravan, taking photos of the home and cars belonging to Moorman and his wife. His wife armed herself with a baseball bat as they arrived, according to the suit.

Pulled up next to him in traffic, blasted a loud horn, rolled down a window and repeatedly screamed "Sean Moorman! Sean Moorman!"

Moorman chose to exercise his First Amendment right to record law enforcement officers in public places out of "concern for his neighbors" and a "determination to see that their suffering is witnessed by others."

In doing so, he joined a loose coalition of observers across the country documenting ICE activity.

ICE has been particularly active in Springfield since the federal government stripped Haitians in the United States of temporary protected status on July 27. An estimated 12,000 to 15,000 Haitians live in Springfield and other Clark County communities.

ACLU seeking 'John Doe' agent names

The ACLU filed Moorman's suit against "John Doe No. 1-7." The suit lists each of their vehicles – six of the seven were driving black SUVs, with one using a black pickup – and the license plate information for each vehicle.

The ACLU did not identify the agents because, "We don't know who they are," Carey said.

Agent identities are a "guarded secret," he said, with most agents wearing masks, sunglasses and hats. "None of them wear name tags," he said.

The ACLU contacted the U.S. Department of Justice, by email, to request the names but did not get a reply, Carey said. Lawyers also filed a motion as part of the lawsuit, seeking the names, he said.

Suit seeks restraining order, expungement of Moorman info

The lawsuit seeks a restraining order to bar ICE agents from "taking further threatening, intimidating and retaliatory action" against Moorman. Agents should not follow Moorman, block his car, photograph him, travel to his home, or shout or honk at him, the lawsuit says.

The suit also asks the government to expunge any records it has collected about Moorman or his family.

text:
INDIANAPOLIS — André Carson has submitted an official Congressional inquiry to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security regarding a purported increase in ICE activity observed in Indianapolis. Carson, a member of the U.S. House of Representatives, is the elected delegate for large portions of Indianapolis.

Carson launched his inquiry by sending a letter to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin and acting U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement Director David Venturella.

In the letter, Carson laid out numerous key areas he’d like DHS to provide a report on by Sept. 9, including:

The name of the operation ICE is conducting in Indianapolis

The geographic scope of ICE’s Indiana operations

The anticipated duration of ICE’s operation in Indianapolis

The objective of ICE’s operation in Indianapolis

Details on the statutory authorization ICE has to carry out operations in Indianapolis

The number of ICE operatives stationed in Indianapolis

The number of state, local or federal law enforcement officers working on ICE’s operation in Indianapolis

The number of people detained by ICE in Marion County from Jan. 1, 2026, to Sept. 1, 2026

Operational guidelines governing how agents identify individuals for questioning, surveillance or arrest

Information on whether or not ICE is receiving assistance with its operation from the Indianapolis Metropolitan Police Department, Marion County Sheriff’s Office and Indiana State Police

Number of Indiana agencies that have agreements in place to assist ICE operations

Number of complaints filed about use-of-force incidents, injuries and vehicle collisions caused by ICE activity

Operational plans, arrest records, internal communications, bodycam videos, dashcam videos and dispatch records related to ICE’s work in Indianapolis

Carson’s letter requested more information than that outlined in the list above. The letter can be read in its entirety here.

Carson has also asked DHS for more information on where individuals detained by ICE in Indianapolis are housed. MCSO told FOX59/CBS4 that, as of Wednesday morning, only one ICE detainee was being housed at the county jail.

A spokesperson for MCSO indicated that fewer than 10 ICE detainees are typically housed at the county jail at any given time. It is currently unclear if ICE is taking individuals detained in Indianapolis to other facilities.

A report published by the New York Times earlier this year suggests ICE had launched a $38 billion initiative to turn dozens of warehouses in the U.S. into detention facilities. Indianapolis was among the cities the agency was reportedly aiming to build one of these detention centers in.

The State of Indiana reached an agreement with DHS last year to expand Miami Correctional Facility and house ICE detainees. The expansion was nicknamed the “Speedway Slammer.”

A February report from the Indianapolis Business Journal also suggested that ICE was vying to lease office space in Carmel. It is currently unclear if ICE’s plans to build a holding facility in Indianapolis or lease office space in Carmel materialized.

Another report from FOX59/CBS4 suggests that at least 31 Indiana law enforcement agencies had brokered 287(g) agreements to help ICE with immigration enforcement.

Carson sent his letter to DHS less than 24 hours after FOX59/CBS4 published a report on ICE ramping up activity in Indianapolis. Video obtained by FOX59/CBS4 showed ICE agents chasing a person across several lanes of traffic on Post Road near Interstate 70.

More video depicted agents detaining a person at a gas station near 38th Street and German Church Road. A witness told FOX59/CBS4 that masked agents rolled up to the gas station in a black Nissan Pathfinder prior to detaining the individual.

Carson addressed the I-70 chase video in his letter, asking DHS to detail the policies it uses to govern pursuits near active roadways, intersections, schools, childcare centers, places of worship and medical facilities.”

FOX59/CBS4 asked DHS for information about its Indianapolis operations. The organization did not provide many specifics about its work in response, only emphasizing that ICE agents uphold immigration laws 24 hours a day, 365 days a year.

DHS also provided information on several people it has detained in Indiana. The agency labeled the detainees as the “worst of the worst,” suggesting they had been convicted of kidnapping, rape and assault.

A release from the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of Indiana also highlighted that a Homeland Security task force secured sentences for 11 “illegal aliens” between March and August. The full release is available here.

text:
INDIANAPOLIS (WRTV) — An Indianapolis woman was searching for answers Wednesday after federal immigration agents detained her brother Tuesday morning at an east-side job site.

Following reports of immigration activity throughout central Indiana Tuesday and Wednesday, Circle City Broadcasting contacted U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to ask whether the agency was conducting a sweep.

An ICE spokesperson declined to confirm or deny the reports, saying in a statement: “ICE agents uphold our nation's immigration laws in all 50 states, seven days a week, 24 hours a day.”

Dulce Morales said agents detained her brother, 27-year-old Milo Morales, while he worked at a job site Tuesday morning.

She tracked his phone’s last location to a parking lot off 38th Street on the far-east side. By the time she arrived, Dulce said he was gone. However, she said she approached a black SUV with tinted windows at the scene and met a man who identified himself as an ICE officer.

“He was wearing this vest, a green vest that says 'Police - ICE'. He did identify himself as ICE as well,” Dulce said. “I asked, 'Have you detained anyone? And he said, 'Yeah, I've detained plenty of illegal immigrants.'”

Dulce said the agent told her they had taken several people into custody at the job site where her brother worked, but would not confirm if her brother was among them.

Hours later, Dulce received a call from Milo, who confirmed agents had detained him. She says that because Milo has no criminal record, he has no assigned federal identification number — often called an “A-number” — meaning the family cannot track where he will be transferred.

“We just want to know if he's OK. We want to make sure he comes home. He's a hard-working man ... and I mean he's going to be a dad soon, too. We just want him to come home,” Dulce said.

As a member of the military, Dulce says she feels disheartened to see what is happening to her brother.

“Working as a servicemember and finding out that they're taking your family left and right, it's really hard to keep showing up,” Dulce said.

Her family says no one has heard from Milo since 2:30 p.m. Tuesday at the east-side location. They remain unsure of his whereabouts or when the government will assign him a tracking number.

text:
WASHINGTON – A federal judge blocked the Trump administration from carrying out for now the president’s latest effort to impose new limits on automatic birthright citizenship after losing an earlier legal fight before the U.S. Supreme Court.

In an order on Wednesday, a U.S. judge in Maryland ruled that President Donald Trump’s August executive order expanding the categories of noncitizen parents whose children would be ineligible for citizenship is likely unlawful as applied to a nationwide class of families whose legal status was already at issue in earlier court fights. The new exclusions would include anyone who took part in a “commercial transaction to ensure” they give birth in the U.S.

The fresh setback to Trump’s hard-line immigration agenda puts the fight over birthright citizenship on a path to return to the Supreme Court. The U.S. Justice Department next could ask a federal appeals court to lift the district judge’s order and allow officials to move ahead with implementing the president’s plan while the legal fights continue to play out.

The Supreme Court “already decided that the children in the class are citizens at birth,” U.S. District Judge Deborah Boardman wrote in her decision imposing a preliminary injunction. “This court must, once again, preliminarily enjoin enforcement of the president’s most recent attempt to strip the right to citizenship from them.”

Boardman wrote that the administration had advanced a “distorted interpretation” of the high court ruling striking down Trump’s original executive order to restrict birthright citizenship. She said the president’s latest action would deny the status to members of the class she’d already certified covering children of noncitizen parents who aren’t legally in the U.S. or who are in the country on temporary visas.

Spokespeople for the White House and the Justice Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Shana Khader, legal director at We Are CASA, one of the groups that brought the case in Maryland, said in a statement that “the White House must recognize it will not succeed in stripping children of their right to citizenship, evading binding court decisions or placing the president’s anti-immigrant agenda above the Constitution.”

The Supreme Court struck down Trump’s original executive order curbing birthright citizenship in June, a major rebuke from a conservative-majority bench that has largely sided with the administration over the past year and a half.

“Citizenship, then and now, was the right to have rights – to freely participate in our political community,” Chief Justice John Roberts wrote for the majority at the time. “The framers of the Fourteenth Amendment extended that promise to every free-born person in this land. We keep that promise today.”

Trump vowed to look for other ways to limit citizenship. He signed two executive orders in early August targeting so-called “birth tourism,” a term that the administration has used to refer to noncitizens coming to the U.S. with the goal of obtaining citizenship for their children.

One of those orders, which isn’t central to the latest legal challenges, directs U.S. agencies to adopt rules or update existing policies to let immigration authorities deny or revoke visas, or otherwise turn away foreign nationals coming to the U.S. “for the purpose of giving birth on American soil.”

The second order addresses the categories of individuals whose children aren’t eligible for citizenship. In addition to the “commercial transaction” exclusion, the order calls for new carve-outs for babies born in the U.S. to a broader class of foreign nationals who work for their governments or other international organizations in the U.S., are members of designated terrorist groups or who engage in fraud.

Opponents accused the administration of ignoring the Supreme Court’s ruling and once again trying to rewrite the Constitution’s guarantee of citizenship to nearly every person born on U.S. soil. They filed challenges to the president’s new policy as part of earlier class action lawsuits in New Hampshire and Maryland contesting Trump’s original, now-defunct citizenship restrictions.

The judge in New Hampshire is also weighing a request to block Trump from carrying out key parts of the new executive order.

The Justice Department argued the challengers lacked legal standing because they hadn’t shown the existing class actions covered families affected by the president’s latest action. The government also claimed the challenges were premature because federal agencies haven’t taken steps yet to implement Trump’s order yet and the Supreme Court didn’t definitively rule out the possibility of expanding exceptions to birthright citizenship.

The case is Casa Inc. v. Trump, 25-cv-201, U.S. District Court, District of Maryland (Greenbelt).

text:
A federal judge has temporarily blocked parts of a new Virginia law designed to limit cooperation between local law enforcement agencies and federal immigration authorities.

However, the ruling allows existing agreements between local agencies and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to remain in place while the legal challenge moves forward.

At the center of the dispute is the federal government’s 287(g) program, which allows ICE to train and authorize local law enforcement officers to perform certain federal immigration duties.

Virginia’s new law took effect Sept. 1, 2026, and sought to impose restrictions on roughly a dozen conditions connected to immigration-related operations. Under the law, agencies that failed to make the required changes could have had their 287(g) agreements declared void.

U.S. District Judge Robert Payne ruled that Virginia cannot enforce those restrictions while the case proceeds through the courts.

SEE ALSO: 19-year-old found dead, staff member hurt in Virginia elementary school shooting

Former U.S. Attorney John Fishwick said the issue ultimately comes down to the relationship between state and federal law.

“Well, I think in this situation where lawmakers have run afoul of the Constitution is they've passed a law that interferes with the federal law,” Fishwick said. “State law cannot interfere or be inconsistent with federal law. Federal law will always take priority.”

Fishwick said Judge Payne’s ruling reflects that principle.

“What the judge is saying here is you've interfered with federal law. You've gone beyond what you can do. And therefore I'm not going to let you enforce this new law,” he said.

Several sheriff’s offices in the region currently participate in the 287(g) program with ICE, including the Amherst County Sheriff’s Office.

Amherst County Sheriff Jimmy Ayers said he was not surprised by the judge’s decision. He also said he was grateful for the work ICE has done in the community to help keep residents safe.

The legal fight, however, is not over.

Attorney General Jay Jones’ office plans to appeal Judge Payne’s ruling. Fishwick believes the case could eventually make its way to the U.S. Supreme Court.

For now, existing agreements between local law enforcement agencies and ICE can continue as the courts determine whether Virginia’s new restrictions can legally be enforced.

text:
The loved ones of a Pittsburgh mother arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents one week ago said they feel helpless as they track her movement from facility to facility on the detainee website.

Katherine Sanchez-Bonilla, known by her friends as "Kathi," was detained by ICE agents while traveling to Rochester, New York, business owner Nicole Velez told KDKA-TV after speaking with Sanchez-Bonilla's husband. Velez said ICE has moved Sanchez-Bonilla three or four times to different detention centers. She's currently in El Paso, Texas, awaiting a hearing.

But Velez said the arrest abruptly disrupted Sanchez-Bonilla's pending asylum case.

"She's an incredibly ethical and conscientious person, so she always talked about doing things the right way," Velez said. "I know she had been working with a lawyer for many years trying to get her papers in line. She had a Real ID, she was paying taxes and managing multiple jobs and going to school."

Nour Chammas, Sanchez-Bonilla's Ohio-based immigration attorney, told KDKA-TV that cases like this are increasingly common. New federal data shows ICE arrested an average of more than 1,580 people a day in July, a new high under the current administration. Only about 4% of those taken into custody in July had previous convictions for violent crimes, according to the federal data.

Chammas said Sanchez-Bonilla has no criminal record and has a pending asylum application after leaving Costa Rica.

"People that do have a fear of being in their country due to some form of persecution, or some form of harm that they've either suffered, or that they fear suffering in the future, they have that availability that they can come here and they can file for asylum, which the law allows," Chammas said.

Since Sanchez-Bonilla is in immigration detention, Chammas said her asylum case will move forward in immigration court.

"If you have a pending asylum application, even though you do have authorization to remain in the U.S. while the application is pending, they can still pick you up, because technically you don't have status," Chammas said. "So ICE can pick you up and put you through immigration court proceedings, and then you would have to pursue your asylum claim in court."

In a statement to CBS News, the Department of Homeland Security said ICE enforces the law as written, adding, "What makes someone a target for immigration enforcement is whether or not they are illegally in the U.S.— full stop."

Chammas said Sanchez-Bonilla is expected to go before an immigration judge on Thursday. Her 12-year-old son is with family in another city.

text:
Private debt collectors are helping the Trump administration impose massive civil penalties on immigrants accused of being in the country illegally as a way to encourage them to leave on their own.

The ongoing Scripps News ICE Inc. investigation found the companies are able to profit off both the tax dollars awarded to them in government contracts and in steep fees they are tacking onto fines that few migrants are actually paying.

A $1.8 MILLION FINE

About a year ago, a piece of paper arrived in the mail that would splinter 22-year-old Eric Amaya’s family.

It was a notice from the Department of Homeland Security saying Amaya’s father owed $1.8 million for ignoring a deportation order from 1996.

Federal law allows DHS to fine immigrants $998 each day they stay beyond an order to leave the country for a maximum of 5 years, equaling $1.8 million.

“It’s insane, right?” Amaya said. “No one can pay that amount of money.”

RELATED STORY | ICE awards contracts for companies to visit homes of child immigrants

The surprise notice led Amaya's father, who Scripps News agreed not to identify by name, to believe he had become a target for deportation. He decided to move to his native El Salvador rather than risk arrest and prolonged detention by ICE, his son said, leaving his family behind in Maryland.

“He said to us that if he stayed, he felt like he was going to die,” Amaya said. “My father suffers from a heart condition. He suffers from heart failure.”

The ongoing Scripps News ICE Inc. Investigation has exposed repeated complaints about inadequate health care among detainees at for-profit immigration lockups around the nation.

THREE COMPANIES AWARDED CONTRACTS

The Amaya family’s experience is part of a much broader effort by the Trump administration to collect immigration fines allowed under federal law but rarely enforced during previous administrations. After Eric’s father left the country, the notices kept coming.

Scripps News has learned that Customs and Border Protection has awarded at least three contracts to private collection agencies to pursue immigration-related debts. One of the contracts went to Continental Service Group or ConServe, a debt collector that sent a bill to Eric’s father.

“They know that they can outsource some of the immigration enforcement functions to private markets in order to scale the scope of the intimidation tactics,” said Charles Moore, a staff attorney at Public Justice, a group representing immigrants in court who are fighting the fees. “If they get private companies who are incentivized by making money from the government, they can target even more people.”

In addition to the hundreds of thousands of tax dollars in the contracts, CBP is also allowing these private debt collectors to charge huge fees.

The bill Amaya’s father received from ConServe added more than $500,000 in administrative costs and more than $60,000 in penalties, according to the bill reviewed by Scripps News.

“You just chalk it up to the rest of the numbers you’ve seen as, okay, it’s ridiculous,” Amaya said.

IN CASE YOU MISSED IT || ICE locking up more parents and children at for-profit detention center in Texas

CBP confirmed ConServe gets to keep at least some of those fees.

“The private collection agency retains funds for administrative costs, interest, and late payment penalty,” an unnamed CBP spokesman said. “CBP supports efforts to ensure that individuals meet their legal obligations, including payment of immigration-related fines and other debts owed to the U.S. government.”

CBP says those who voluntarily leave the country using the CBP Home app will have their fines forgiven.

“Not only are the fines forgiven, but illegal aliens receive a free flight home and an exit bonus of $2,600,” a CBP spokesperson said in a statement.

But the government plans to seek payments from more than 66,000 immigrants who have already left the U.S. and are now in Guatemala, Honduras or Mexico, according to contracting documents.

Few immigrants appear to be paying the fines, according to data provided by DHS.

As of July 16, ICE had issued more than 103,000 civil fines totaling more than $84 billion but had collected only $1.2 million.

THE IMPACT

Moore said CBP is sending bill collectors after some immigrants who should not be subject to civil penalties, a claim the government disputes.

“Those are folks who are seeking lawful status, who have orders of supervision with ICE or have some other reason to remain in the country,” Moore said. “The point of all of this is to scare people.”

That fear comes across in declarations filed by immigrants in federal court.

“I live in panic due to this fine,” wrote one person going by the initials A.S. “The fines have made me afraid to live. I am trying to be like a ghost so nobody sees me.”

In another declaration, an immigrant says “It is so much money and I can never pay that. I could not sleep or eat or concentrate at work. My oldest child, who is 10 years old ... she cried and stopped going to school for a week and did not want to eat.”

MORE FROM OUR ICE INC. INVESTIGATION | 'Mom, what did we do?' Parents recall weeks in ICE family detention

CBP issued a fine for more than $900,000 to a woman who came to the U.S. from Guatemala to escape domestic violence.

“I’ve had days when I don’t sleep, thinking that at any moment they can knock on my door, arrest, me, leave my children alone,” she said in an interview with Scripps News. “I couldn’t pay off all that money even with my whole life.”

Eric Amaya graduated this year from college with his bachelor's degree. In a video taken of the ceremony, he is seen on the stage telling his parents he loves them.

His father had already been back in El Salvador for months. With fees, he owes $2.4 million.

“The hope is that my father comes back one day,” Amaya said. “My father was the primary breadwinner of the family. His income alone paid for the mortgage and the food. I find myself having to work more and to face all of those charges by myself now.

“I find my journey being more difficult without my father here,” he said.

A 10-year-old Honduran immigrant who came into the United States as an unaccompanied minor carries her baby cousin on April 25, 2021, after reuniting with extended family in Sellersburg, Indiana. (Photo by John Moore/Getty Images)WASHINGTON— More than 20,000 unaccompanied immigrant youth remain at risk of losing their legal representation, one month after the Trump administration ended a federal contract with an organization that provided legal services to migrant children, advocates and attorneys said Tuesday.

Most of those children who initially had attorneys through funding provided by Congress still have access to lawyers because the Acacia Center for Justice and its network of 100 nonprofits have continued to represent the children without pay.

But unaccompanied immigrant children who have been placed into federal custody since the contract expired after July 31 are likely without attorneys as they appear in immigration court, said Michael Lukens, the executive director of the Amica Center for Justice, which is part of Acacia’s network.

“Many nonprofits are not taking on new cases,” Lukens said. “We have not closed any case of a child we were already representing — that obviously is not a sustainable model. We feel both ethically and morally obligated to continue as long as we can.”

Without a lawyer, fewer than 10% of immigrant children win the right to remain in the United States while their cases go through immigration court.

Roxana Avila-Cimpeanu, the deputy director of Florence Immigrant & Refugee Rights Project, said the organization is currently representing 600 children, and cannot represent several children who have recently arrived in Arizona, where the group is based.

“This is something that is happening across the nation,” she said.

Contract expired

The Department of Health and Human Services’ Office of Refugee Resettlement, which cares for unaccompanied children, let a contract with Acacia for legal services expire July 31.

The center has a network of roughly 100 organizations it works with that provide legal aid and representation to immigrant children across the country in their immigration court appearances. Acacia has provided legal services for unaccompanied minors for decades.

Additionally, since December, HHS has not released $65 million that Congress appropriated for legal representation of unaccompanied children in immigration cases, meaning that Acacia and its legal providers have gone for months without reimbursement.

Leaders of Acacia have said the funds were withheld because attorneys refused to hand over to the Trump administration sensitive case data from the unaccompanied children, such as medical records and the types of legal relief the minors are seeking.

After the contract expired in July, HHS initially awarded a single $150 million contract to a small Texas firm, headed by a former Trump official who served during the first administration. But the law firm, which only had two attorneys that specialized in immigration law and primarily focused on regulatory work, backed out of the contract.

New contract

In August, the Trump administration awarded a $158 million no-bid contract to a controversial anti-human-trafficking organization called Our Rescue, a Utah-based company that was previously known as Operation Underground Railroad.

The group was founded by Tim Ballard, who presented it as an “anti-sex-trafficking” organization. The group was featured in the conservative film “Sound of Freedom” that promoted several QAnon conspiracy theories.

After the movie’s release, Ballard was accused of sexual misconduct by several employees and has since left the organization.

Our Rescue now specializes in working with law enforcement related to child trafficking cases and is run by a former Department of Homeland Security official, Derek Benner. It’s unclear if there are any immigration attorneys on staff and the group does not have a history of providing legal representation to unaccompanied immigrant youth in immigration court.

Our Rescue did not respond to States Newsroom’s request for comment.

Bilal Askaryar, the communications director for Acacia, said Our Rescue has not been in contact with Acacia to transfer over case information.

Avila-Cimpeanu said she has also not heard from Our Rescue to start the transition process for representing the children’s cases.

“I think it’s very unclear what their role is,” she said.

The Our Rescue contract will run from Aug. 7 until Feb. 6, 2027, according to its award.

The Office of Refugee Resettlement did not respond to States Newsroom’s request for comment.

text:
Local police reported hundreds of migrants to immigration enforcement in the past few years. Forty-three agencies in Michigan made at least one referral to federal agents, including six Michigan State Police units and local departments across metro Detroit and elsewhere in the state.

Use our searchable database to see where law enforcement reported people to immigration authorities, or see a full list below.

Here are some more key points from our investigation.

Michigan police made at least 388 immigration referrals

Law enforcement agencies across the state recorded at least 388 encounters involving federal immigration agencies between 2021-26.

This is the most comprehensive available count of police calls to immigration authorities in Michigan in recent years, but it almost certainly undercounts the full scale of the practice. We don’t know whether every person in the dataset was ultimately detained or deported.

Local police collaboration intensified after Trump returned to office

Cooperation between local police and federal immigration authorities isn’t new. But the number of recorded arrests and referrals surged after Donald Trump’s second inauguration in 2025.

Some agencies made dozens of referrals in 2025 and 2026, compared with few or none from 2021 through 2024.

Many encounters began with minor violations or no violation

People were reported to immigration authorities after encounters involving issues like a cracked windshield, jaywalking, a broken-down car or simply an officer's “suspicion.”

In some cases, officers appeared to use a minor violation as a pretext to investigate a person’s immigration status, according to experts who reviewed records for this story.

Police advocates offered a different interpretation, saying officers were generally responding to violations they observed and were not necessarily acting with an ulterior motive.

Some chiefs warn immigration arrests damage trust

Experts and some police chiefs say these interactions can discourage migrants and others from reporting crimes or cooperating with investigations.

Melvindale Police Chief Chris Egan said he wants residents to “know that law enforcement isn’t going to automatically lead to immigration or deportation,” because that trust is necessary to “encourage crime reporting and cooperation for investigations.”

title: At Two Restaurants' Parking Lots in Peekskill, ICE Detains Two Men; Owners Caught Off Guard
description:
A separate photo shared with the Herald showed ICE agents detaining the same man in shackles in the parking lot of the Taormina Trattoria restaurant.
Anthony Pietrosanti, owner of Taormina Trattoria, told the Herald he learned on Facebook that ICE had detained an individual in his parking lot.
“Apparently, they pulled someone over in a van that was going to work and they just put his car, his van in our parking lot and took him away,” Pietrosanti said.
It’s just by coincidence they used our parking lot as a facility to put that person’s van off the street.
The officer stopped his vehicle to investigate what was occurring and learned ICE agents detained two individuals.
text:
Two men were detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) on Welcher Avenue at two separate restaurant parking lots in the City of Peekskill on Tuesday, Sept. 1 around 8:30 a.m.

Video of the incident shared with the Peekskill Herald showed several ICE agents escorting the two men, one wearing handcuffs and the other in shackles, into unmarked vehicles in the parking lot of NY Firehouse Grille.

A separate photo shared with the Herald showed ICE agents detaining the same man in shackles in the parking lot of the Taormina Trattoria restaurant.

ICE did not respond to a request for comment on why the men were detained.

Anthony Pietrosanti, owner of Taormina Trattoria, told the Herald he learned on Facebook that ICE had detained an individual in his parking lot. He said it occurred around 8:40 a.m. to 9 a.m. on Sept. 1, prior to the restaurant’s opening at noon.

“Apparently, they pulled someone over in a van that was going to work and they just put his car, his van in our parking lot and took him away,” Pietrosanti said. “It had nothing to do with us. It’s just by coincidence they used our parking lot as a facility to put that person’s van off the street. That’s the way it seemed to me.”

Alex Asadoorian, owner of NY Firehouse Grille at 63 Welcher Ave., told the Herald in a phone call he did not know ICE was using his parking lot until an employee alerted him early that morning. He said he was informed by agents at the scene that one man was a “woman beater” and was threatening people with knives, and a second man was allegedly trying to run ICE over with a vehicle.

Peekskill Chief of Police Adam Renwick told the Herald in an email that ICE agents did not provide the Peekskill Police Department with the names, charges, or any details on the individuals detained.

Renwick said that around 8:30 a.m. an officer was on patrol in the area of Hudson Avenue and South Street when they observed two unmarked federal vehicles conducting a traffic stop. The officer stopped his vehicle to investigate what was occurring and learned ICE agents detained two individuals. Renwick said the officer did not participate in the apprehension and resumed his patrol responsibilities after learning what had occurred.

Pietrosanti said he did not know much about the incident other than that ICE came and went.

“They said there was two vehicles and they blocked the guy off,” Pietrosanti said. “So they targeted him. They knew where he was and one person stopped one way and one blocked the other way, so that’s not by coincidence, that’s for sure.”

After being alerted to unoccupied unmarked cars in his parking lot, Asadoorian said he rushed to his restaurant around 8:30 a.m., where he found the two cars parked prior to the restaurant’s opening at around 10:30 a.m. He said normally he would leave the cars alone but that they were parked incorrectly, making half the lot unusable for the day.

As a result, he called the Peekskill Police Department to inform them he was going to get the cars towed. The department then told him the vehicles were coming back as unregistered vehicles.

“At that point, my neighbor called me right next door and she said, ‘I know whose cars those are,’” Asadoorian said. “I said, ‘Well, please let me know because I’m about to have them towed.’ She goes, ‘Good, have them towed.’ I said, ‘Well, are they yours?’ She goes, ‘No, they’re ICE.’ So I said, ‘Well, I would rather not start an argument with a federal agency and tow their vehicles so I don’t think that I’m going to do that.’”

Asadoorian said he did not want to start a fight with a federal agency that could possibly bother him, his business or staff, and decided to wait for them to return.

“They did show back up and I said, ‘I’m assuming that these are your cars, gentlemen,’” he said. “And they said, ‘Yes. Peekskill police did call and inform us that you were calling about these vehicles.’ I said, ‘Yeah. They’re parked incorrectly’ and this is what I tell every single person: ‘If you’re going to park here, just do it correctly so we can utilize the lot the best that we can.’”

Asadoorian said he called his landscaper, asking them to install bollards and ropes or chains to avoid the situation in the future. He said he changed his policy a couple months ago to allow everyone to use his lot since he shares a lot of customers with the deli across the street, but is now reconsidering that practice.

“I have opened it up to everyone at this point, but now I’m obviously questioning that decision because I don’t want stings operating out of here when we’re not here,” Asadoorian said.

After video of the incident was posted online that showed him shaking an agent’s hand, Asadoorian said there were several online rumors alleging that he was conspiring with ICE by letting them use the parking lot.

“I had that conversation [about parking] and I did shake their hand. And I said, ‘Thank you for understanding about the lot’ and that was that,” Asadoorian said. “I shake everyone’s hands. I’m a community person and obviously I appreciate law enforcement as a whole. I offer 10 percent off to firefighters and police officers in general, but as far as coordinating or anything of that nature, that’s obviously just made up.”

Asadoorian described the activity at his parking lot as a “confusing,” “scary situation,” “very crazy morning” and overall terrible situation.

“I was trying to make the best decision for the business and my staff, obviously,” Asadoorian said. “Overall, I don’t want any issues with ICE. I don’t want issues with the community. I just want to sell burgers and make a living.”

In a similar incident on Aug. 15, ICE used the Peekskill City Police Department’s lower parking lot for about 12 minutes on the same day a man was detained. Chief Renwick told the public on Aug. 17 the department was reviewing why federal agents used the police department’s lot.

Renwick told the Herald on Sept. 1 that he is still awaiting a call back from ICE for further explanation.

[Editor’s Note > The above story was updated at 10:30 a.m. on Wednesday, Sept. 2, to clarify certain facts about the incident].

title: Visa Processing Pause Declared Unlawful
description:
On August 21, 2026, a federal judge in Manhattan struck down the Trump administration’s decision to suspend the issuance of immigrant visas to people from 75 countries.
Background The State Department (DOS) announced the pause on January 14, 2026, and took effect on January 21.
The policy prevented consular officers from granting immigrant visas to applicants from 75 countries.
The pause applied only to immigrant visas and never included the nonimmigrant categories such as H-1B, F-1, and B1/B2.
Judge Vargas stated that the policy constituted a “direct abrogation” of the statutory scheme that Congress established for the adjudication of visas.
text:
On August 21, 2026, a federal judge in Manhattan struck down the Trump administration’s decision to suspend the issuance of immigrant visas to people from 75 countries. The judge stated that the policy exceeded the legal powers of the Secretary of State and violated the prohibition in federal immigration law against discrimination based on nationality. U.S. District Judge Jeannette Vargas delivered the verdict in the case Catholic Legal Immigration Network, Inc. v. Rubio, filed in the Southern District of New York.

Background

The State Department (DOS) announced the pause on January 14, 2026, and took effect on January 21. The policy prevented consular officers from granting immigrant visas to applicants from 75 countries. The rationale for this is concerns that people from those countries were more likely to become a ‘public charge’, that is, to depend on government assistance once they had arrived in the United States. The pause applied only to immigrant visas and never included the nonimmigrant categories such as H-1B, F-1, and B1/B2.

Details of the Ruling

Judge Vargas identified two flaws in the policy. The first was that it went beyond the powers Congress has granted to the Secretary of State, since the INA mandates that each applicant be assessed individually rather than rejecting entire nationalities as a group. The second was that the INA prohibits discrimination against people on the grounds of their national origin in immigrant visa processing, and therefore a general ban applied is in direct conflict with that provision. Judge Vargas stated that the policy constituted a “direct abrogation” of the statutory scheme that Congress established for the adjudication of visas.

Public charge remains a valid reason for refusing a visa; the court merely stipulated that it should be assessed on a case by case basis rather than being assumed from a person’s passport.

Impact

The State Department can no longer rely on the 75 country list to withhold visas. Consular officers must evaluate applicants individually again, as the law has always required. Families and employers with pending cases in the affected countries should see their applications resume movement, though it’s worth watching whether the administration appeals or tries a narrower version of the same policy later on.

title: Jury splits verdict for Charlotte protesters charged in ICE confrontation
description:
In an immigration protest case that hinged on bystander video and federal agents’ conduct and credibility, a federal jury sided mostly with the U.S. government Wednesday.
In a split verdict, the jury found two protesters arrested outside a south Charlotte Department of Homeland Security office last fall guilty as charged on all three petty offenses.
The jury found both Morrow and Stanley guilty of petty misdemeanor charges of obstructing federal property, disrupting government officials’ duties and failing to comply with officials’ orders.

In the analogy, ICE officers were their parents.
text:
In an immigration protest case that hinged on bystander video and federal agents’ conduct and credibility, a federal jury sided mostly with the U.S. government Wednesday. In a split verdict, the jury found two protesters arrested outside a south Charlotte Department of Homeland Security office last fall guilty as charged on all three petty offenses. They found one guilty and the other innocent of assaulting and impeding officers.

Heather Morrow, a 45-year-old Charlotte-Mecklenburg Schools bus driver and unsuccessful county commissioner candidate, is guilty of misdemeanor assaulting or impeding officials when she touched an officer who was trying to arrest William Donovan Stanley outside a building that housed DHS and Immigration and Customs Enforcement offices on Nov. 16.

Stanley, a 25-year-old local college student, faced the same misdemeanor assault charge but was found not guilty by the nine-woman, three-man jury after a three-day trial in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of North Carolina Wednesday afternoon.

The jury found both Morrow and Stanley guilty of petty misdemeanor charges of obstructing federal property, disrupting government officials’ duties and failing to comply with officials’ orders. Those charges are each punishable by a maximum of a month in prison or a $5,000 fine.

Morrow’s misdemeanor assault charge is punishable by a maximum of a year in prison or a $100,000 fine.

In a statement, a spokesperson for Russ Ferguson’s U.S. Attorney’s Office said: “The facts supported a conviction in this case, which is why we brought and tried the case, and ultimately the jury unanimously agreed. There was a clear violation of the law here, and we always seek to pursue justice where the law is violated.”

Other U.S. citizens charged with assaulting officials during that weeklong operation in November saw their charges dropped soon after they were arrested. Morrow, too, saw her original felony assault case dropped when cellphone video contradicted ICE officers’ claims that she tried to jump on a federal agent’s back.

Morrow and Stanley will be sentenced at a later date set by the court. Both have been out on bond for 10 months, and Morrow has continued to work as a CMS bus driver as this case — the last one tied to “Operation Charlotte’s Web” — played out in the uptown federal court.

On Wednesday, Morrow was in uniform and prepared to go to work in the afternoon. But the clock ticked past normal dismissal times as the jury deliberated for four hours — until 3:47 p.m.

ICE in uptown Charlotte court

While they faced the same charges, the case against Morrow was built on allegations that she blocked the office entrance at 6130 Tyvola Centre Drive with her car and body and touched an officer who was trying to arrest Stanley. Federal prosecutors said Stanley did not follow orders to move out of the entrance and instead put his hands on the hood of an officer’s car, punched the car’s window and resisted arrest.

Assistant U.S. attorneys Caryn Finley and Kenneth Smith told jurors during closing arguments that ”this is a simple case.” Morrow and Stanley went to an area they knew was federal property, did not follow the rules, failed to comply when officers asked them to move and disrupted ICE officers from being able to carry out orders from the Trump administration.

“You can protest,” Finley told jurors in her closing argument. “You can’t keep a federal officer from doing their job.”

Finley at one point compared Morrow and Stanley to children who threw temper tantrums when their parents said they couldn’t have cookies. In the analogy, ICE officers were their parents.

One of Morrow’s attorneys, Xavier de Janon rebutted in his closing argument: If they were children, then they were children playing on a public driveway when their parents showed up, cursed at them, threatened them with pepper spray, tackled them and then made false statements about what happened.

Jim Cooney, one of Stanley’s attorneys, also argued that the signs identifying the area as federal property were not visible from where the protesters were and reminded jurors that the protesters did not go past the “no trespassing” signs they could see. Officers also gave inadequate warnings, Cooney argued, and did not specifically tell Morrow and Stanley that they were on federal property.

When Officer Jason Rajabi first arrived, video shows, he told protesters through his car’s speakers that they were “hindering my duties” and would be arrested if they did not move.

Defense attorneys argued that the protesters did move, and video shows the same. Video also shows Stanley ran back in front of Rajabi’s car and put his hands on the hood.

Rajabi told FBI agents that Stanley punched his window, too, but video did not show that. Footage does show a detail Rajabi did not offer to FBI agents investigating the case:

When he got out of the car to arrest Stanley, Rajabi did not tell him he was under arrest, video shows. He said “come here motherf—er,” and then grabbed Stanley from behind and picked him up. While testifying, Rajabi said it was reasonable for Stanley to try to protect himself — perhaps by initially resisting — if someone he didn’t know came up from behind, cursed at him and grabbed him.

During opening arguments, attorneys Rob Heroy (representing Morrow) and Claire Rauscher (representing Stanley) repeated the officer’s explicit phrase to jurors. Eventually, U.S. District Judge Matthew Orso put a “motherf—er” moratorium over the trial. During closing arguments, attorneys on all sides simply said “m” and “f.”

Finley acknowledged that “we may not like” their word choice, but at the end of the day, officers were doing their jobs and trying to protect their property.

Outside the courtroom, Rauscher told The Charlotte Observer she was “really happy our client was acquitted.” Stanley, accompanied by his mother and father, declined to comment.

Morrow’s mother told the Observer she was “shocked” by the jury’s decision. She cried as the courtroom deputy read out that her daughter had been convicted on all counts. Her son and protesters from Indivisible Lake Norman, who were at the trial or outside the courthouse every day this week, comforted her.

Barbara Morrow said she was glad her daughter had so much support from the community. Outside the courthouse, de Janon echoed the same to reporters and said they plan to appeal the jury’s verdict.

In a statement after the verdict came in, de Janon said: “Over several months, we witnessed … how the federal government loses evidence [and] covers up lies from ICE. We know, and saw firsthand, that these prosecutions are designed to enable fascism and the police state: another protest against ICE has been criminalized, another set of people standing up for immigrants will be punished.”

Lease details, lost video kept from jury

Judge Orso rejected arguments from defense attorneys that the lease between the federal government and the owners of the office building did not extend to the parking lot entrance. Attorneys unsuccessfully argued the government only had jurisdiction power over a specific square-footage and some parking lots.

Jurors also were not privy to the fact the ICE officers failed to follow FBI orders to preserve building surveillance video that may have more fully captured parts of the protest — a detail that came out during a lengthy interview of the special agent in charge of the case before trial.

Orso, recently appointed by President Donald Trump, also shot down Morrow’s attorneys’ argument that the case should be dismissed because Morrow, specifically, was protected by the First Amendment. It was not her words that were on trial, Orso said; it was her actions.

title: A judge blocks Trump's new bid to curb birthright citizenship, citing Supreme Court precedent
description:
“The Supreme Court has spoken: Children in the certified class are ‘citizens at birth,’” Boardman, appointed by President Joe Biden, wrote in Wednesday's ruling.
Birthright citizenship is guaranteed under current law for anyone who is born on U.S. soil, with a few exceptions.
The law stretches back to 1868, when the 14th Amendment was ratified in the aftermath of the Civil War.
But Trump has long wanted to end birthright citizenship, issuing a previous executive order declaring that children born to people who are in the United States illegally or temporarily are not American citizens.

text:
A federal judge has blocked President Donald Trump's latest attempt to limit birthright citizenship, granting a preliminary injunction against an executive order that the administration said would target “birth tourism.”

U.S. District Judge Deborah L. Boardman in Maryland on Wednesday issued the injunction until a class-action lawsuit brought by immigrant families and advocacy groups is resolved.

“The Supreme Court has spoken: Children in the certified class are ‘citizens at birth,’” Boardman, appointed by President Joe Biden, wrote in Wednesday's ruling.

Birthright citizenship is guaranteed under current law for anyone who is born on U.S. soil, with a few exceptions. The law stretches back to 1868, when the 14th Amendment was ratified in the aftermath of the Civil War.

But Trump has long wanted to end birthright citizenship, issuing a previous executive order declaring that children born to people who are in the United States illegally or temporarily are not American citizens. The Supreme Court struck down that attempt in June.

In August, the president tried again with a narrowed executive order that appeared to restrict automatic citizenship for specific categories of people, including children born to adults with connections to foreign embassies or organizations or to anyone considered an “alien enemy” of the United States.

The order defined birth tourism as someone who enters the United States on a “nonimmigrant visa for the purpose of giving birth on American soil.” Birth tourism is already considered fraud and grounds to restrict a visa if someone seeks one specifically to obtain U.S. citizenship for a child.

The order sought to deny citizenship to children born to adults who “engaged in a commercial transaction to purchase or access birthright citizenship,” and some families said they feared their children could be denied citizenship simply because they purchased airfare to come to the U.S. and got pregnant after they arrived.

Families and organizations who sued over the birthright citizenship restrictions told the court that the executive branch has taken a broad view of who qualifies as an alien enemy, sometimes relying on speculation or misinformation to make that determination.

Others said they feared their children would be denied citizenship because a member of the parents' extended family was connected to a gang in their home country, even though the parents were not gang members.

Uncertainty surrounding the order left them with confusion and fear, the families said.

They were joined in the lawsuit by We Are CASA, the Asylum Seeker Advocacy Project and the Institute for Constitutional Advocacy and Protection.

The administration's attorneys argued that the request to block the order was premature and said the federal agencies tasked with enforcing it would use “appropriate measures” to do so, relying on official guidance that hasn't been issued yet.

The judge rejected that argument.

“No matter what the guidance says, the 2026 Executive Order commands agencies to deny citizenship documents to several broad categories of children,” Boardman wrote.

“The White House must recognize it will not succeed in stripping children of their right to citizenship, evading binding court decisions or placing the president’s anti-immigrant agenda above the Constitution,” Shana Khader, legal director at We Are CASA, said in a prepared statement.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

___ Associated Press reporter Valerie Gonzalez contributed.

text:

title: UPDATE: ICE sightings reported across Columbus, Seymour; two businesses temporarily close
description:
Social media reports of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents popped up on Columbus area Facebook groups Wednesday afternoon.
The Columbus Human Rights Commission posted that multilingual “Know Your Rights” cards and “I Speak” cards are available in their office free of charge following the reports of ICE activity.
Lt. Skylar Berry, a Columbus Police spokesperson, did not know more about ICE being in the city.
The Bartholomew County Sheriff’s Office was not officially made aware of any ICE activity in the county, and they did not request its assistance, said Lt. Dane Duke, a sheriff’s office spokesperson.
ICE activity has also been taking place in the Indianapolis area.
text:
UPDATE: 6:36 p.m. Sept. 2

The city of Columbus released the following statement following reports of ICE activity in the city:

“We are aware of the recent reports of Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity at a local restaurant earlier today. Neither the city administration nor the Columbus Police Department received any advance notice about this operation, and we were not aware it was happening. Because federal agencies like ICE operate independently, they are not required to notify local municipalities or law enforcement within their jurisdictions.

“At this moment, we still do not know if anyone was taken into custody or how long these operations might continue in our area. We want to reassure the community that, in line with our local policies, the Columbus Police Department does not participate in federal immigration enforcement sweeps and have not entered into any agreement with federal law-enforcement to participate in such action. We are committed to keeping everyone informed and safe, and we will share verified updates as soon as we have more information.”

ORIGINAL STORY

Reports of federal immigration enforcement activity in Columbus and Seymour on Wednesday prompted at least two Columbus restaurants to temporarily close and fueled concern among some residents.

Social media reports of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents popped up on Columbus area Facebook groups Wednesday afternoon. One video showed what appeared to be ICE agents outside Camila’s Mexican Restaurant on 25th Street, reportedly around 12:45 p.m. Wednesday. One agent can be seen on video wearing a tactical vest with ERO emblazoned on it, with ERO referring to ICE’s Enforcement and Removal Operations directorate. Another video showed the agency performing a traffic stop on a vehicle on what appeared to be State Road 46 near Interstate 65.

While The Republic could not independently verify the video, the tactical vest worn by an individual in the footage appeared consistent with vests marked “ERO,” an acronym used by ICE’s ERO directorate in publicly available photographs.

After the Camila’s video was posted on social media, the restaurant suddenly closed. When The Republic called the restaurant, an unnamed employee said some of the employees were scared about ICE being outside the restaurant. These employees talked to the owner, saying that they wanted to be safe and not at risk.

The employee said that Camila’s plans to reopen tomorrow should employees show up. Camila’s also posted on Facebook at 3:15 p.m. that every employee is safe and that they will be back in business Thursday.

Less than an hour later, TaColumbus announced on Facebook that they would be closed for the rest of the day due to “unforeseen circumstances.” An employee told The Republic by phone the restaurant closed “because of what’s happening with ICE” and that they want to protect their Hispanic customers, especially since they are Hispanic themselves.

The employee said that he and his wife have been giving people rides and picking up groceries from the store for people so that they don’t have to be seen outside. He said he does not know if TaColumbus will reopen Thursday, but they just want to help out the community.

The Columbus Human Rights Commission posted that multilingual “Know Your Rights” cards and “I Speak” cards are available in their office free of charge following the reports of ICE activity.

Lt. Skylar Berry, a Columbus Police spokesperson, did not know more about ICE being in the city. CPD is not involved in the operation to the best of his knowledge, he said.

The Bartholomew County Sheriff’s Office was not officially made aware of any ICE activity in the county, and they did not request its assistance, said Lt. Dane Duke, a sheriff’s office spokesperson.

Stuart Mora, executive director of the Indiana Organizing Project, which has campaigned to end ICE detention at Miami Correctional Facility in northern Indiana, told The Republic he couldn’t independently verify any ICE sightings, but did hear reports of ICE being active in the Seymour area for the past three days.

Reports in the Seymour area on social media include a reported detainment at an Aisin plant. A GoFundMe was set up by a Seymour woman for a family member who was reportedly detained by ICE early Tuesday morning, which was later shared on Facebook. The Republic and our sister newspaper, The Tribune, have not been able to independently confirm this.

Seymour Police Chief Greg O’Brien said he heard about ICE being in the city on Monday, but the department was not notified and is not involved in any operations. The Jackson County Sheriff’s Department did not immediately respond to an inquiry.

When The Republic contacted ICE about the reports of activity, asking whether the agency was conducting operations in the Bartholomew and Jackson County areas, a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson did not answer the question directly. The spokesperson said that “ICE agents uphold our nation’s immigration laws in all 50 states, seven days a week, 24 hours a day,” before sending photos and names of a selection of what the spokesperson said were “some of the worst of the worst arrested by ICE in Indiana.” The five people, who hailed from Mexico, Niger, Haiti and Honduras, were reportedly convicted of charges like kidnapping, identity theft, rape, child neglect and aggravated assault.

ICE activity has also been taking place in the Indianapolis area. Volunteer watchdog organizations like Indy Rapid Response have reported a surge in sightings of ICE agents and people being detained around the city since Aug. 31, the Indianapolis Star reported.

This story may be updated.
